cards.title: Powell scraps the Fed's post-2020 inflation playbook in his final Jackson Hole speech
cards.what_happened: Federal Reserve Chair **Jerome Powell** used his keynote address at the Jackson Hole economic symposium to release the Fed's revised long-run policy framework, confirming the central bank is **abandoning flexible average inflation targeting** and reverting to its older, more conventional approach of anchoring inflation expectations tightly around a 2% target. Powell said the labor market remains near maximum employment but that officials are increasingly attentive to signs of a slowdown in hiring. He reiterated language from a day earlier that the 'baseline outlook and shifting balance of risks may warrant adjusting' the Fed's policy stance — code for an imminent rate cut — while acknowledging tariff-driven inflation pressures are 'clearly visible'. The framework announcement adds a structural, longer-lasting element to what markets had already been treating as a near-certain September rate cut after Thursday's remarks sent the Dow up **800 points** and gold to **$3,419 an ounce**.
key_points: Powell formally **abandoned** the Fed's 2020-era 'flexible average inflation targeting' framework in his last Jackson Hole address as chair.
The Fed reverts to a **conventional flexible inflation-targeting** approach, anchoring policy back to a plain 2% inflation goal.
Powell flagged a **weakening labor market** as a growing worry, even as he said inflation risks stay 'tilted to the upside'.
The speech built on yesterday's rate-cut signal, which had already pushed odds of a **September cut above 91%**.
This is widely read as **Powell's legacy-setting moment** before his term as chair ends.

thread.previously: Yesterday Powell's Jackson Hole remarks were read as an unusually strong hint of a September rate cut, sending the Dow up 800 points, gold to $3,419/oz, and pushing rate-cut odds from about 70% to over 91% in a single day.
thread.changed: Today's fuller readout of the speech shows Powell went beyond the rate-cut signal: he formally released the Fed's revised long-run framework, abandoning the 2020-era 'flexible average inflation targeting' regime and reverting to conventional inflation targeting, while flagging labor-market weakness as a growing concern.

depth.background: The Fed adopted 'flexible average inflation targeting' (FAIT) in 2020, a framework that let inflation run above 2% for a while to make up for earlier undershoots — a response to a decade of too-low inflation before the pandemic. That framework was blamed by critics for making the Fed slow to react when inflation actually surged in 2021-22. Every five years the Fed reviews its long-run strategy, and this Jackson Hole symposium — an annual gathering of central bankers in Wyoming — was Powell's venue to unveil the results, in what commentators are calling his **'swan song' speech** as his chairmanship nears its end.

cards.title: Blackstone pitches a $36 billion loan to keep Anthropic's AI chips running
cards.what_happened: **Blackstone**, the world's largest alternative-asset manager, has begun sounding out investors about arranging a roughly **$36 billion debt package** to help Anthropic pay for the Google-made AI chips (TPUs) it depends on to run its models. Banks are reportedly already lining up investor meetings for the financing. This would mark Anthropic's **second large debt financing tied specifically to chip consumption**, following a similar structure used earlier this year. The debt talks are happening in parallel with Anthropic's push toward an **IPO it is targeting for as early as October 2026**, with bankers pricing the company's potential market value as high as **$2 trillion** on its first day of trading. Anthropic's losses ballooned to nearly **$42 billion in 2025**, underscoring just how much cash the company burns to stay competitive with rivals like OpenAI.
key_points: Blackstone is in early talks to arrange roughly **$36 billion** in debt for Anthropic's AI computing buildout.
The money would fund the **Google chips** (TPUs) Anthropic rents to train and run its Claude models.
It would be Anthropic's **second major debt deal** this year, on top of billions already raised in equity.
The news lands as Anthropic preps a blockbuster **IPO as early as October**, at a valuation investors are pricing near **$2 trillion**.
Anthropic's 2025 net losses hit nearly **$42 billion** — a five-fold jump from 2024 — showing how costly the AI arms race has become.

depth.background: Training and running large AI models like Anthropic's Claude requires enormous amounts of specialized computing power — mostly rented from cloud providers like Google and Amazon rather than owned outright. That rented compute is expensive enough that AI labs increasingly borrow money (debt) to pay for it, instead of only relying on investors buying equity (ownership stakes). Anthropic has already raised **tens of billions** from investors, including a $65 billion round earlier this year, but its cash burn has kept pace with its growth. Wall Street banks — Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan — are also working on Anthropic's IPO in parallel, meaning the company is trying to lock in both debt and public-market capital at the same time.

cards.title: Bessent to unveil 'the toughest sanctions in history' on Iran this Monday
cards.what_happened: Bessent announced Thursday that the Treasury Department will hold a press conference **this coming Monday** to detail a new round of sanctions he describes as among the **toughest ever imposed on any nation**. He told reporters the goal is 'the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world,' explicitly saying both US allies and rivals — including **China** — will be forced to choose whether to keep doing business with Iran or with the US-led coalition. Separately, the **State Department** has already sanctioned six entities and one individual it accuses of helping Iran move illicit funds using cryptocurrency, moving ahead of Monday's bigger announcement. Bessent argues the cumulative effect of these measures should cause Iran's economy to **'collapse.'**
key_points: Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** says Monday's sanctions package will be among the **toughest ever imposed** on any country.
He's calling it **'the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world'** and says allies and adversaries alike will have to pick a side.
The State Department has already sanctioned **six entities and one individual** accused of moving Iranian funds through crypto.
Bessent claims the new measures are designed to make Iran's economy **'collapse.'**
It comes as ship traffic through the **Strait of Hormuz** has fallen to roughly **8 vessels a day**, down from about 130 before the war began.

depth.background: The US and Iran have been in an escalating standoff since a US-Israel military campaign against Iran began in **February 2026**, after which Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow waterway through which a huge share of the world's oil and gas passes — 'closed' and began attacking ships and laying mines. Washington has already leaned heavily on sanctions (financial penalties that cut a country off from global trade and banking) to pressure Iran, and Trump has separately claimed the US now has **'total control'** of the strait. Treasury Secretary Bessent is the official in charge of designing and enforcing US economic sanctions.

cards.title: Trade talks with Canada collapse — Trump slaps 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods
cards.what_happened: Trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed late Friday night, and the 50% tariffs on Canadian goods that had been threatened — then paused — went into effect at midnight. The duties apply under **Section 338** of the Tariff Act of 1930 and cover about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian exports, including hockey sticks, building materials, liquor, and certain clothing categories. Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'important progress' had been made in the talks but that it 'has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians,' and pledged Canada would match the US tariffs dollar for dollar. Because Section 338 has never been used before, legal experts expect Canada or affected US importers to challenge it in court almost immediately.
key_points: Talks broke down late Friday night, triggering **50% tariffs** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian goods at the stroke of midnight
Trump invoked **Section 338** of the 1930 Tariff Act — a presidential power that has **never been used before**
The duties hit everyday goods: **hockey sticks, building materials, liquor, and clothing**
Canadian PM **Mark Carney** vowed to **'match those tariffs dollar for dollar'**
The move is expected to be **challenged in court almost immediately**

depth.background: Trump has spent 2026 waging an on-again, off-again tariff war with dozens of trading partners, using emergency economic powers to impose duties without Congress. In **February 2026**, the **Supreme Court struck down** his use of the **IEEPA** (a law meant for genuine national emergencies) to impose country-specific tariffs, ruling it unconstitutional — forcing the White House to hunt for other legal tools. Section 338 is one of those tools: a Depression-era clause that lets a president slap duties of up to 50% on any country found to 'discriminate' against US commerce, and it had literally never been invoked until now. Trump had already paused a threatened 50% Canada tariff once, on **August 18**, after Carney announced what looked like a breakthrough — but that truce didn't hold.

prev_ref.title: China rejects Trump's demand to join the 'economic D-Day' campaign against Iran

cards.title: Trump doubles down on 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz as Iran warns of a 'devastating' response to new sanctions
cards.what_happened: Trump repeated and expanded his claim that the US has **'total control'** over the Strait of Hormuz, saying **'I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!'** and suggesting the US could formally claim the waterway as its own territory once the war against Iran is 'finished.' He described the ongoing US naval blockade as a **'wall of steel'** that Iran cannot counter. In response, officials on Iran's side, including its paramilitary Revolutionary Guard Corps, warned of a **'devastating'** response if the US presses ahead with the sanctions campaign due to be formally announced **Monday** — the plan Bessent has called the most extensive coordinated sanctions effort ever attempted against a single country. China has already declined to take part.
key_points: Trump says the US has **'total control'** of the Strait of Hormuz and floated **declaring it US territory**
The formal rollout of Bessent's **'toughest sanctions in history'** against Iran is due **Monday**
Iran's side warned of a **'devastating' response** if the new sanctions go ahead
The US-Iran war, which began **February 28, 2026**, has already produced **56 reported vessel-damage incidents** in the strait
China has already refused to join the sanctions push, calling it counter-productive

thread.previously: China's foreign ministry publicly refused to join the new US sanctions campaign against Iran, calling pressure tactics 'not the solution' and urging a diplomatic resolution instead — a rebuff that came the same day Iran's foreign ministry warned any official enforcing the new US sanctions could face prosecution.
thread.changed: With the formal sanctions rollout due Monday, Trump escalated further — declaring the US has 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz and floating the idea of declaring it US territory — while Iran's side warned of a 'devastating' response if Washington follows through.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil** passes through — meaning any disruption there ripples straight into gas prices everywhere. Since a US-Iran war broke out on **February 28, 2026**, Washington has run a naval blockade of Iranian ports and carried out repeated strikes, while pairing the military pressure with an escalating economic campaign Trump has branded **'economic D-Day.'** Treasury Secretary Bessent has said the goal is to **'collapse this regime'** by cutting off Iran's oil and banking channels, with China — the biggest buyer of discounted Iranian crude — seen as the campaign's real test.

cards.title: Yemen edges toward all-out war as Houthi attacks trigger the bloodiest clashes since the 2022 truce
cards.what_happened: On August 6, Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone strikes on Yemeni government military camps in Hadramout and Marib provinces, killing at least **30 soldiers** and wounding 15 more — one of the deadliest single attacks since the 2022 truce. A military source told AFP the toll may have reached **58 dead**; the Houthis claim to have killed or wounded 'hundreds,' though that figure is unverified. Fighting has since spread across multiple fronts — Taiz, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, al-Dhale and Lahj — with the government reporting it carried out more than **100 military operations** against Houthi positions in a single 24-hour stretch, using drones, artillery and rocket launchers. On Friday, UN special envoy **Hans Grundberg** told the UN Security Council that Yemen faces its highest risk of returning to full-scale civil war since the 2022 truce took hold. The truce itself was never formally renewed after it lapsed in October 2022, but had mostly held on the ground until this month's escalation.
key_points: Houthi forces launched their biggest offensive since the 2022 truce, killing at least **30 government soldiers** and wounding dozens in strikes on Hadramout and Marib on **August 6**.
Government sources say the real toll from that first wave may have reached **58 dead**; the Houthis claim they killed or wounded 'hundreds,' unverified.
Fighting has since spread to **Taiz, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, al-Dhale and Lahj**, with Yemeni forces claiming **100+ retaliatory strikes in a single 24-hour period**.
UN special envoy **Hans Grundberg** told the Security Council Yemen faces its **highest risk of all-out war since the 2022 truce**.
The truce that has held, imperfectly, since **April 2022** paused eight years of civil war between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognized government.

depth.background: Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthi movement, an armed group backed by **Iran**, seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north, pushing the internationally recognized government into exile in the south. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the government, and the war killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises before a **UN-brokered truce in April 2022** mostly paused the front-line fighting, even though it was never formally renewed. Since then, sporadic clashes have continued, but what's happening now is different in scale: since **August 6**, Houthi attacks have killed dozens of government soldiers in a single push, and the government has responded with over a hundred strikes of its own.

cards.title: Fed Chair Powell all but promises a September rate cut, sending stocks and gold to fresh highs
cards.what_happened: Federal Reserve Chair **Jerome Powell** delivered his keynote speech at the Jackson Hole symposium on Friday, saying the 'baseline outlook and the shifting balance of risks may warrant adjusting our policy stance' — widely read as a strong signal the Fed will cut its benchmark interest rate at its September meeting. He acknowledged inflation risks remain 'tilted to the upside' as tariff-related price pressures become 'clearly visible,' but said he was increasingly worried about a weakening job market. Markets reacted immediately: the **Dow Jones** jumped **800 points (1.9%)** to a fresh record, the **S&P 500** rose about 1.5%, and the **Nasdaq** gained 1.9%, led by gains in Nvidia, Tesla, Meta and Broadcom. Gold rose 1.1% to **$3,419 an ounce** and Bitcoin climbed 2.7%, while the dollar weakened. Interest-rate traders raised their odds of a September rate cut from about 70% in the morning to **over 91%** by the end of the day.
key_points: Powell said the economic outlook '**may warrant adjusting**' the Fed's policy stance — market-speak for a rate cut is coming.
Traders' odds of a **September rate cut** jumped from **70% to over 91%** within hours of the speech.
The **Dow rose 800 points (1.9%)** to a record close; the Nasdaq gained **1.9%**; gold rose to **$3,419/oz**.
Powell flagged **two-sided risk** — a cooling job market alongside inflation that's still '**tilted to the upside**' from tariffs.
The US dollar weakened on the news, a classic signal that traders expect **cheaper borrowing** ahead.

depth.background: The Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium is an annual gathering of the world's top central bankers in Wyoming, and the Federal Reserve Chair's speech there is one of the most closely watched events on the global economic calendar because it often previews the Fed's next move. Coming into this year's speech, investors were split on whether the Fed would cut interest rates at its **September meeting**, given a US economy showing both a cooling labor market and inflation that remains above the Fed's **2% target**, partly due to import tariffs. Interest rates are the tool the Fed uses to speed up or slow down the economy: cutting them makes borrowing cheaper, which usually boosts stocks and growth but can also fuel inflation.

cards.title: Russia says it's open to 'new ideas' on ending the Ukraine war — but only ones that fit Putin's terms
cards.what_happened: Speaking on Thursday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said Moscow is willing to hear 'new ideas' for ending the war, but stressed any proposal must align with **President Vladimir Putin's** own goals and the 'realities on the ground' — meaning battlefield gains Russia already holds. The remarks come as the Kremlin says it currently has no update on when US mediators Kushner and Witkoff, who led earlier negotiations, might return to the table. Ukraine, for its part, is still awaiting the mediators' return and has repeated it will not unilaterally pull troops from the **Donbas**, insisting any territorial discussion happen based on the current line of contact rather than Russia's maximalist claims. The statement reads publicly conciliatory but changes nothing about the substance of Russia's position.
key_points: Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister **Sergey Ryabkov** said Moscow will consider 'new ideas' to end the war, but only if they match **'realities on the ground'** — diplomatic code for Russia's own terms.
The Kremlin says it has **no new information** on a return visit by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who led earlier rounds of talks.
The two core sticking points are unchanged: Russia wants **all of the Donbas region** ceded, while Ukraine refuses to withdraw troops unilaterally.
This is the latest twist in over a year of on-again, off-again truce attempts, including short-lived ceasefires earlier in 2026 that both collapsed within weeks.

depth.background: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in **February 2022**. Since then, repeated rounds of US-brokered talks — including a push earlier this year involving envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff — have produced brief truces but no lasting peace, largely because Moscow and Kyiv want fundamentally different things from any deal. **Territory and security guarantees** remain the two issues neither side will bend on: Russia wants Ukraine to formally cede the Donbas region it has only partly captured by force, while Ukraine says it won't hand over land it still controls without a fight at the negotiating table.

cards.title: Scientists built an AI that predicts how well your body will respond to a vaccine — before you even get the shot
cards.what_happened: The study pooled blood samples from thousands of participants, including both healthy volunteers and people with weakened immune systems from conditions like **HIV, multiple myeloma, and autoimmune disease**. Researchers fed the data — antibody levels against dozens of unrelated microbes — into a deep-learning model, which found that people with higher baseline levels of antibodies to common germs like Staphylococcus aureus, RSV, and human respirovirus 3 tended to mount stronger COVID-19 vaccine responses. The team is calling these 'sentinel' antibodies, since they seem to signal overall immune readiness rather than anything specific to the vaccine itself. Roughly 5–6% of otherwise healthy people turned out to be weak responders, while some immunosuppressed participants surprised researchers with robust responses — suggesting readiness is about the immune system as a connected whole, not any one number.
key_points: Researchers analyzed **8,687 blood samples from 4,089 people** to find a pre-vaccine antibody 'fingerprint' that predicts immune response.
People with higher pre-existing antibodies to unrelated everyday bugs like **Staph aureus and RSV** — dubbed 'sentinel' antibodies — turned out to have stronger COVID-19 vaccine responses.
About **5–6% of healthy people** had unexpectedly weak vaccine responses, while some immune-suppressed patients (HIV, cancer, autoimmune disease) responded strongly — defying assumptions.
A **deep-learning model** spotted the predictive pattern across many antibody measurements at once — a signal invisible to any single test.

depth.background: Not everyone's immune system reacts the same way to the same vaccine — some people build strong, lasting protection, others barely respond, and doctors have long struggled to know which is which **before** the shot is given rather than after. Researchers set out to see whether a person's *existing* antibody profile — built up from a lifetime of ordinary infections — could hint at how 'ready' their immune system is to mount a strong response to something new, like a vaccine.

prev_ref.title: Russia's overnight barrage kills a dozen in Kyiv as its missile war on Ukraine hits its bloodiest stretch since the invasion began

cards.title: Russia hits Kyiv again before dawn, killing one and wounding a 7-year-old girl
cards.what_happened: In the early hours of Saturday, Russian missiles and drones struck central Kyiv, killing one person and wounding six others, including a 7-year-old girl who was among four people hospitalized, according to mayor Vitali Klitschko. A residential building took a direct hit, and the blast wave also damaged the compound of a nearby kindergarten. This is the fourth time in five days that Russia has struck the Ukrainian capital: Thursday's attack alone killed 16 people and injured more than 40 after Russia launched dozens of missiles and 168 drones overnight, of which Ukraine's air force says it intercepted roughly 90%. A separate strike on Saturday in central Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district killed three more people. City officials say this is now the most sustained and deadly run of attacks on Kyiv since the war began.
key_points: Russian missiles and drones hit **central Kyiv** before dawn, killing **one person** and wounding **six**, including a **7-year-old girl**.
A **residential building** was hit directly and the blast also damaged a **kindergarten compound**, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
It is the **fourth major strike on Kyiv in five days** — Thursday's barrage alone killed **16 people** and wounded more than 40.
Kyiv officials describe this run of attacks as the **bloodiest stretch of the war** for the capital since Russia's 2022 invasion began.

thread.previously: We reported that Russia's overnight barrage on Kyiv killed a dozen people, part of what officials called the bloodiest stretch of the missile war on Ukraine since the invasion began.
thread.changed: Russia struck Kyiv again before dawn today, a fourth major hit on the capital in five days. This time the toll was smaller — one dead, six wounded — but the pattern of near-daily strikes on the same city is what has officials alarmed.

depth.background: Russia has spent nearly three and a half years grinding through a war it launched by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Since mid-2025 the front lines have moved slowly, so Russia has leaned harder on long-range **missile and drone strikes** deep inside Ukraine — hitting cities far from the front, including the capital, Kyiv — to pressure the government and wear down civilian morale and infrastructure. Peace talks brokered by outside powers have repeatedly stalled without a ceasefire. This week's cluster of strikes on Kyiv is the most intense since the war's early months.

cards.title: New York overtakes Silicon Valley in raw tech headcount for the first time in 13 years
cards.what_happened: CBRE's latest annual tech-talent report finds that the New York metro area now employs 394,300 tech workers, narrowly surpassing the San Francisco Bay Area's 375,730 — the first time New York has taken the lead in the study's 13-year history. The shift reflects diverging trends over 2022–2025: the Bay Area's tech workforce fell 6% amid waves of layoffs at major tech companies, while New York's grew more than 8%. A big driver is New York's finance sector, which has been aggressively hiring tech and AI talent directly into banks and asset managers rather than pure tech firms. Even so, when CBRE weighs a broader set of 13 factors — including wages, talent concentration, rents, and the supply of new graduates — the Bay Area still ranks first overall, followed by Seattle, Toronto, New York, Austin, and Washington DC. Separately, workers with AI-specific skills across the US and Canada grew 45% year-over-year to about 751,000 by mid-2026, with both San Francisco and New York each adding more than 20,000 AI-specific jobs since mid-2025.
key_points: New York's metro area now counts **394,300 tech workers**, edging past the San Francisco Bay Area's **375,730** — the first time that's happened in **13 years** of this industry tracking.
From **2022 to 2025**, the Bay Area's tech workforce **shrank 6%** while New York's **grew more than 8%**, per real-estate firm CBRE.
The shift is driven largely by **Wall Street hiring AI and tech talent directly** into finance roles, even as pure tech companies kept cutting jobs in the Bay Area.
Despite losing the headcount lead, the Bay Area still ranks **first overall** on CBRE's broader scorecard, which also weighs wage levels, talent depth and graduate supply.

depth.background: For as long as the modern tech industry has existed, the San Francisco Bay Area — Silicon Valley plus San Francisco itself — has been synonymous with the biggest concentration of tech workers in the US. Real-estate firm **CBRE** has tracked this 'tech talent' competition across US metro areas for 13 years using a scorecard of factors like headcount, wages, and graduate pipelines. New York has long been a strong second city for tech, but has never actually had more tech workers than the Bay Area — until now.

cards.title: Russia's overnight barrage kills a dozen in Kyiv as its missile war on Ukraine hits its bloodiest stretch since the invasion began
cards.what_happened: In the early hours of **August 20**, Russian forces launched a fresh wave of ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, striking residential and other buildings and triggering fires across the capital. UN OCHA and local officials reported **at least a dozen people killed** and close to 50 injured. It came days after a separate assault killed 17 people when Ukrainian defences failed to intercept a single one of the ballistic missiles fired at the city, managing to stop only drones. Ukrainian officials say the pattern reflects a deliberate Russian strategy: Moscow appears to be probing and exploiting the exact gap in Ukraine's air defences — interceptors for ballistic missiles — that allies have been slowest to fill. July's death toll of 377 civilians was already the worst monthly total in more than four years of war, and August's attacks suggest the trend is worsening rather than easing.
key_points: Russian ballistic missiles and drones hit Kyiv overnight, killing **at least a dozen civilians** and wounding nearly 50, per UN humanitarian office OCHA.
Ukraine has effectively **run out of Patriot interceptors** — the only weapon in its arsenal that can shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.
**July was the deadliest month since April 2022**, with 377 civilians killed as Russian missile volumes surged.
Kyiv's top drone commander says Moscow plans to push toward **200 missiles per attack**, more than double earlier barrages.
President Zelenskyy says lives 'could have been saved' had allies resupplied interceptor stocks faster.

depth.background: Russia has bombarded Ukrainian cities with missiles and drones since its **2022 invasion**, but the campaign has intensified sharply through 2026 as Moscow leans harder on long-range strikes while ground fighting grinds on. Ukraine's air-defence net relies heavily on **US-made Patriot batteries** — the only system that reliably intercepts ballistic missiles — but the interceptor rounds they fire are expensive, slow to manufacture, and controlled by Washington's allocation decisions. Kyiv has spent months pleading with the US and NATO allies to speed up interceptor supplies, with mixed results, even as President Trump has periodically floated and then walked back pledges to let Ukraine build Patriot interceptors domestically.

cards.title: Google secures the right to buy a $12.2 billion stake in chipmaker Marvell as Big Tech locks up its AI supply chain
cards.what_happened: On **August 19**, Marvell disclosed that it had granted Google a stock warrant — an option to buy shares at a fixed price in the future — covering up to **58.97 million shares at $206.58 apiece**, worth about **$12.2 billion** if Google exercises the full amount. Rather than vesting on a calendar, the bulk of the warrant unlocks in direct proportion to how much Google actually spends buying chips from Marvell, meaning Google's ownership stake grows only as real business volume grows. The agreement spans a broad range of technology used alongside Google's TPUs — processors, data-storage silicon, and networking chips that move data between AI servers. Marvell's stock jumped nearly 8% on the news, and the deal could be worth roughly $120 billion in revenue for Marvell by fiscal 2033 if Google hits its purchasing targets.
key_points: Marvell gave Google a **warrant to buy up to 58.97 million shares** at $206.58 each — worth **$12.2 billion** if fully exercised.
Marvell shares **jumped nearly 8%** on the news, as it signals a top cloud provider's confidence in the chipmaker.
The stake **doesn't vest on a fixed schedule** — it unlocks only as Google hits cumulative spending milestones with Marvell (roughly 240,000 shares per **$500 million** in chip purchases).
The deal could bring Marvell **~$120 billion in revenue through fiscal 2033** if Google hits its targets.
It covers chips used with Google's custom **TPU** AI processors, plus data-storage and networking silicon.

depth.background: Google, like Amazon and Microsoft, designs its own custom AI chips — called **TPUs (Tensor Processing Units)** — to run its AI models more cheaply than relying solely on Nvidia's GPUs. But designing a chip is only half the job: it still needs a specialist manufacturing and engineering partner to actually build and integrate it, which is where **Marvell Technology**, a chipmaker known for high-speed data and networking silicon, comes in. Big Tech companies have increasingly been taking equity stakes or offering warrants to their key suppliers this year, tying supplier fortunes directly to how much AI infrastructure spending actually happens.

cards.title: Israeli settlers and troops kill two Palestinians, including a teenager, in separate West Bank shootings
cards.what_happened: On Friday, a confrontation broke out in the West Bank town of **Sa'ir** after Palestinians threw stones at a group of Israelis who had entered the area without official authorization. Israeli soldiers were dispatched to the scene; in the chaos, a security official opened fire, and a **17-year-old Palestinian, Karim Sanad Raja Shalaldeh, was killed**, with another man wounded. The teen's father said at the hospital that it was **settlers who killed his son**, not soldiers — a distinction Israeli authorities have not fully clarified. In a **separate incident** the same day elsewhere in the West Bank, Israeli forces killed another Palestinian, bringing the day's West Bank death toll to two.
key_points: A **17-year-old Palestinian**, named locally as Karim Sanad Raja Shalaldeh, was shot dead in the town of **Sa'ir**, north of Hebron, after Palestinians threw stones at Israelis present in the area.
A **second Palestinian was killed** the same day in a separate shooting involving Israeli forces elsewhere in the West Bank, according to wire reports.

The Israeli military said soldiers were sent to Sa'ir after Palestinians threw rocks at **Israeli civilians who were there without prior authorization**; some Israelis were hurt before a security official opened fire.
The teenager's father told the Associated Press at the hospital that it was **settlers, not soldiers**, who killed his son.
The killings add to a documented **rise in settler violence** across the West Bank that rights monitors and the UN have tracked through 2026.

depth.background: The **West Bank** is Palestinian territory that Israel has militarily occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 **Israeli settlers** now live there in communities most of the world considers illegal under international law, alongside about 3 million Palestinians. Settler violence against Palestinians — attacks on people, homes, and farmland — has escalated sharply since the Gaza war began in 2023, often with **little accountability** from Israeli authorities, according to human-rights groups. Sa'ir, near Hebron, sits in an area with a long history of friction between Palestinian residents and nearby settlements.

cards.title: Anthropic's investors are reportedly targeting a $2 trillion IPO in October — the largest ever
cards.what_happened: According to Bloomberg and other outlets, Anthropic's investors are pushing for the company to go public in **October 2026** at a valuation of **$2 trillion or more** — a figure that would make it the **biggest IPO in history**, eclipsing SpaceX. The company confidentially filed IPO paperwork with the SEC back in **June** and is expected to file publicly by the **end of August**. Its **annualized revenue run rate** (current monthly revenue multiplied by 12) reached **$65 billion** at the end of July, and backers expect that to climb to **$100–120 billion by the end of 2026** — more than **ten times** its level at the start of the year. **Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley** are reportedly running the offering, which could raise more than **$60 billion**. The one wrinkle: revenue growth slowed in June after **US export controls** temporarily restricted sales of Anthropic's top AI models.
key_points: Anthropic's backers are said to be targeting a **$2 trillion valuation** for an **October IPO**, which would make it the **largest public listing in history**, topping SpaceX's record.
The AI company confidentially filed its **S-1** (the core IPO disclosure document) with the US SEC in **June**, and could file publicly as soon as **end of August**.
Its annualized revenue **run rate hit $65 billion** by end of July, and backers reportedly expect **$100–120 billion by year-end** — over **10x** where it started 2026.
**Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley** are the lead underwriters ("bookrunners") on a deal that could raise upward of **$60 billion**.
Growth actually **slowed in June** after the **US Commerce Department** imposed a temporary export control on Anthropic's most advanced AI models.

depth.background: **Anthropic**, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is one of a handful of AI labs (alongside OpenAI and Google DeepMind) racing to build the most capable AI systems, and has raised money at eye-watering valuations — its last private round (Series H) reportedly valued it near **$965 billion**. Going public via an **IPO** (initial public offering — a company's first sale of shares to the general public on a stock exchange) would let ordinary investors buy into that growth, but also expose the company to public quarterly scrutiny for the first time. SpaceX currently holds the record for the largest-ever IPO benchmark investors are measuring Anthropic against.

cards.title: A magnitude-6.7 earthquake shakes Peru's southern Andes, injuring at least two
cards.what_happened: A magnitude-6.7 earthquake struck Peru's southern Andes on Thursday afternoon, according to the **US Geological Survey (USGS)**. The epicenter was 38 kilometers northwest of the city of Upahuacho in Parinacochas province, at a depth of 66.7 kilometers. At least two people were injured, and the quake damaged homes, health centers, and schools in the affected area. Shaking was felt across a wide radius, including in the Ica and Arequipa regions of southern Peru.
key_points: The quake struck at **1 p.m. local time (18:00 GMT)** on Thursday.
It was centered **38 km northwest of Upahuacho**, in the Parinacochas province of the Ayacucho region.
At least **2 people were injured** and homes, health centers, and schools were damaged.
The quake had a depth of **66.7 km** and was felt as far away as Ica and Arequipa.
Peru sits on the **Pacific 'Ring of Fire'**, making quakes like this routine but never risk-free.

depth.background: Peru lies along the Pacific 'Ring of Fire,' a horseshoe-shaped zone circling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur, because it traces the edges of tectonic plates that are constantly grinding against each other. The Ayacucho region, in Peru's southern highlands, is largely rural and mountainous, with older adobe-and-brick construction that is especially vulnerable to shaking. Peru has a history of far more destructive quakes, including a 2007 magnitude-8.0 quake near Ica that killed hundreds, which is the scale authorities watch for whenever a strong tremor hits.

cards.title: Somali pirates hijack a suspected Iranian 'shadow fleet' oil tanker off Yemen
cards.what_happened: On Thursday, six armed individuals hijacked the oil tanker SIBU 1 roughly **136 nautical miles east of Al Mukalla, Yemen**, according to UKMTO. The tanker broadcast a distress call before the attackers signaled intent to sail it toward Bosaso in Somalia. SIBU 1 flies an Eritrean flag but is believed to be part of Iran's sanctions-evading shadow fleet, having repeatedly delivered fuel to a Houthi-controlled terminal at Ras Isa. It was one of **29 vessels the US Treasury's OFAC sanctioned in December 2025** for moving hundreds of millions of dollars of Iranian petroleum. This is the second tanker hijacking in the region in just four days, and the 13th attack of the year — more than double the total for all of 2025.
key_points: The Eritrea-flagged tanker **SIBU 1** was seized by **six armed men** east of Yemen's coast.
It is the **second hijacking in four days** — the worst piracy surge off Somalia in **over a decade**.
SIBU 1 is at least the **13th vessel attacked** this year in the area, versus just **five in all of 2025**.
The US Treasury had already **sanctioned the ship in December 2025** as part of Iran's oil-smuggling 'shadow fleet'.
Attackers reportedly plan to sail it toward **Bosaso, Somalia**, a known pirate staging port.

depth.background: A 'shadow fleet' is a group of aging, often unregistered or falsely-flagged tankers that sanctioned oil exporters like Iran and Russia use to sell crude while dodging Western sanctions and insurance rules. SIBU 1 had been routinely ferrying fuel to a Yemeni port controlled by the **Houthi militia**, an Iran-backed group. Somali piracy, which was largely stamped out by international naval patrols a decade ago, has been quietly resurging in 2026 as those patrols thinned out and instability in Yemen created cover. The **UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO)** body, which tracks these waters, confirmed the distress call.

cards.title: Tens of thousands in Indiana enter a second week without power after a deadly storm
cards.what_happened: Beginning **August 11**, a powerful storm system dropped more than **11 inches of rain** on parts of Indiana over three days, causing record flooding and knocking down large numbers of trees and power lines. As of **August 21**, tens of thousands of residents are entering their **second week without electricity**, with some describing day nine as 'survival mode.' The prolonged outages have forced school closures: Gary's district, serving about **4,300 students**, shut down on **August 13**, just weeks into its school year, and remains closed through at least today, while Portage Township Schools — which had to cancel its planned August 12 opening — now doesn't expect to resume classes until **August 25**. Local officials say the delay in restoring power comes from ongoing safety hazards: downed trees across properties and infrastructure damage crews still need to clear and repair before lines can be safely re-energized. Businesses in affected areas have also been unable to reopen.
key_points: A storm dumped more than **11 inches of rain** over three days starting **August 11**, triggering record floods and toppling trees onto power lines.
Some residents are now on their **ninth straight day** without electricity, describing conditions as 'survival mode.'
Gary's school district, serving about **4,300 students**, has been closed since **August 13** and remains shut through at least today.
Portage Township Schools, forced to cancel its Aug 12 start, now aims to reopen on **August 25**.
Officials blame the drawn-out outages on ongoing **downed trees and property damage** crews still have to clear.

depth.background: Indiana sits in the US Midwest, a region increasingly hit by intense, fast-moving storms that dump extreme rainfall in short bursts — a pattern many climate scientists tie to a warmer atmosphere holding more moisture. When a storm's winds and rain bring down large numbers of trees onto power lines across a wide area at once, utility crews can't just flip a switch: they often have to clear debris and rebuild sections of the wire network street by street, which is why outages after severe storms can stretch past a week even in a wealthy country with a modern grid.

cards.title: Nevada clears Tesla, Uber and Waymo to run up to 8,000 robotaxis in Las Vegas
cards.what_happened: On **August 20**, the Nevada Transportation Authority voted unanimously to grant Tesla, Uber and Waymo permits to run commercial, paid autonomous-vehicle service across Clark County, home to Las Vegas. The permits let the three companies put up to **8,000 robotaxis** on the road combined over the next 12 months: Tesla can scale to as many as **5,000** vehicles, while Waymo and Uber were each capped at **1,000** — Uber's fleet will actually run through partnerships with Hyundai's self-driving unit Motional and Amazon-owned Zoox, rather than Uber's own cars. This is separate from, and vastly larger than, the **10-vehicle** state DMV testing permit Tesla had received just days before for supervised trials. Despite the generous cap, Tesla's own robotaxi chief engineer, Eric Early, said the company would be 'extremely happy' to reach **2,500** cars in the first year — about half of what it's now allowed. Local taxi and limousine operators pushed back at the hearing, warning regulators about market oversaturation and congestion in Las Vegas's already-busy tourist corridor.
key_points: Nevada's Transportation Authority unanimously approved permits for **Tesla, Uber and Waymo** to run paid robotaxi service in Clark County (Las Vegas).
Combined, the three companies can deploy up to **8,000 driverless taxis** over the next 12 months.
Tesla's ceiling is **5,000 vehicles**; Waymo and Uber (via Motional and Zoox) were each capped at **1,000**.
Tesla's own robotaxi chief engineer admits the company will likely field only **~2,500** cars in year one — far under its cap.
Local taxi operators objected at the hearing, warning of **oversaturated, gridlocked roads** on the Las Vegas Strip.

depth.background: Nevada has spent years positioning itself as one of the most permissive US states for autonomous-vehicle testing. Just days earlier, Tesla received a separate, much smaller Nevada DMV permit — capped at only **10 vehicles** — for supervised testing; a Transportation Authority permit like this one is the much bigger, separate approval a company needs before it can legally *charge the public* for driverless rides. Waymo already runs commercial robotaxis in cities like Phoenix and San Francisco, while Tesla has spent years promising a 'Cybercab' robotaxi business that investors are still waiting to see at real scale. Las Vegas — dense, tourist-heavy, and open around the clock — is now set to become one of the most closely watched live tests of competing self-driving bets.

cards.title: China rejects Trump's demand to join the 'economic D-Day' campaign against Iran
cards.what_happened: China's foreign ministry publicly rejected Washington's request to join or support the new sanctions campaign. Spokesman Lin Jian said **sanctions and pressure tactics 'are not the solution'** to the underlying dispute, and that 'military force and pressure tactics will only lead to escalation that serves no one's interests.' Beijing instead called for a political and diplomatic resolution between Iran and the US. The rebuff came the same day Iran's foreign ministry warned that any official who orders or carries out the new US sanctions could face prosecution — a largely symbolic but pointed signal of defiance. Bessent had directly named China days earlier as the key holdout whose cooperation the sanctions campaign needs to actually bite.
key_points: China's foreign ministry spokesman **Lin Jian** said sanctions and pressure tactics are 'not the solution' to the Iran standoff.
Beijing called instead for a **'political and diplomatic approach'** and dialogue between Tehran and Washington.
Treasury Secretary **Scott Bessent** had urged China — Iran's biggest oil customer — to 'get with the program' on sanctions.
Analysts note the **US has little real leverage** over Beijing, which buys the bulk of Iran's sanctioned oil exports.
Iran's own foreign ministry separately warned that officials who **order or enforce the new US levies are liable to prosecution**.

thread.previously: We reported that the US had branded Hezbollah an Iranian proxy and imposed sanctions on it as the first concrete step in Trump's 'economic D-Day' campaign against Iran.
thread.changed: China — Iran's largest oil customer — has now publicly refused to join the campaign, calling sanctions 'not the solution,' exposing the biggest gap in Washington's isolation strategy.

depth.background: On Wednesday, President Trump declared what he called an 'economic D-Day' against Iran — a sweeping sanctions push meant to cut off the country's remaining trade lifelines after the two nations' recent military confrontation. The campaign leans heavily on pressuring third countries, especially **China**, which has continued buying discounted Iranian crude oil despite years of US sanctions, keeping Iran's economy afloat. Treasury Secretary Bessent has been the public face of the push, calling it potentially 'the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world.' China has historically shrugged off US secondary sanctions threats tied to Iran, treating its energy relationship with Tehran as a matter of sovereign trade policy.

cards.title: Nvidia strikes a $7 billion deal for AI coding startup Poolside — without buying it
cards.what_happened: Nvidia agreed to pay Poolside **$6 billion** for a non-exclusive license to its 'Model Factory' platform, which generates AI models tailored for software development. Alongside the licensing fee, Nvidia is investing **$1 billion in equity** directly into Poolside, valuing the startup at **$12 billion** before the new money. As part of the arrangement, **109 of Poolside's roughly-similar-sized staff** received job offers to move to Nvidia, though Poolside's founders will remain and keep running the company independently. The deal was first reported by tech-industry outlets citing a letter Poolside sent to its investors. Poolside can still license its technology to other buyers since the Nvidia deal is non-exclusive, unlike a typical acquisition that would lock the technology to one buyer.
key_points: Nvidia is paying **$6 billion** to non-exclusively license Poolside's AI model-building technology, its 'Model Factory'.
Nvidia is also investing **$1 billion** directly into Poolside at a **$12 billion** pre-money valuation.
**109 Poolside employees** received job offers to join Nvidia as part of the arrangement.
Poolside's founders explicitly said **'this is not an acquisition and it is not an acquihire'** — the startup keeps operating independently.
The license is **non-exclusive**, so Poolside can still sell its AI coding models to other companies too.

depth.background: Poolside is an AI startup that builds large language models specialized in writing, debugging, and optimizing software code — essentially AI co-pilots for programmers. Nvidia, the dominant maker of the chips that train and run AI models, has increasingly used its cash pile to strike deals that secure access to cutting-edge AI software and talent without the regulatory scrutiny a full acquisition would trigger. This 'license-plus-investment' structure has become a favored workaround in the AI industry — Google's move with Windsurf and other similar deals set the template — letting a giant like Nvidia effectively absorb a startup's technology and staff while the startup remains a separate legal entity.

cards.title: NASA's Swift telescope is doomed to a fiery crash after its $30 million rescue mission fails
cards.what_happened: NASA and **Katalyst Space Technologies** announced the rescue mission for Swift has been called off, more than a month after Katalyst's **Link** spacecraft launched to attempt the save. Katalyst said Link would not attempt to capture Swift and lift it to a safer orbit because the rescue spacecraft itself went into an **uncontrollable spin** a few weeks after its early-July liftoff, making it impossible to safely dock. NASA had paid **$30 million** for the attempt, hoping to extend the life of a telescope that has already outlasted its planned mission by two decades. **Intense solar activity** this year caused Swift's orbit to decay faster than predicted, and it now sits at just **345 km altitude** — dangerously low. With the rescue abandoned, Swift is expected to **reenter Earth's atmosphere and burn up no earlier than October**.
key_points: NASA and startup **Katalyst Space Technologies** called off their mission to save the **Swift Observatory**, a 22-year-old space telescope.
The rescue spacecraft, called **Link**, went into an **uncontrollable spin** a few weeks after launching in early July.
Swift is now expected to **reenter Earth's atmosphere no earlier than October**, burning up in the process.
NASA had paid Katalyst **$30 million** to boost Swift into a higher, safer orbit.
**Intense solar activity** dragged Swift down faster than expected — it now orbits at just **345 km altitude**.

depth.background: The **Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory** launched in **2004** and has spent over two decades detecting **gamma-ray bursts** — the most powerful explosions in the universe, often signaling a dying star's collapse into a black hole. Ageing satellites naturally lose altitude over time as they brush against the thin upper atmosphere, and the Sun's activity (which expands the atmosphere when strong) speeds that decay up. Rather than let a scientifically productive telescope simply burn up, NASA turned to a newer approach: paying a private company to fly out and physically boost it into a longer-lasting orbit.

cards.title: Charter plane crashes at a remote US military radar site in Alaska, killing all 8 aboard
cards.what_happened: A Cessna 441 charter aircraft departed Anchorage on Thursday bound for the Cape Newenham radar site and crashed just before reaching its destination, around 12:15 p.m. local time. All eight people aboard — two pilots and six passengers — were killed, according to the US military, which oversees the radar site. The charter, operated by Security Aviation, had been booked by the US Army Corps of Engineers, and two of the passengers killed were USACE employees traveling to the site for work. The crash site sits roughly 450 miles west of Anchorage, in one of the most remote parts of the state, complicating recovery and investigation efforts. No cause has been confirmed publicly as of Friday.
key_points: A charter Cessna 441 crashed near **Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site**, about **450 miles west of Anchorage**, killing all 8 people aboard.
The flight, chartered by the **US Army Corps of Engineers**, had two pilots and six passengers, including two USACE employees.
It crashed around **12:15 p.m. Thursday**, local time, shortly before reaching its destination, operated by charter company Security Aviation.
Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that **tracks aircraft in Alaska's airspace and along its borders** — relevant to US homeland air defense.
The cause of the crash has **not yet been determined**; investigators are examining the wreckage in a remote, hard-to-reach location.

depth.background: Alaska's vast, sparsely populated interior is served by small charter aircraft for tasks ordinary infrastructure can't reach — ferrying engineers, contractors, and supplies to remote military and civilian sites. Cape Newenham is one of a chain of Cold War-era **Long Range Radar Sites** built to watch for aircraft approaching North America from the north and west, a role that has taken on new relevance amid heightened US vigilance around North Korean and Russian military activity. Small-plane crashes are a recurring hazard in Alaska given the terrain, weather, and reliance on short backcountry runways.

cards.title: British Columbia's Bald Range wildfire: evacuation lifted for almost all of Summerland, but 150 structures are gone
cards.what_happened: The fire ignited on August 7 and within three hours had already burned **5,000 hectares**; by August 10 it covered 15,600 hectares, and the province declared a state of emergency ordering roughly 20,000 people out of Summerland and Peachland. An 80-year-old woman died attempting to evacuate the Meadow Valley area northwest of Summerland as the fire advanced. Over the following two weeks, roughly 500 firefighting personnel battled the blaze, which peaked at **22,693 hectares** by August 20. Preliminary estimates put the damage at about **150 structures** damaged or destroyed, with around 40 of those in Summerland proper and the rest scattered outside town — officials cautioned the count doesn't yet distinguish homes from sheds and outbuildings. Evacuation orders have now been lifted for roughly 90% of Summerland's properties, letting most residents return home even as some areas remain on alert.
key_points: The **Bald Range fire** broke out on **August 7** near Summerland, BC and exploded to **5,000 hectares within three hours**.
At its peak it forced roughly **20,000 people** to evacuate Summerland (pop. 12,000) and nearby Peachland (8,000), under a declared state of emergency.
An **80-year-old woman died** while trying to evacuate the Meadow Valley area — the fire's only reported fatality.
About **150 structures were damaged or destroyed**, roughly 40 of them in Summerland itself.
By August 20, evacuation orders were lifted for almost all of Summerland as the fire's growth slowed, though it has now burned **22,693 hectares** (about 227 sq km).

depth.background: British Columbia has faced increasingly severe wildfire seasons in recent years as hotter, drier summers linked to climate change extend the fire season and make blazes harder to control. The Bald Range fire started in rugged terrain near **Summerland**, a town of about 12,000 in the Okanagan Valley wine region, and grew explosively in its first days, prompting Prime Minister **Mark Carney** to put the Canadian military on standby to help provincial firefighting crews.
