cards.title: Trump declares 'Economic D-Day' against Iran, threatening sanctions on any country that helps it
cards.what_happened: President Trump posted on Truth Social on Wednesday evening, August 19, that he was escalating economic pressure on Iran, calling it **'ECONOMIC D-DAY'** and describing it as the **'MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY.'** He said any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities provide any kind of lifeline to Iran would face 'TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences.' He specifically named the channels Iran has historically used to evade sanctions — **oil smuggling, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies** — as targets of the new measures. Trump said he had 'no choice' but to tighten the squeeze after Iran 'TRAGICALLY' let his 60-day deadline for a deal expire without an agreement. The announcement did not name specific countries or companies to be sanctioned.
key_points: Trump announced on Truth Social Wednesday evening that the US would launch its **'most crushing' economic operation ever** against a country
Any nation whose **banks, businesses, airports or government** help Iran will face 'tremendous' new US sanctions
The move specifically targets **oil smuggling, cash transfers, exchange houses and ship registries** Iran has used to dodge existing sanctions
It follows the **expiry of Trump's 60-day deadline** for a US-Iran deal, which he said Iran let pass 'tragically'
Comes as the US Navy already backs a **rerouting of Hormuz shipping** through Oman, sidelining Iran's own claimed route

thread.previously: Trump had threatened to bomb Oman if it interfered with US efforts to control Hormuz shipping, as his 60-day deadline for a US-Iran deal expired without an agreement.
thread.changed: Trump has now followed through with a concrete escalation: a threat of sweeping US sanctions on any country or company that helps Iran evade existing sanctions, which he's calling 'Economic D-Day.'

depth.background: Since mid-2026, the US and Iran have been locked in an escalating standoff after talks aimed at a nuclear and shipping-security deal broke down. Trump had set a **60-day deadline** for Iran to reach an agreement, and separately threatened to 'bomb' Oman if it interfered with US efforts to keep the **Strait of Hormuz** — the narrow waterway that a fifth of the world's oil passes through — open on US-backed terms. Shipping data already show more than **80% of Hormuz traffic** now moves via the Omani route rather than the path Iran claims to control. Iran has for years faced US sanctions on its oil exports; this new push threatens to extend the pain to any outside country or firm that helps Iran evade them.

cards.title: Trump hosts crypto executives at the White House, pushes Congress to pass the CLARITY Act
cards.what_happened: On Wednesday, August 19, Trump gathered top cryptocurrency and finance executives at the White House — including Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, and Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev — alongside SEC Chairman Paul Atkins and CFTC Chair Michael Selig. He called on Congress to pass the **Digital Asset Market Clarity Act**, saying clear rules would give the fast-growing crypto industry the legitimacy it needs. The Senate is scheduled to vote on the bill on **September 15**, but it needs **60 votes** to pass and Republicans hold only 53 seats, meaning it needs Democratic votes it hasn't yet secured. The bill has drawn pushback from members of both parties over unresolved details.
key_points: Trump hosted a **White House crypto summit** with SEC Chair **Paul Atkins** and CFTC Chair **Michael Selig**
Executives from **Coinbase, Ripple, Robinhood, Nasdaq and CME Group** attended
Trump pushed Congress to pass the **Digital Asset Market Clarity Act**, to set clear rules for crypto
A Senate vote is set for **September 15**, needing **60 votes** — Republicans hold only **53 seats**
**Bitcoin jumped** on the news as investors bet on clearer regulation ahead

depth.background: US crypto firms have long operated in a legal gray zone because it's unclear which regulator — the **Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)**, which oversees stocks and other securities, or the **Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)**, which oversees commodities and derivatives — has authority over which digital tokens. Congress has debated for over a year how to resolve this, and the Trump administration has pushed to make the US a crypto-friendly hub. The proposed **Digital Asset Market Clarity Act** would give the CFTC primary oversight of most 'digital commodities,' leaving securities-like tokens to the SEC, but the bill has stalled in the Senate amid disagreements from both parties over investor protections.

cards.title: Liberia agrees to take 1,200 deportees from the US who aren't Liberian
cards.what_happened: Liberia's government confirmed it will accept up to **1,200 deportees from the United States** who are not Liberian nationals — a mix of people from other African countries as well as North America, South America, and the Caribbean. Liberia's Information Minister, **Jerolinmek Piah**, said the first group of **20 deportees** was expected to land on **August 20, 2026**. Most of those being sent reportedly have immigration violations or other offenses on record, according to officials. The deal operates under an **Asylum Cooperative Agreement** that Liberia and the US signed in September 2025, which stayed confidential until details emerged in March 2026. It's part of a wider, largely secretive US push to route deportees who can't easily be sent home through third countries willing to take them, with roughly a dozen African nations now participating.
key_points: Liberia will accept up to **1,200 people** deported from the US who are **not Liberian citizens** — a 'third-country' deal.
The first batch of **20 deportees** was expected to arrive on **August 20, 2026**.
The arrangement runs under an **Asylum Cooperative Agreement** signed in **September 2025** and only made public in March 2026.
It's one of roughly **two dozen** such secretive US deals, about **10 of them in Africa**, raising due-process concerns.

depth.background: Normally, a country deports people back to their own nation. A **'third-country' deportation deal** is different: the US sends people it wants to remove — often from countries that won't take them back — to a different country that agrees to accept them instead. Under the Trump administration, the US has expanded this practice sharply, striking roughly **two dozen** such agreements, about **10 of them with African nations**. Liberia signed its own **Asylum Cooperative Agreement** with the US in **September 2025**, though the deal wasn't publicly disclosed until **March 2026**.

cards.title: Astronomers find a star orbiting close enough to our galaxy's black hole to measure its spin
cards.what_happened: A team using the **European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope Interferometer** discovered a faint star, designated **S301**, orbiting Sagittarius A* on a tight **8.7-year path**. At its closest approach, S301 comes within roughly **1.7 billion kilometers** of the black hole — about as far as Saturn sits from the Sun — and it reaches speeds of about **25,000 kilometers per second**, making it the fastest-moving star ever tracked in the Milky Way. That proximity is what makes it valuable: it orbits close enough for the star's path to be visibly warped by the black hole's spin through **frame-dragging**. By observing S301 through at least two complete orbits, the researchers expect to directly calculate Sagittarius A*'s spin for the first time. The findings were published in the journal *Nature* on **August 19, 2026**, by a team led by K. Abd El Dayem, and covered by NPR, The Washington Post, and other outlets the same day.
key_points: A newly found star, S301, orbits Sagittarius A* — the **supermassive black hole** at the center of our galaxy — once every **8.7 years**.
At its closest pass it comes within about **1.7 billion km** of the black hole, roughly Saturn's distance from the Sun, hitting **25,000 km/s**, a galactic speed record.
Because it orbits so close, astronomers can now measure the black hole's **spin** for the first time — never done before for a 'quiet' (non-feeding) black hole.
The discovery, using the **European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope Interferometer**, was published in *Nature* on **August 19, 2026**.
Tracking at least two full orbits (17+ years) should reveal how Sagittarius A* formed and grew over cosmic time.

depth.background: Every large galaxy, including the Milky Way, is thought to have a **supermassive black hole** at its heart — for us, that's **Sagittarius A***, an object about **4 million times the mass of the Sun** sitting 26,000 light-years away. Black holes don't just have mass and location; they also **spin**, and that spin drags the fabric of space-time around with it, an effect called **frame-dragging**. Measuring a black hole's spin is far harder than measuring its mass, because you need something orbiting close enough, and predictably enough, to detect that subtle space-time drag. Until now, nobody had found an object near Sagittarius A* precise enough to do that.

cards.title: Zimbabwe's Lake Kariba ferry disaster death toll climbs to 94, its deadliest boat sinking ever
cards.what_happened: On August 11, the Mbuya Nehanda ferry left with **at least 114 adults, 5 crew, and an unspecified number of children** aboard — far beyond its authorized capacity of 90. Passengers had already raised concerns about deteriorating weather before the boat departed. About 30 minutes into the crossing, waves began washing over the vessel, which was running on **only one functioning engine**. Survivors say their pleas to turn back or seek shelter were refused by the crew. The ferry eventually turned side-on to the waves and capsized. Recovery teams have spent more than a week pulling bodies from the lake, and the toll has climbed steadily — from 72, to 84, to 94 as of August 19 — because Lake Kariba's currents and crocodile population make recovery slow and dangerous.
key_points: The ferry **Mbuya Nehanda** capsized on **Lake Kariba** on August 11 after being overloaded well past its **90-passenger limit**.
The confirmed death toll has risen to **94** as recovery teams keep pulling bodies from the water over a week later.
At least **18 of the dead are children**, the youngest just **1 year old**; 16 victims were 10 or younger.
Survivors say passengers begged to turn back or shelter from rising waves, but were **refused**.
**Pope Leo** offered prayers for the victims as the toll passed 90, drawing global attention to the disaster.

depth.background: Lake Kariba is a vast reservoir on the Zambia-Zimbabwe border used daily by rural ferries to move people between villages that have no road access. The **Mbuya Nehanda** was operated by Zimbabwe's **Rural Infrastructure Development Agency**, a government body responsible for keeping remote communities connected. Zimbabwe has a history of poorly regulated, overcrowded ferry and bus services, and this is now the **deadliest boat disaster in the country's history**, surpassing prior tragedies on the same lake.

cards.title: China lands its first reusable orbital rocket, as Unitree becomes the first humanoid-robot stock on China's markets
cards.what_happened: On Wednesday, LandSpace's **Zhuque-3** rocket delivered a satellite to orbit and then, for the first time, guided its own first-stage booster back down to a **controlled landing on solid ground using extendable legs** — the same basic technique SpaceX uses for Falcon 9. It's the rocket's second flight; an earlier attempt at recovery had failed. On the same day, **Unitree Robotics** opened its **share subscription process** ahead of a listing on the Shanghai stock exchange, positioning it to become the **first dedicated humanoid-robot company to trade as an A-share** (a mainland Chinese stock). Industry data shows Chinese manufacturers already accounted for **more than 97% of humanoid robot shipments worldwide** in the first half of 2026.
key_points: Chinese startup **LandSpace** landed its **Zhuque-3** rocket's first stage on solid ground after launching a satellite — China's **first-ever land recovery** of an orbital-class booster.
It was the rocket's **second flight**; the first landing attempt had failed.
Separately, **Unitree Robotics** began its share sale to list on **Shanghai's stock market**, becoming China's first pure-play humanoid-robot stock.
**Chinese vendors made over 97% of global humanoid robot shipments** in the first half of 2026.
Reusable rockets are the technology that let SpaceX slash launch costs — China is now chasing that same economics.

depth.background: For nearly a decade, SpaceX's Falcon 9 has been the only rocket regularly landing and reflying its first stage, which let it cut launch costs and fly far more often than any rival. China's state and private space sector — including LandSpace — has spent years trying to replicate that trick with methane-fueled rockets. On the robotics side, China has poured state and private capital into humanoid robots as a strategic industry, with firms like Unitree becoming globally recognized for viral demo videos of robots doing backflips and martial arts.

cards.title: Attacks on aid workers hit a record high in 2025, and the UN blames the rise of cheap armed drones
cards.what_happened: The **UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs** reported that violence against aid workers hit another grim record in 2025, with **907 killed, injured, or kidnapped** worldwide. Of those, **350 died**, a slight improvement from 2024's record of **387** deaths. **UN aid chief Tom Fletcher** said the growing use of cheap, adaptable **armed drones** in conflict zones is a major driver of the rising risk. In March, drone strikes hit **Goma** in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, killing at least three people including a French aid worker, while aid convoys in **Sudan** and **Ukraine** were repeatedly hit through the year. **Gaza** was again the single deadliest location, with **186** humanitarians killed there in 2025, followed by Sudan. In **Colombia**, attacks involving weaponized drones **quadrupled** between 2024 and 2025.
key_points: **907** humanitarian workers were killed, injured, or kidnapped worldwide in 2025 — a new record
**350** aid workers were killed, slightly down from the all-time high of **387** in 2024
**Gaza** was the deadliest place for aid workers, with **186** killed there in 2025 alone
In **Colombia**, attacks using weaponized drones **quadrupled** between 2024 and 2025
The report was released on **World Humanitarian Day**, August 19

depth.background: Humanitarian workers — people from the UN, Red Cross, and NGOs who deliver food, medicine, and shelter in conflict zones — have historically relied on their neutral status to operate safely near frontlines. That protection has eroded over the past decade as more conflicts involve armed groups who don't respect humanitarian law, and now the spread of cheap, easy-to-operate armed drones is adding a new and harder-to-defend-against threat. The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) tracks these attacks every year, and 2024's total was already a record before 2025 broke it again.

cards.title: Trump pauses new 50% tariffs on Canada for three days as a trade deal nears
cards.what_happened: President Trump had set a new round of **50% tariffs** on about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian imports — including cement and hockey sticks — to take effect Wednesday, August 19. Just hours before the deadline, he announced a **three-day pause**, pushing the effective date to **August 21**, citing a phone call with Canadian Prime Minister **Mark Carney** and a pending agreement. Trump said the pause was granted **'subject to the finalization of documents'** confirming a deal between the two countries. Carney, for his part, said **'substantial progress'** had been made but cautioned that **'important work'** still needs to be done before anything is final. The reprieve is the latest in a series of last-minute delays in this dispute.
key_points: Trump paused a fresh **50% tariff** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian goods just hours before it was due to hit
The pause runs until **August 21**, giving negotiators three more days to lock in a deal
PM **Mark Carney** says 'substantial progress' has been made, but 'important work' remains
The targeted goods ranged from **cement to hockey sticks** — everyday inputs for US builders and retailers
Trump says the delay is conditional on 'finalization of documents' confirming the two sides 'have a DEAL'

depth.background: The US and Canada have been locked in an on-again, off-again **tariff standoff** for months, part of Trump's broader push to use tariffs — taxes charged on imported goods, usually paid by the importing company and often passed on to consumers — as leverage to force trading partners into new terms. Canada is the **US's largest goods trading partner**, and the two economies are deeply intertwined, from cars to lumber to energy, so new tariffs ripple quickly into US supply chains and prices. Talks between Washington and Ottawa have dragged on for weeks without a final signed agreement, even as deadlines came and went.

cards.title: Moderna and Merck's personalized mRNA cancer vaccine succeeds in a major melanoma trial, and Moderna's stock more than doubles
cards.what_happened: Moderna and Merck announced on **Wednesday** that in a late-stage (Phase 3) trial, melanoma patients who had their tumors surgically removed and then received the **personalized mRNA vaccine plus Keytruda** had a lower rate of cancer **recurrence** and lower rate of the cancer **spreading to other parts of the body**, compared with patients who got Keytruda alone. The trial met both its main goal (reducing recurrence) and a secondary goal (reducing spread) — the first time an individualized, mRNA-based cancer therapy has succeeded at this late a trial stage. The full data has not been published yet; the companies say results will be shared at an upcoming medical meeting. **Moderna's stock surged as much as 60%** in premarket trading on the news.
key_points: The vaccine, paired with Merck's **Keytruda**, cut skin-cancer recurrence in a **late-stage (Phase 3) trial**.
It is the **first-ever positive Phase 3 result** for an mRNA-based cancer treatment.
**Moderna's shares jumped as much as 60%** in premarket trading on the news.
The treatment is **personalized** — built from each patient's own tumor — not a one-size-fits-all shot.
Full detailed results will be presented at a **future medical conference**, not released in full yet.

depth.background: Moderna is best known for its **COVID-19 mRNA vaccine**, which works by giving cells temporary instructions to build a piece of a virus so the immune system learns to recognize it. Since 2016, Moderna has partnered with pharmaceutical giant **Merck** to apply that same mRNA technology to cancer, not infectious disease — using it to build a **personalized vaccine**, called intismeran, that trains a patient's immune system to recognize the specific mutations in their own tumor. It is paired with **Keytruda**, Merck's existing immunotherapy drug that helps the immune system attack cancer cells more broadly.

cards.title: NASA images reveal a 60-foot crater where a discarded SpaceX rocket stage slammed into the Moon
cards.what_happened: The rocket stage struck the Moon on **August 5, 2026**, slamming into the surface at an estimated **5,400 miles per hour**. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), a satellite that has been circling and mapping the Moon since 2009, flew over the impact site on **August 11 and 12** and photographed the aftermath — engineers had to tilt the spacecraft's cameras while it moved at **1 mile per second**, 60 miles above the surface, just to get a clean shot. NASA released the before-and-after images on **Tuesday, August 18**, showing a fresh crater roughly **60 feet wide** gouged into the lunar dust. It is the clearest confirmed picture yet of a piece of Earth-launched hardware hitting the Moon.
key_points: A defunct **Falcon 9 upper stage** hit the Moon on **August 5** at roughly **5,400 mph**.
NASA's **Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter** photographed the site on **August 11-12**, six days after the crash.
The impact carved a fresh crater about **60 feet (18 meters) wide** into the lunar surface.
Engineers had to **tilt the orbiter** mid-flight, 60 miles up, so its camera could catch the crater.
The stage began its journey in **January 2025**, launching two commercial Moon landers before being discarded.

depth.background: In January 2025, a **SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket** launched two commercial lunar landers into space. Once its job was done, the rocket's spent upper stage — the second, smaller segment that fires after the main booster falls away — was released into orbit, as is routine after most launches. Nobody aimed it at the Moon on purpose; instead, the **slow drift of orbital mechanics** — the gravitational tug-of-war between Earth, the Moon, and the Sun — gradually bent its path until it was on a certain collision course, a phenomenon astronomers had been tracking and predicting for months.

cards.title: Indiana declares a statewide disaster as historic flooding kills at least seven and FEMA moves in
cards.what_happened: Severe storms and flash flooding began hitting Indiana on **August 11** and continued for days, leaving **at least seven people dead** and forcing widespread evacuations. Governor **Mike Braun** issued a statewide disaster emergency declaration on August 13, and two days later President Trump approved a **federal emergency declaration** that lets FEMA directly support the response across **53 of Indiana's counties**. On **August 18**, Indiana's homeland security agency and FEMA personnel began **aerial preliminary damage assessments** — flying over affected areas to catalog the damage, which is the required first step before the state can request a full federal **major disaster declaration** (the designation that unlocks individual household aid, not just emergency response funding). The state has also activated its own disaster relief fund, offering **$5,000 grants** to individuals who need immediate help, and flooding has spilled over into neighboring Ohio and Kentucky.
key_points: **At least 7 people have died** in Indiana since thunderstorms began dumping record rain on August 11.
Governor Mike Braun declared a **statewide disaster emergency**, and President Trump approved a federal emergency declaration covering **53 counties**.
FEMA and state crews began **aerial damage assessments on August 18** — the first step toward a full federal disaster declaration with individual aid.
The state activated a **disaster relief fund** offering **$5,000 grants** to affected households.
Flooding also spread into **Ohio and Kentucky**, and the storms followed an unusually wet stretch across the central US this summer.

depth.background: Indiana sits in the US Midwest, a region built around farmland, small towns, and rivers that normally rise and fall gently with the seasons. Starting **August 11, 2026**, repeated rounds of thunderstorms dumped what officials are calling **historic rainfall** on the central and southern parts of the state, overwhelming rivers and drainage systems built for much smaller storms. This is part of a broader pattern climate scientists have flagged for years: a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, so when it does rain, it tends to rain harder and faster than the infrastructure below it was designed for.

cards.title: Meta's child-safety trial opens with a whistleblower now cleared to testify against the company
cards.what_happened: Opening statements began August 18 in the consolidated child-safety trial against Meta. California deputy attorney general Megan O'Neill argued Meta's core business model depends on exploiting the attention and data of young users, and that internally the company knew and hid the risks. Meta's lawyers are expected to counter that the company has built extensive parental-control and safety features and that youth mental health has many causes beyond social media. In a significant pretrial ruling, the judge denied Meta's motion to exclude **Arturo Bejar**, a former senior engineer who became a prominent whistleblower after telling the Senate in 2023 that Meta knew its platforms harmed teenagers and chose not to act. His testimony is now expected to feature prominently over the trial's six-plus weeks, alongside planned testimony from **Zuckerberg** himself and top Instagram executives.
key_points: The trial, in **US District Court in Northern California**, opened August 18 with attorneys general from **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** leading the case on behalf of **29 states** total.
California deputy AG **Megan O'Neill** told the court Meta's business "relies on exploiting young people's data and attention" and that it **lied about known risks** to teen mental health.

The judge refused Meta's request to bar former senior engineer and whistleblower **Arturo Bejar** from testifying — he told the US Senate in 2023 that Meta knew about harms to teens and failed to act.
The trial is expected to run **at least six weeks**, with testimony expected from **Mark Zuckerberg**, Instagram head **Adam Mosseri**, and Meta's global safety chief **Antigone Davis**.
Meta **denies the allegations** and is expected to argue it has invested heavily in safety tools and that broader youth mental-health trends aren't its doing.

thread.previously: We reported the trial opened this week, with a coalition of US state attorneys general accusing Meta of deliberately engineering Instagram to be addictive to teenagers, in a case that could cost the company up to $1.4 trillion.
thread.changed: Opening statements were delivered on August 18: a California deputy attorney general laid out the states' core allegation that Meta's business model depends on exploiting kids' data and attention, and the judge rejected Meta's attempt to block whistleblower Arturo Bejar from testifying — a ruling that lets the trial's most damaging insider witness take the stand.

depth.background: This case is the product of years of state-level investigations into how Instagram and Facebook are designed, following 2021 leaks (the "Facebook Files") showing Meta's own internal research found Instagram worsened body-image issues for a meaningful share of teen girls. Roughly **29 US states** sued Meta separately, and this trial — with four states as the lead plaintiffs — is the first to actually reach a courtroom. The stakes are unusually high: penalties and damages sought could theoretically total **$1.4 trillion**, though such maximalist figures rarely survive intact even when plaintiffs win.

cards.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda becomes the fastest-growing on record, topping 5,000 cases
cards.what_happened: In just over three months since being declared a PHEIC, this Ebola outbreak has grown faster than any previous one on record. As of the WHO's August 18 update, confirmed cases stand at 5,021 with 2,378 deaths, concentrated in DRC's Ituri province (4,257 cases, 1,878 deaths) but now confirmed in North Kivu, South Kivu, and three other provinces. Uganda has also reported cases linked to the same outbreak. In response, five Central African countries — DRC, Uganda, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo, and South Sudan — are coordinating tighter border surveillance and information-sharing to try to stop the virus crossing into new territory.
key_points: The WHO reports **5,021 confirmed cases** and **2,378 deaths** as of August 18 — a fatality rate near **47%**
The outbreak has spread from Ituri province to **five more provinces**, including North Kivu and South Kivu
WHO declared a **Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)** on May 17; it's now the **fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record**
**Five Central African nations** are tightening cross-border surveillance to stop further spread
The strain is **Bundibugyo virus**, striking remote, hard-to-reach areas of DRC and Uganda where conflict complicates the response

depth.background: Ebola causes severe fever and internal bleeding and has repeatedly emerged from this part of Central Africa, where past outbreaks — including the 2018-2020 DRC epidemic — showed how armed conflict and mistrust of health workers can let a virus spread for months before it's contained. A **PHEIC** is the World Health Organization's highest alarm level, reserved for outbreaks serious enough to need a coordinated global response; declaring one in May was meant to fast-track funding and expert deployment. Response efforts are also being complicated by recent cuts to US health-aid programs (CDC and USAID), which have historically funded much of the region's outbreak response.

cards.title: Ukraine fires nearly 800 drones at Moscow region in one of its largest attacks of the war
cards.what_happened: Overnight, Ukraine launched close to **800 drones** toward the Moscow region in what Russian officials called the second-largest such attack since January 2025. Moscow's air defense claimed to intercept 791 of them, with the city's mayor saying 197 were shot down over Moscow Oblast specifically. Despite the intercepts, fires broke out at the **Severnoye Domodedovo warehouse complex**, and Russian state media confirmed a Wildberries facility was damaged — the second Wildberries site hit in three days after a similar wave struck the company's largest warehouse, in Koledino, on August 16. Three people were wounded in the strikes. The same day, Russia hit back with a missile strike on a village in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, killing at least 10 civilians and wounding 17, demolishing homes in the process.
key_points: Ukraine launched **almost 800 drones** at the Moscow region overnight — its **second-largest** drone attack since January 2025
Russia says it intercepted **791 of the drones**, with **197 shot down over Moscow Oblast** alone
A **Wildberries warehouse** — Russia's biggest online retailer — caught fire for the **second time in three days** as Ukraine keeps targeting Russian logistics
**Three people were wounded** near Moscow; hours earlier a Russian missile strike killed **10 civilians** in a Kharkiv-region village
Ukraine has now hit **about a dozen Wildberries sites since July 18**, part of a deliberate campaign to disrupt Russia's supply chains

depth.background: Ukraine has spent the past year building long-range attack drones capable of reaching deep into Russia, in response to Russia's own nightly missile-and-drone barrages on Ukrainian cities. Rather than only hitting military targets, Ukraine has increasingly aimed at **logistics hubs that keep Russia's civilian economy — and war effort — running**, including warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia's version of Amazon. The goal, Ukrainian officials say, is twofold: disrupt supplies the military depends on, and erode public and economic support for the war at home. This overnight attack came just two days after a similarly sized wave of roughly 600 drones hit the same region.

prev_ref.title: Iran declares a shift to 'fully offensive' policy in the Strait of Hormuz as its US ceasefire formally lapses

cards.title: Shipping data shows Iran has lost control of the Strait of Hormuz to the US-backed Omani route
cards.what_happened: Maritime intelligence firm **Kpler** found that more than 80% of vessel transits through Hormuz over the past two weeks took the UN-authorized Omani route rather than the path Iran claims to control, according to CNN Business reporting. That shift has stopped Iran from charging tolls on shipping through the strait, something it was still doing as recently as spring. Iran has attacked ships attempting the Omani route, but most vessels are now crossing anyway, trusting **US naval forces** to protect them. "It increasingly looks like Iran has at least partially lost control of the strait," said Kpler's head of crude oil analysis, Homayoun Falakshahi. Separately, Oman and Iran are holding talks to restore normal freedom of navigation through the strait on their own terms — without US involvement — a prospect reports say frustrates Trump.
key_points: More than **80% of ships** crossing the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks used the Omani route, not Iran's, per tracking firm Kpler.
Iran can no longer collect **tolls** on strait traffic, cutting off a revenue stream it relied on during the standoff.
Analysts say Iran has "**at least partially lost control**" of the world's most important oil chokepoint.
Iran has attacked ships taking the Omani route, but most now cross anyway, betting on **US naval protection**.
Oman and Iran are quietly negotiating to restore free navigation **without the US involved** — a move Trump reportedly dislikes.

thread.previously: Yesterday, Iran formally declared a 'fully offensive' policy to enforce control over the Strait of Hormuz after its ceasefire with the US lapsed, vowing to attack ships using the rival route past Oman.
thread.changed: New shipping-tracking data shows that declaration hasn't worked as intended — over 80% of tankers are now bypassing Iran's route entirely, leaving Tehran unable to collect tolls and effectively sidelined from the strait it claims to control.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow shipping lane between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** passes through every day — there is no practical way around it for tankers leaving the Gulf. The current standoff escalated after a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire deadline expired without a deal, Trump claimed the strait as effectively **US-controlled territory**, and Iran responded by declaring a "fully offensive" policy to enforce its own claim over the waterway, attacking ships that used the rival route past Oman's coast.

cards.title: The UAE cuts off all trade with Iran after accusing it of firing two missiles at its territory
cards.what_happened: The UAE's Ministry of Defence said its air defense systems detected and intercepted two ballistic missiles fired from Iranian territory on Tuesday evening, describing them as targeting maritime navigation; one fell outside UAE waters and the other landed within them. In response, the UAE's Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced an **indefinite halt** to all trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran, saying the move reflected **'escalations that undermine peace and security in the region.'** Iran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei called the accusation **'completely unfounded'** and suggested the incident was a staged **'false flag'** operation meant to damage regional trust. This is the first such strike alleged against the UAE since May, and it comes just days after Abu Dhabi accused Tehran of attacking two of its state-owned ADNOC oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
key_points: The UAE says its air defenses intercepted **two ballistic missiles** launched from Iran on Tuesday evening.
One missile fell in the sea outside UAE waters; the other landed **inside** its territorial waters.
Abu Dhabi responded by halting **all trade, commerce and financial transactions** with Iran indefinitely.
Iran **denies** launching anything, calling the claim a **'false flag'** operation.
It's the first strike alleged against the UAE since **May**, days after Abu Dhabi accused Iran of hitting two of its state oil tankers.

depth.background: The UAE and Iran sit on opposite sides of the **Strait of Hormuz**, the narrow waterway that roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through, and tensions between them have been rising for weeks as a US-brokered ceasefire between Washington and Tehran expired without a deal. Iran has already seized a UAE-owned oil tanker and a ship was struck by an unidentified projectile in the strait earlier this week, with Iran vowing to go **'fully offensive'** after the ceasefire lapsed. The UAE is one of the Gulf's biggest trading and financial hubs, so cutting off Iran commercially is a serious economic weapon, not just a symbolic gesture.

cards.title: Trump orders US troops to scale back drills with South Korea, saying Seoul wouldn't help with his Iran war
cards.what_happened: On Sunday, Trump announced in a social media post that he was ordering the Pentagon to **'substantially reduce'** joint exercises with South Korea, saying the drills are costly and send a **'totally inappropriate and hostile'** signal to North Korea, which he described as having been **'unthreatening and respectful'** during his presidency. He said the decision followed South Korea's refusal to actively join his push to denuclearize Iran, and he pointed to his rapport with North Korean leader **Kim Jong Un** as a further reason to ease up. The announcement came just as US and South Korean troops began this week's Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, designed specifically to sharpen readiness against a North Korean attack. South Korea's foreign ministry said it hoped the warmer Trump-Kim relationship could **'pave the way'** for actual talks between Washington and Pyongyang. President Lee Jae Myung, at a cabinet meeting the next day, called for South Korea to build **stronger independent defense capabilities**, while insisting the allied drills were purely defensive and not aimed at provoking the North.
key_points: Trump told Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to **'substantially reduce'** the annual joint US-South Korea military exercises.
He said South Korea had **declined to help** the US effort to denuclearize Iran.
Trump cited his **'very good' relationship with Kim Jong Un** as another reason for the pullback.
The order landed just as **Ulchi Freedom Shield**, the allies' biggest annual drill, was starting.
South Korea's President **Lee Jae Myung** responded by calling for stronger **independent** national defense.

depth.background: The US has stationed troops in South Korea since the **1950-53 Korean War** ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty, and the two countries still hold large joint military drills every year to keep their forces ready against North Korea. Those drills, including this week's Ulchi Freedom Shield, are the clearest daily proof that Washington's defense promise to Seoul is real. Trump has separately been leading a US military campaign pressuring Iran to give up its nuclear program, including threats around the **Strait of Hormuz**, and has been asking allies around the world to back that effort.

prev_ref.title: Meta goes on trial today in a case that could cost it up to $1.4 trillion over child safety

cards.title: Meta's $1.4 trillion child-safety trial opens with a bipartisan coalition of states accusing it of engineering Instagram to hook kids
cards.what_happened: Opening arguments began on August 18 in a landmark federal trial pitting Meta against a bipartisan coalition of **29 US states**, with lawyers for **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** leading the case. They allege Meta deliberately engineered Instagram and Facebook features — **infinite scroll, photo filters, and the 'like' button** — to be compulsively addictive for minors, and that it collected data from children under 13 without parental consent, violating child privacy law. Meta's defense rejects the claims, pointing to years of investment in teen safety tools like age checks and screen-time limits. The financial stakes are enormous: potential penalties have been estimated as high as **$1.4 trillion**, close to Meta's entire Nasdaq market value, though any final number would likely be far lower after negotiation or appeal. This builds on precedent — a New Mexico court already ordered Meta to pay **$567 million**, on top of an earlier $375 million fine, over similar child-safety allegations.
key_points: **29 US states** are suing Meta; opening arguments from **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** kicked off the trial in federal court.
States allege Meta built **Instagram and Facebook** to be addictive to minors using **infinite scroll, filters, and the 'like' button**, and collected data from under-13s without parental consent.
The potential penalty is estimated as high as **$1.4 trillion** — roughly equal to Meta's **entire market value** on the Nasdaq.
Meta says it has **spent years building teen protections** and denies deliberately designing addictive products.
A **New Mexico court already fined Meta $567 million** this year on top of an earlier $375 million child-safety penalty — a preview of the financial risk here.

thread.previously: We reported the trial was beginning today, outlining the up-to-$1.4-trillion stakes and the child-safety allegations against Meta.
thread.changed: Opening arguments have now actually been delivered, naming the four lead states, detailing the specific design features (infinite scroll, filters, the like button) at the center of the case, and confirming Meta's formal defense.

depth.background: For several years, whistleblower leaks and internal research (like the 2021 Facebook Papers) have alleged that Meta knew its platforms could harm teen mental health but prioritized engagement and growth anyway. That evidence fed a wave of state lawsuits, and this case — a bipartisan coalition of 29 states, with four leading the opening arguments — is the biggest test yet of whether Meta can be held financially liable for how it designed its apps. The case matters far beyond Meta: a loss could set a legal template for regulating addictive app design across the whole tech industry.

cards.title: Russia knocks out a major Ukrainian power plant in its 230th strike on the same site, part of a 147-drone night ahead of winter
cards.what_happened: On August 18, Russian forces struck one of DTEK's thermal power plants so heavily that it was forced to **completely halt electricity generation**; DTEK didn't disclose the plant's location for security reasons but confirmed **significant equipment damage**. It was the **230th attack** on DTEK's thermal plants since the war began. The strike was part of a wider night of bombardment: Ukraine's air force said Russia fired **147 drones**, of which **111 were shot down or jammed**, while a separate missile strike on **Pechenihy** in Kharkiv Oblast killed at least **10 civilians** and injured others. DTEK said no plant employees were hurt and repair crews were mobilizing immediately alongside national grid operator Ukrenergo to keep the wider system stable.
key_points: A Russian strike forced one of **DTEK's thermal power plants** to completely **halt electricity generation**, with equipment severely damaged.
It was the **230th time** DTEK's plants have been attacked since Russia's **2022 full-scale invasion** began.
Russia launched **147 drones overnight** on August 18 as part of the same barrage; Ukraine says it downed or jammed **111** of them.
A separate missile strike on **Pechenihy, Kharkiv Oblast**, killed at least **10 civilians** the same day.
**No plant staff were injured**, but DTEK says repair crews are already coordinating with grid operator **Ukrenergo**.

depth.background: **DTEK** is Ukraine's largest private energy company, running thermal power plants that keep millions of homes and businesses supplied through the country's brutal winters. Since Russia's invasion, Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's power grid in the cold months, trying to freeze the country into concessions by knocking out heat and electricity rather than only fighting on the front line. This has happened before: past winters saw rolling blackouts across Ukraine after waves of strikes on exactly this kind of infrastructure.

cards.title: Asian chip stocks crash as 30-year US Treasury yields hit a 19-year high, with Samsung and SK Hynix both losing over 7%
cards.what_happened: Asian markets sold off sharply as trading opened on Wednesday, with **Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix** — the two biggest suppliers of memory chips to AI data centers — both losing more than **7%** of their value in a single session. The **KOSPI**, South Korea's benchmark index, fell so fast that the exchange had to **briefly halt trading** after a 5% slide. The proximate trigger was the **US 30-year Treasury yield surging to 5.33%**, its highest point since 2007, driven by a mix of escalating Middle East tensions (including the Strait of Hormuz standoff) and persistent worries about US government debt and inflation. Investors also cited growing skepticism about whether the **trillions of dollars** Big Tech is pouring into AI data centers and chips will generate returns fast enough to justify current stock prices. The damage wasn't confined to Korea — **MSCI's broader Asia-Pacific index** fell around 2% as the selloff spread across the region.
key_points: The **30-year US Treasury yield** jumped to **5.33%**, its highest level since **2007** — 19 years ago.
**Samsung Electronics** fell as much as **7.17%** and **SK Hynix** tumbled **8.42%**, dragging South Korea's market down.
South Korea's stock exchange **briefly halted trading** after the KOSPI index slid **5%** in a single session.
**MSCI's Asia-Pacific equities benchmark** slid about **2%** as the rout spread beyond Korean chipmakers.
The selloff blends **rising bond yields**, **Middle East tensions**, and doubts about whether massive **AI infrastructure spending** will ever pay off.

depth.background: A **Treasury yield** is the interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for a set period — 30 years, in this case. When that yield rises, it means investors are demanding more compensation to lend long-term, often because they expect higher inflation, more government borrowing, or more risk ahead. Higher yields matter enormously for **AI and chip stocks** specifically because their sky-high valuations are built on profits investors expect years from now — and the more it costs to borrow today, the less those distant future profits are worth in today's dollars. Samsung and SK Hynix are the world's two biggest makers of the memory chips that power AI data centers, so they sit at the center of the same AI-spending boom that has driven markets for the past two years.

cards.title: Trump threatens to bomb Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, as the 60-day US-Iran deadline expires without a deal
cards.what_happened: President Trump said in a Fox News interview with Trey Yingst that the US would **'bomb the [expletive] out of'** Oman if it 'gets in the way' of American efforts to reopen and control shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. His comments came as the **60-day memorandum of understanding** between the US and Iran — meant to produce a lasting deal — expired this week without one. At the same time, **Iran's foreign ministry said Tehran had separately reached an agreement with Oman** on managing shipping traffic through the strait, even describing the talks as continuing but complex. Shipping data show the practical toll of the standoff: **only 13 ships** passed through Hormuz over the weekend, including just three on Sunday, compared with dozens on a normal day. Trump added that no further talks with Iran were currently scheduled.
key_points: Trump said **'we'll bomb the [expletive] out of them'** if Oman interferes with US efforts in the Strait of Hormuz, in a Fox News interview.
The **60-day window** for a US-Iran deal, agreed back in June, **expired this week** with no resolution.
Iran says it has reached a **separate agreement with Oman** over shipping traffic through the strait, even as Trump threatens Oman.
Shipping through Hormuz has **nearly ground to a halt** — only **13 ships** passed through over the weekend, a fraction of normal traffic.

thread.previously: We reported that Iran declared a shift to a 'fully offensive' posture in the Strait of Hormuz as its ceasefire with the US formally lapsed, and that Iran had seized a UAE-owned oil tanker in the days after.
thread.changed: The 60-day window the US and Iran had set in June to reach a deal has now expired with no agreement. Trump responded by threatening to bomb Oman — a neutral country that has long mediated between Washington and Tehran — if it 'gets in the way' of US efforts in the strait, even as Iran said it has separately struck its own arrangement with Oman on shipping traffic.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil** passes through — making it one of the most important chokepoints in the global economy. The US and Iran agreed a **60-day ceasefire and negotiation window** in June after weeks of strikes, but that truce has been unraveling for days: Iran declared a 'fully offensive' posture as the ceasefire lapsed and seized a UAE-owned tanker. **Oman** has historically played the role of neutral back-channel between Washington and Tehran, hosting talks neither side could hold directly — which is what makes Trump now threatening Oman itself such an unusual escalation.

cards.title: An Israeli strike kills at least six in Gaza City as Kushner's talks with Netanyahu fail to revive a US ceasefire plan
cards.what_happened: An Israeli strike on Monday hit a crowded cafe near Gaza City's port — an area now serving as a **displacement camp** for civilians — killing at least **six people** and injuring 14, according to Palestinian reports. Israel's military said the strike targeted commanders and operatives of Hamas's elite **Nukhba force** while they were meeting at the site. The strike came the same day Kushner held talks with Netanyahu in an effort to get Israel to implement a US-backed ceasefire framework that **Hamas had already agreed to** — but the meeting ended with **no agreement**. Separately, the UN's Lebanon peacekeeping mission (UNIFIL) reported an average of **137 projectiles a day** fired into southern Lebanon by Israel over the last two weeks, well above the pace since the June truce there.
key_points: An Israeli strike hit a **crowded cafe at Gaza City's port**, an area turned into a **displacement camp**, killing at least **six people** and wounding 14.
Israel's military said the strike targeted **commanders of Hamas's elite Nukhba force** who were meeting there.
Trump's envoy **Jared Kushner met Netanyahu** but the talks did **not produce an agreement** to implement a US-backed ceasefire framework Hamas had already accepted.
The UN's peacekeeping force in Lebanon separately reported an average of **137 projectiles fired daily** into southern Lebanon over the past two weeks, calling the surge 'alarming'.
Netanyahu continues to **reject the US-backed plan** to end hostilities in Gaza.

depth.background: The war in Gaza has continued despite repeated rounds of US-brokered diplomacy, with a framework previously agreed to by Hamas still not implemented by Israel. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, has taken on an informal envoy role pushing both sides toward a deal. Separately, southern Lebanon has seen a fresh spike in Israeli strikes even after a truce reached there in June, displacing families who had only recently returned home.

prev_ref.title: Trump threatens to 'bomb' Oman as the US-Iran ceasefire deadline expires with no deal

cards.title: Trump claims the Strait of Hormuz as 'new' US territory and rules out extending Iran's ceasefire deadline
cards.what_happened: President Trump escalated the standoff on Tuesday by posting a map that labels the Strait of Hormuz as **'new' US territory** — a claim with no legal basis, since the strait runs through Iranian and Omani territorial waters under international law. He simultaneously said **no negotiations with Iran are underway or scheduled**, a day after his own administration said it had opened an informal channel with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Iran's government accused Washington of using the deadline's expiry to **'squeeze' concessions** out of Tehran rather than negotiate in good faith. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that, with diplomacy stalled, Iran would consider a **'timely and precise' military strike** aimed at breaking the US naval blockade around the strait if it has to.
key_points: Trump posted a map labeling the **Strait of Hormuz** as **'new' US territory**, an unprecedented claim over a waterway that has never been US soil.
He said **no talks are taking place** with Iran, contradicting his own administration's claim just a day earlier of a **back-channel with the IRGC**.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters Iran will launch a **'timely and precise' military strike** to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy keeps failing.
The **60-day ceasefire negotiation window** with Iran expired this week with **no agreement reached**.
About **one-fifth of the world's oil** transits the Strait of Hormuz daily, and traffic through it is already running below normal.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Trump threatened to 'bomb' Oman if it obstructed US efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as the 60-day negotiation window with Iran expired with no deal in place.
thread.changed: Trump has now escalated further: he posted a map labeling the Strait of Hormuz as 'new' US territory, and said no talks with Iran are currently taking place or scheduled — a day after his own administration claimed it had opened a back channel with Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Iran, in turn, says it will go 'fully offensive' and threatens a 'timely and precise' strike to break the US naval blockade of the strait.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that ships must pass through to move oil out of the Persian Gulf — it is the world's single most important oil transit route. A **temporary US-Iran ceasefire**, reached after weeks of naval and drone confrontations, gave both sides a **60-day window** to negotiate a lasting deal; that window expired this week without one. In the days since, Iran has seized a UAE-owned tanker, an unidentified projectile struck another vessel in the strait, and Iran formally declared a shift to a **'fully offensive' military posture**.

prev_ref.title: Wall Street is jittery over an unusual three-way revolt inside the Federal Reserve

cards.title: The Fed publishes today's minutes from the meeting where three policymakers revolted
cards.what_happened: The Federal Reserve is releasing its official minutes from the July 28-29 FOMC meeting this afternoon, the standard three-week-lagged transcript-style summary the Fed publishes after every rate decision. Markets already know the headline outcome — a hold at **3.50%-3.75%** with three dissents for a hike — but the minutes are the first place the Fed explains, in its own words, the reasoning of both the majority and the dissenters. Analysts are watching specifically for how much weight policymakers put on **tariff-driven price increases** versus the risk of over-tightening into a softening jobs market, since that balance will shape expectations for the Fed's next meeting on September 15-16. The July dissent was the first time in roughly a decade that three FOMC members pushed in the same direction against the majority, so the minutes carry more market-moving weight than a typical release.
key_points: The Federal Reserve releases the **official minutes** from its July 28-29 meeting today, its standard **three-week-later** disclosure.

That meeting saw **three regional Fed presidents** — Beth Hammack, Neel Kashkari, and Lorie Logan — dissent in favor of an immediate rate **hike**, the first same-direction triple dissent in **a decade**.
The minutes are expected to spell out **why** each dissenter wanted to raise rates, giving markets their clearest look yet at how deep the split runs.
Traders currently price roughly a **50/50** chance the Fed holds rates steady again at its **September 15-16** meeting.
Any hawkish language in the minutes could push **bond yields** and the dollar higher; dovish language could do the opposite.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported that three regional Fed presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) dissented at the July meeting to push for a rate hike instead of a hold — the first three-way same-direction dissent in a decade — and that markets were already jittery, with stocks dipping and gold rising.
thread.changed: Today the Fed publishes the actual minutes explaining that dissent in detail, giving markets their first real look at the dissenters' reasoning rather than just the fact that they dissented.

depth.background: At its July meeting, the Fed's rate-setting committee (the **FOMC**) voted to hold its benchmark interest rate at **3.50%-3.75%** for a fifth straight meeting, but three of its members broke ranks to argue for a hike instead — an unusually visible crack in a body that normally moves in near-unanimous lockstep. The Fed publishes a detailed account of each meeting's discussion **three weeks later**; today is that day for July's meeting. Since the vote, softer-than-expected inflation and jobs data have shifted market sentiment back toward the Fed holding steady, but the dissent itself signaled real disagreement inside the institution that sets the price of borrowing for the entire US economy.

cards.title: A Chinese robotaxi startup just lined up more than 4,000 self-driving cars for cities outside China
cards.what_happened: Pony.ai announced this week that its pipeline of planned and potential robotaxi deployments outside China has expanded to more than **4,000 vehicles**, all already under contract, with the actual rollout pace depending on local permits and regulatory approval in each city. The centerpiece is an expanded partnership with **Uber** covering more than 2,000 robotaxis across Europe, layered on top of a public launch in **Singapore** through ComfortDelGro's Zig app. The company also reported strong Q2 financial results: total revenue rose **68.8%** year-on-year to **$36.2 million**, and robotaxi-specific revenue jumped **691.2%** to **$12.1 million**, making up a third of total revenue for the first time. CEO James Peng framed the milestone as proof the company can scale internationally by plugging into partners' existing apps rather than building demand city by city on its own.
key_points: **Pony.ai** says its pipeline of planned and contracted overseas robotaxi deployments has grown past **4,000 vehicles**.
A single deal with **Uber** covers more than **2,000 robotaxis across Europe**, announced just last week.
The company also just launched publicly in **Singapore** through the ComfortDelGro-owned Zig ride-hailing app.
Robotaxi revenue **surged 691%** year-on-year in Q2, now a third of Pony.ai's total revenue for the first time.
Rollout still depends on **regulatory approval** city by city — the 4,000 figure is contracted capacity, not cars on the road yet.

depth.background: **Pony.ai** is a Chinese autonomous-driving company that already runs robotaxi services in several Chinese cities and has been racing rivals like Baidu's Apollo Go and WeRide to prove the technology works at commercial scale before expanding abroad. Robotaxis are cars that drive themselves and pick up paying passengers with no human safety driver, and building trust with regulators — who must certify the software is safe enough for public roads — is normally the slowest part of expanding into a new country. Partnering with an established ride-hailing app, rather than building its own consumer brand from scratch in each new market, is the strategy Pony.ai is using to get there faster.

cards.title: Russia is secretly shipping explosives and drone parts to Iran through the Caspian Sea, document shows
cards.what_happened: NBC News reported, based on a European government document, that Russia has been shipping **trinitrotoluene (TNT)**, drone parts, and ammunition to Iran via the Caspian Sea. The material is intended to help Iran **replenish weapons stockpiles** that were degraded during months of US and Israeli airstrikes earlier this year. Analysts note the Caspian route was deliberately chosen because Western naval forces have **no legal access** to intercept cargo moving between Russian and Iranian ports, and vessels can disable identification transponders without the attention that would draw elsewhere. Separately, US intelligence has reportedly shown Russia is helping build a **new drone factory** in Iran that could be operational early next year.
key_points: A European government document obtained by **NBC News** shows Russia is shipping **TNT, drone components, and ammunition** to Iran.
The route runs through the **Caspian Sea**, which no Western navy has legal access to — making the shipments effectively **untouchable**.
The material is meant to help Iran **rebuild stockpiles** destroyed by US and Israeli strikes during this year's war.
Ships can switch off tracking transponders in the Caspian **without drawing the scrutiny** they would on the open ocean.
It's the latest evidence of a **deepening Moscow-Tehran alliance**, on top of a US intelligence downgrade showing Russia is helping Iran build a new drone factory.

depth.background: Iran and Russia have grown closer for years, most visibly through Iran supplying Russia with attack drones for its war in Ukraine. That relationship now appears to run both ways: after this year's US-Israel war against Iran destroyed much of its missile and drone-production capacity, Russia is stepping in to help rebuild it. The Caspian Sea is a landlocked body of water bordered by Russia, Iran, and three Central Asian states — no NATO or US warship can legally enter it, making it a **blind spot** for Western monitoring and interdiction that open ocean routes don't offer.

cards.title: Iran seizes a UAE-owned oil tanker as the US-Iran ceasefire officially lapses
cards.what_happened: Iranian state media (Fars News) reported that the **IRGC (Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps)** boarded and seized a UAE-owned oil tanker near Qeshm Island on August 17, claiming the vessel had refused to use Iran's designated northern shipping route and hadn't paid a service fee. It is the **first confirmed seizure**, following drone and missile strikes on two other Abu Dhabi National Oil Company tankers around August 14-15. Separately, the temporary US-Iran ceasefire's deadline passed with no renewal; **Trump ruled out extending it** and told reporters Iran was unlikely to accept the deal on offer, calling instead for its surrender. Trump also threatened to **'bomb' Oman** — a key mediator — if it obstructs reopening the strait to normal traffic. Oil prices jumped **above $90 a barrel** and US pump prices hit a **mid-August record**, reflecting fears that a fifth of the world's oil supply route is now a live conflict zone.
key_points: Iran's Revolutionary Guard **seized a UAE-owned oil tanker** near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz — its first outright ship seizure of this crisis.
Iran claims the tanker **skipped a mandatory fee and route**, but it comes days after Abu Dhabi's state oil firm reported **drone and missile strikes** on two of its tankers.
The **US-Iran ceasefire deadline expired with no deal**, and Trump ruled out extending it, telling Iran to effectively **surrender**.
Trump separately threatened to **'bomb' Oman** if it obstructs efforts to reopen the strait, where **~20% of global oil trade** passes daily.
Crude oil jumped past **$90 a barrel** and US gasoline hit a **mid-August record** near $4.06/gallon on the news.

thread.previously: We reported Trump was threatening to 'bomb' Oman as the ceasefire deadline approached with no deal in sight.
thread.changed: The deadline has now formally expired, Trump has ruled out an extension and called for Iran's surrender, and Iran has carried out its first actual tanker seizure of the crisis — moving this from threats to action.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's seaborne oil must pass through — there's no way around it for tankers leaving the Gulf. Iran and the US fought a war earlier this year after American and Israeli strikes hit Iranian nuclear and military sites; a **shaky ceasefire** has held since, but always had a deadline attached. Since then Iran has repeatedly harassed shipping linked to the **UAE**, a US ally that hosts American forces, as a way to pressure Washington without directly re-engaging its military. Oman has tried to broker a deal on how ships transit the strait, which is what Trump is threatening to blow up if it doesn't go the US's way.

cards.title: AI chip startup Etched doubles its valuation to $21 billion in under a month
cards.what_happened: Etched announced it raised **$700 million** in a funding round led by **Jane Street**, valuing the company at **$21 billion** — nearly double its **$10.3 billion** valuation from just one month earlier. Jane Street, a major trading firm, is also Etched's first customer and received its first rack of Etched's AI hardware last month, which is now running live workloads. Etched says the AI chips it builds are designed specifically for **inference** — running trained AI models efficiently — rather than for training new ones, aiming to make it cheaper for companies to actually deploy AI products at scale. The company says it has signed more than **$1 billion** in contracts with AI companies and cloud providers.
key_points: Etched raised **$700 million** at a **$21 billion** valuation, led by trading firm Jane Street.
Its valuation has **more than doubled in about a month** — it was $10.3 billion in July and just $5 billion last December.
The company builds chips specialized for AI **'inference'** — running already-trained models — not for training them.
Etched says it has already signed **over $1 billion** in customer contracts across AI companies and cloud providers.
Jane Street, its first customer, put its first rack of Etched hardware into production last month.

depth.background: Most of the AI chip boom so far has been about **training** — the expensive, one-time process of teaching a model, dominated by Nvidia. Etched, a San Jose startup, is betting the next bottleneck is **inference**: the ongoing, everyday cost of actually running a trained model to answer a query, generate an image, or power an AI agent — a cost companies pay every single time someone uses the product. Etched's valuation has climbed at an unusual pace: **$5 billion in December**, **$10.3 billion in a Series C this past July**, and now **$21 billion**, reflecting investor belief that specialized chips built only for inference can run AI dramatically cheaper and faster than general-purpose chips.

cards.title: Meta goes on trial today in a case that could cost it up to $1.4 trillion over child safety
cards.what_happened: Opening statements began Tuesday, **August 18**, in a California federal courtroom, kicking off what is expected to be a **six-to-eight-week trial**. Attorneys general from **California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey** are leading the case on behalf of the 29 states, arguing Meta built features like infinite scroll and push notifications specifically to maximize the time children spend on its apps. The states are asking for financial penalties that could theoretically reach **$1.4 trillion**, along with court-ordered changes to how Meta designs and operates Facebook and Instagram. Meta CEO **Mark Zuckerberg**, along with other current and former executives, is expected to take the stand during the trial.
key_points: **29 US states** sued Meta in 2023, accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook features that deliberately hook children.
Opening arguments began **August 18** in an Oakland federal court before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers.
States are seeking damages that could total as much as **$1.4 trillion**, plus forced changes to how Meta runs its apps.
The trial is expected to run **six to eight weeks**, with **Mark Zuckerberg** among the executives set to testify.
A separate group of **25 more states** has its own child-safety case against Meta still waiting for trial.

depth.background: Twenty-nine US states filed suit against Meta in **2023**, arguing the company knowingly built addictive features into Instagram and Facebook that fueled a youth mental-health crisis, and that it collected data on children under 13 without parental consent in violation of federal privacy law. Meta has faced years of similar accusations from parents, researchers, and its own former employees, some of whom have testified that internal research showed the company knew its products harmed teenagers' wellbeing. This is the **first of the 29-state cases to reach trial**; a related group of 25 additional states is pursuing its own case separately. A federal jury already ordered Meta to pay **$375 million** in a related child-safety verdict earlier this year.

cards.title: A ship is struck by an 'unknown projectile' in the Strait of Hormuz, wounding a crew member, hours after Iran vows to go 'fully offensive'
cards.what_happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) reported that a vessel was struck by an **unknown projectile** while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz at **01:35 UTC on August 18**, causing **engine room damage and a crew casualty** — it remains unclear whether the crew member was killed or wounded. The rest of the crew was assisted by the **Omani Coast Guard**. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities are still investigating who or what fired the projectile. Hours later, President Trump posted on Truth Social that the strait is **'open and operating'** and that 'all water mines have been removed or detonated,' while also saying there are **no talks scheduled** with Tehran. US Central Command declined to confirm his demining claim and referred questions to the White House. Iran's top negotiator countered that the strait will **not reopen** until the US lifts its naval blockade and releases frozen Iranian assets — directly contradicting Trump's account.
key_points: A vessel was hit by an **unknown projectile** exiting the Strait of Hormuz at **01:35 UTC**, damaging its engine room.
**One crew member was hurt**; survivors were assisted by the **Omani Coast Guard**, per the UK's UKMTO monitor.
**No group has claimed responsibility** — the attack came hours after Iran declared a 'fully offensive' posture.
Trump posted the strait is **'open and operating'**, but **US Central Command would not confirm** his claim that mines were cleared.
Iran's top negotiator says the strait **stays shut** until the US lifts its naval blockade and unfreezes Iranian assets.

thread.previously: We reported Iran had formally declared a shift from a defensive to a 'fully offensive' posture in the strait after its ceasefire with the US lapsed, warning it was ready for a 'timely and precise' military attack to break the US naval blockade, while ship transits had already begun falling.
thread.changed: That declared posture has now produced an actual attack: a vessel was hit by an unclaimed projectile and a crew member hurt, and the US and Iran are now giving directly contradictory public accounts of whether the strait is safe to use at all.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** passes through by tanker — there is no practical detour. A 60-day US-Iran ceasefire (the Islamabad Memorandum) lapsed on **August 16** with no permanent deal on Iran's nuclear program, and Iranian officials told Reuters the same day that Tehran was formally shifting from a defensive posture to a **'fully offensive'** one in the strait. Weekly ship transits had already fallen from 118 to 95 as owners grew wary of the chokepoint even before this strike.
