cards.title: Cadillac's owner denies selling the F1 team amid a federal probe into $16-20 billion in loans, as a new team boss takes over
cards.what_happened: TWG Global issued a firm public statement denying it is considering selling the Cadillac F1 team or any other part of TWG Motorsport, pushing back directly on weeks of sale speculation. That denial comes as a federal investigation into owner **Mark Walter** widens: authorities are examining roughly **$16-20 billion** in private-credit loans made by insurance companies Walter controls — **Delaware Life** and **Clear Spring Life and Annuity** — to entities linked to Walter himself or TWG Global, with grand jury subpoenas issued to Walter's Guggenheim Partners and the two insurers back in **February**. Separately, Cadillac abruptly fired team principal **Graeme Lowdon** last week and replaced him with **Marcin Budkowski**, a well-known former Alpine and FIA figure. Budkowski said the ongoing investigation had not come up in discussions around his own hiring, and pointed instead to the team's continued spending as evidence of stability.
key_points: **TWG Global**, which co-owns Cadillac's F1 team, issued a firm statement denying it is considering any sale of the team.
Owner **Mark Walter** faces a federal investigation into roughly **$16-20 billion in private-credit loans** made by insurers he controls to entities linked to himself or TWG Global.
Grand jury subpoenas were issued in **February** to Walter's Guggenheim Partners and two insurance companies, **Delaware Life** and **Clear Spring Life and Annuity**.
Team principal **Graeme Lowdon was fired** last week and replaced by **Marcin Budkowski**.
Budkowski says the investigation was not part of the discussions around his own appointment.

thread.previously: We reported that Horner was edging closer to a Cadillac move, only on the condition of an ownership stake, as owner Mark Walter faced mounting financial pressure — including selling the LA Lakers and reportedly looking to offload his Chelsea FC stake — with TWG Global under a US government and SEC investigation into undisclosed loans, and Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss denying any talks with Horner.
thread.changed: TWG has now gone further with a firm public denial that any team sale is being considered at all, new reporting details the investigation is specifically about $16-20 billion in loans with February grand jury subpoenas, and Cadillac has already fired team principal Graeme Lowdon and replaced him with Marcin Budkowski.

depth.background: **Cadillac** is Formula 1's newest team, only in its debut season, co-owned by **TWG Motorsport**, a subsidiary of billionaire **Mark Walter's** TWG Global. Walter also controls **Guggenheim Partners** and made headlines this year by selling the **LA Lakers for a record $12.5 billion**, just over a year after buying the team — a deal that put a spotlight on his broader business empire. Speculation had built for weeks that financial pressure on Walter could force a sale of Cadillac or a stake in it, fueled partly by reports he was also looking to offload his stake in Chelsea FC, and partly by talk that former Red Bull boss **Christian Horner** was eyeing a return to F1 there.

cards.title: Ferrari to give Hamilton an all-new chassis for the Dutch Grand Prix as its title push escalates
cards.what_happened: Ferrari confirmed it will fit **Lewis Hamilton's car with an entirely new chassis** for this weekend's **Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort, as part of a broader package of upgrades the team is introducing for the second half of the 2026 season. The move comes as Ferrari tries to close the gap to championship leader **Kimi Antonelli**, who holds a **50-point cushion** in the drivers' standings coming out of F1's summer break. Team principal **Fred Vasseur** said the team has 'recharged our batteries' over the break and is focused on 'maximising the opportunities' at a track that has historically been tough for Ferrari. The chassis change is a rare and costly mid-season step, signaling how seriously the team is treating its remaining title chances.
key_points: Ferrari is fitting Lewis Hamilton with an **all-new chassis** for this weekend's **Dutch Grand Prix**
The upgrade is part of an **aggressive development push** to close the gap in the drivers' title fight
Hamilton trails championship leader **Kimi Antonelli by 50 points** heading into the race weekend
Team boss **Fred Vasseur** says Ferrari has 'recharged' over the break and is targeting a strong second half

depth.background: Formula 1 teams operate under a **cost cap** that limits how much they can spend on car development each season, so swapping in a brand-new chassis mid-season is a significant, expensive commitment rather than something teams do lightly. Hamilton joined Ferrari for the 2025 season after more than a decade at Mercedes, and his time with the team has been a mix of struggle and recent improvement, including his first win in red earlier this year.

prev_ref.title: Verstappen reportedly wants only a one-year Red Bull deal, resisting the team's push to erase his exit clause

cards.title: Max Verstappen signs Red Bull contract extension through 2030, ending exit speculation
cards.what_happened: Red Bull announced today that Max Verstappen has signed a contract extension keeping him with the team through the end of the **2030 season**, two years beyond his previous deal and with the exit clauses removed. New team principal Laurent Mekies called it 'fantastic news for everyone at Red Bull... his impact on our team and on Red Bull's motorsport story has been transformational.' The announcement comes the day before Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, and follows a stretch of reported tension over his future — as recently as this week, Verstappen had reportedly been resisting signing anything beyond a single year, wary of the team's push to lock him in longer term.
key_points: **Max Verstappen** has signed a new Red Bull deal running through the **end of 2030** — two years beyond his previous 2028 contract.
The extension **removes the performance-related exit clauses** that had fueled months of speculation he could leave.
The announcement lands the day before his **home Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort, ending talk of a possible move to McLaren.
It comes despite a **rough 2026 season** — Verstappen is currently sixth in the standings and winless through the first half of the year.
The deal follows **major turnover at Red Bull**, with Christian Horner, Helmut Marko, and Adrian Newey all having left and Laurent Mekies now running the team.

thread.previously: Verstappen was reportedly resisting Red Bull's push for a long-term commitment, wanting only a one-year deal and to keep his exit clause intact, after the team had tabled a five-year, ~$80 million-a-season offer to scrap it.
thread.changed: He has now signed — extending through 2030 and giving up the exit clauses entirely, ending the standoff before his home race.

depth.background: Verstappen, a four-time world champion with 71 career wins, had been at the center of prolonged contract uncertainty this year. His existing deal, running to 2028, carried performance-related exit clauses, and reports emerged that his management had held talks with McLaren about a possible 2027 move — talks that intensified as Red Bull went through a leadership shake-up with the departures of team boss Christian Horner, advisor Helmut Marko, and design chief Adrian Newey.

cards.title: Mercedes brings a 'sizeable' upgrade to Zandvoort — but engine penalties now look 'almost inevitable' for both drivers
cards.what_happened: Mercedes confirmed it will introduce a 'sizeable' upgrade package at the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, including a reworked floor (revised floor edge, corner sections, and diffuser) and a new front wing with a more integrated mainplane and footplate design, aimed at recovering performance against a closing Ferrari and McLaren. Because Zandvoort runs F1's Sprint weekend format this year, teams get only a single practice session before Sprint Qualifying — leaving little time to validate whether the new parts actually work before they count. Separately, team principal Toto Wolff said engine-component penalties are now 'almost inevitable' for both championship leader Kimi Antonelli and teammate George Russell later this season, with Monza's long straights seen as the preferred venue to absorb Antonelli's penalty since overtaking is easier there.
key_points: Mercedes is bringing a **major floor and front-wing upgrade** to the Dutch Grand Prix as Ferrari and McLaren close the gap.
The Dutch GP runs F1's **Sprint format**, meaning only **one practice session** to validate the new parts before they matter competitively.
Team boss **Toto Wolff** says grid penalties are now 'almost inevitable' for both **Kimi Antonelli** and **George Russell** later this season.
**Monza** is being floated as the preferred track to take Antonelli's penalty, since its long straights make it easier to recover lost grid positions.
Russell, whose season has trailed his rookie teammate Antonelli, said he's **'past the point of disappointment'** with how the year has gone.

depth.background: Formula 1 caps how many engine and gearbox components each driver can use per season before incurring automatic grid-position penalties — a rule meant to control costs and reliability risk. Mercedes has struggled to keep pace with Ferrari and McLaren in the second half of the season, and rookie Kimi Antonelli currently leads the championship despite Russell, the team's more experienced driver, underperforming relative to him.

cards.title: Honda's first major Aston Martin engine upgrade could decide Fernando Alonso's F1 future
cards.what_happened: Honda has deployed a substantially reworked power unit for Aston Martin this weekend at Zandvoort — the first race back after F1's summer break — featuring a faster-burning pre-chamber, a redesigned piston shape, and modified lubrication systems to reduce friction, together believed to be worth roughly **30 additional horsepower**. It follows a 16-part chassis upgrade the team introduced in Hungary that had already shown promise. Aston Martin and Honda's stakes are unusually high this weekend: Fernando Alonso is reportedly weighing three options for his future — signing a new Aston Martin contract, moving to a rival team, or retiring from Formula 1 altogether — and how the car performs with this new engine is expected to be a significant factor in that decision.
key_points: Honda is bringing its **first major power-unit upgrade** of the season to Aston Martin at this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.
The new engine spec is believed to be worth as much as **30 extra horsepower**, after changes to the pre-chamber, piston shape, and lubrication system to cut friction.
**Fernando Alonso**, 45, is weighing whether to sign a new Aston Martin deal, move teams, or **retire from F1 entirely** — and Honda's progress is a key factor.
Aston Martin's car was over **five seconds off the pace** at the first race of 2026, one of the biggest disappointments of the season.
A **16-part chassis upgrade** introduced at the Hungarian Grand Prix before the summer break already showed signs of progress.

depth.background: Honda supplies Aston Martin's power unit under a partnership central to the team's long-term plan, built around design chief Adrian Newey and two-time world champion Fernando Alonso. The 2026 season introduced all-new aerodynamic and engine regulations, and Aston Martin's car — the AMR26 — struggled badly out of the gate, with Honda's engine underperforming on both power and reliability, contributing to a season that opened over five seconds off the pace at round one in Australia. The team began clawing back performance with a major chassis upgrade at the Hungarian Grand Prix, and this weekend's engine upgrade is the next, and arguably more important, piece of that recovery plan.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz signs new multi-year Williams contract, completing the team's 2027 lineup
cards.what_happened: Williams announced on **August 19** that Carlos Sainz has signed a new multi-year contract to continue racing for the team, with reports indicating a significantly improved salary compared to his current deal. The announcement came just one day after Williams confirmed his teammate **Alex Albon** had also signed on for 2027, meaning the team has now locked in its full driver pairing for next season. In a statement, Sainz said: **"I'm thrilled to announce my continued journey with the Atlassian Williams F1 Team family... We have what it takes to turn this around together."** The timing, just before this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, removes one of the lingering question marks hanging over the 2027 driver market.
key_points: **Carlos Sainz** has agreed a new **multi-year contract extension** with Atlassian Williams, the team announced on **August 19**.
It comes **one day after** Williams confirmed teammate **Alex Albon** would also stay on through 2027.
The two signings **complete Williams' 2027 driver lineup** and take both drivers off the market for next season.
The deal eases pressure on team boss **James Vowles** after a difficult start to F1's new aerodynamic and engine rules cycle.
Sainz called it a continuation of his "journey" with the team, citing belief in the **investment and work happening in the background** at Williams.

depth.background: Carlos Sainz moved to Williams for the 2025 season after being dropped by Ferrari, joining a historic team that has spent years rebuilding after a prolonged slump. F1 entered a new **aerodynamic and engine regulation cycle** in 2026, which reset the competitive order and gave teams like Williams a chance to close the gap on the front-runners — but also created a difficult transition that put pressure on team leadership. With Sainz's future uncertain for much of this year amid speculation linking him elsewhere, and rival Sergio Perez's camp reportedly opening talks with Williams as a possible alternative, the team's 2027 driver lineup had been one of the open questions of this year's driver market, or "silly season."

cards.title: Yuki Tsunoda returns to Racing Bulls for Zandvoort as F1's driver domino chain completes
cards.what_happened: Racing Bulls officially confirmed that **Yuki Tsunoda** returns to race for the team at this weekend's **Dutch Grand Prix**, taking over the seat vacated by **Liam Lawson**. Lawson is stepping up to **Red Bull's main team** to substitute for **Isack Hadjar**, who is out with a wrist injury and will miss the Zandvoort race — F1's emotional farewell to the Dutch circuit. Tsunoda will line up alongside rookie **Arvid Lindblad** at Racing Bulls for the weekend. Tsunoda publicly wished Hadjar a speedy recovery and said he's happy to be back behind the wheel. The move completes the full domino chain triggered by Hadjar's injury: Hadjar out, Lawson up to Red Bull, Tsunoda back into Racing Bulls.
key_points: **Yuki Tsunoda** officially returns to race for **Racing Bulls** at the Dutch Grand Prix, replacing **Liam Lawson**.
Lawson steps up to **Red Bull** to cover for the injured **Isack Hadjar**, who has a wrist injury and will miss Zandvoort.
Tsunoda will race alongside rookie **Arvid Lindblad** at Racing Bulls this weekend.
Tsunoda publicly wished Hadjar a speedy recovery, saying he's 'happy to get back behind the wheel this weekend.'

depth.background: Red Bull runs two F1 teams — its main **Red Bull Racing** team and a junior sister team, **Racing Bulls** — and regularly moves drivers between them depending on form and circumstance. **Isack Hadjar** was racing for Red Bull's main team this season; **Liam Lawson** was at Racing Bulls after being demoted from Red Bull last year following a difficult start; and **Yuki Tsunoda** had been out of a race seat after Lawson took his spot at Racing Bulls. When Hadjar suffered a wrist injury that ruled him out of the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort**, it triggered a chain reaction across the whole junior program.

cards.title: FIA clears F1's rotating 'Macarena' rear wings to keep racing, but Red Bull had to fix a safety flaw
cards.what_happened: The **FIA** completed a **Failure Mode and Effects Analysis** — a formal engineering safety review — of the rotating rear-wing concept used by Ferrari, Red Bull, and soon McLaren under 2026's active-aerodynamics rules. FIA Single-Seater Director **Nikolas Tombazis** confirmed the FIA will **not ban** the design, but said **Red Bull's version required additional mechanical work** after it failed twice on **Max Verstappen's** car — causing his high-speed crashes in Austria qualifying and at the British Grand Prix. Ferrari's own version has had no reported reliability issues. **McLaren** is expected to introduce its own version of the wing by the **Italian Grand Prix at Monza**, while **Mercedes** has opted not to develop one this season, choosing instead to focus its engineering budget on the **2027 car**.
key_points: The FIA completed a formal safety review and will **not ban** the rotating rear-wing design nicknamed the '**Macarena wing**.'
**Red Bull's** version needed extra mechanical fixes after it **failed twice on Max Verstappen's car**, causing high-speed crashes in Austria qualifying and at the British GP.
**Ferrari's** version — which coined the nickname — has had no reported issues; **McLaren** plans to race its own version by **Monza**.
**Mercedes** has chosen to skip developing the device this year, putting its budget into the **2027 car** instead.

depth.background: F1's 2026 rules introduced **active aerodynamics** — car parts, like the rear wing, that can move to change drag and downforce depending on the situation. Several teams built rotating rear wings that flex or spin in a distinctive way, which Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur nicknamed the '**Macarena wing**' after the dance. Safety is governed by the **FIA**, motorsport's governing body, which reviews any new mechanism that could fail at high speed — a wing failure at 300+ km/h can cause a serious crash. Max Verstappen suffered two high-speed crashes this season, in Austria qualifying and at the British Grand Prix, both linked to failures of Red Bull's version of the wing.

cards.title: FIA sets August 25 court date for McLaren and Red Bull's appeal over Gasly's overturned Monaco penalties
cards.what_happened: McLaren and Red Bull, whose drivers were affected by Gasly's promotion, jointly lodged a formal appeal with the FIA against both of the stewards' decisions from that Monaco weekend (**Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09**, over Document 99 issued June 12). The FIA has now confirmed the **International Court of Appeal** will hear the case on **August 25 at 09:00 local time in Paris**, at FIA headquarters. Both sides asked for the hearing to be held behind closed doors, so the arguments won't be public, but the FIA says it will publish a written decision as soon as possible afterward.
key_points: The **FIA's International Court of Appeal** will hear the case in **Paris on August 25** at 09:00 local time.
**McLaren and Red Bull** are jointly appealing a decision that wiped out **Pierre Gasly's** pit-lane speeding penalties from the **Monaco Grand Prix**.
Gasly was originally penalized for two pit-lane speeds of **60.1 km/h and 60.4 km/h**, breaching the pit-lane speed limit rule.
**Alpine** successfully used its 'Right of Review' to get those penalties overturned, promoting Gasly to **3rd place**.
The hearing will be held **behind closed doors** at both teams' request; a ruling follows afterward.

depth.background: Monaco's pit lane has one of F1's strictest speed limits because its exit merges directly with a blind, narrow racing line, making speeding there a real safety risk rather than just a technicality. During the June Monaco GP, stewards penalized Alpine's Pierre Gasly for exceeding that limit twice. Alpine later invoked its **'Right of Review'** — a formal process teams can use to ask stewards to revisit a decision if new evidence emerges — and succeeded in getting the penalties thrown out, which bumped Gasly up to third place at the expense of drivers who had finished ahead of him under the original penalties.

cards.title: A near-certain washout could scramble the title race at F1's emotional farewell to Zandvoort
cards.what_happened: Weather forecasts for this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort point to a **wet, unpredictable farewell** for the venue. Friday's single practice session and sprint qualifying face up to a **91% chance of rain**, with an **18% chance of thunderstorms**. Saturday's **Sprint** — the first ever held at Zandvoort — carries a **45-75% chance** of precipitation, meaning teams and drivers could face a genuine wet-weather shootout with no prior dry running to learn the car's balance. Sunday's main race looks calmer, with rain risk dropping to around **20%**. The stakes are high: **Kimi Antonelli** leads Lewis Hamilton by **50 points** and George Russell by roughly **59-69 points**, and unpredictable wet conditions raise the chance of a shake-up in the standings at a circuit already known for being difficult to overtake on.
key_points: Forecasters give Friday practice and sprint qualifying up to a **91% chance of rain** at Zandvoort
Saturday's sprint race carries a **45-75% chance** of rain — Zandvoort's **first-ever** F1 Sprint
Sunday's race looks drier, with rain risk dropping to roughly **20%**
Championship leader **Kimi Antonelli** holds a **50-point cushion** over Lewis Hamilton heading in
It's the **final** Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort, with the race not renewed beyond this year

depth.background: Zandvoort, a narrow, banked coastal circuit near Amsterdam, returned to the F1 calendar in 2021 after decades away and quickly became a fan favorite for its tight, high-speed corners — but the contract to host the Dutch Grand Prix has **not been renewed**, making this weekend's race the **last one** at the venue for the foreseeable future. It's also the first time Zandvoort hosts a **Sprint** — a shorter, standalone Saturday race worth its own championship points, run as part of six such weekends this season. Reigning-form rookie **Kimi Antonelli** leads the drivers' championship, with a resurgent **Lewis Hamilton** at Ferrari the closest challenger.

cards.title: FIA confirms F1's contentious 5-second start procedure is staying for 2027 — even though it says the safety issue is fixed
cards.what_happened: The FIA has confirmed that F1's five-second pre-start procedure — introduced for the 2026 season to manage turbo-lag risk at race starts — will remain in place for **2027**, even though the FIA itself says the safety concern that originally justified it has largely been fixed. As of August 2026, teams were told a new **'low-power start detection'** protocol has been built to identify cars accelerating unusually slowly off the line, automatically triggering extra electric power (via the car's MGU-K) to prevent a stall without handing the driver a competitive advantage. **Ferrari** remains frustrated: an engine design choice that had briefly given the team a strong start-line advantage was neutralized once the FIA stepped in, and team principal **Frederic Vasseur** has previously said the team's patience with further changes to the procedure was wearing thin.
key_points: F1's **five-second pre-start procedure**, introduced in 2026, will continue into **2027**
The FIA now admits the original safety concern behind the rule has **largely been resolved**
A new **'low-power start detection'** system triggers an automatic power boost to stop cars stalling off the line
**Ferrari** remains angry that the rule neutralized a start-line advantage from its engine design
Ferrari boss **Frederic Vasseur** has previously said **'enough is enough'** on further tweaks to the procedure

depth.background: F1's 2026 cars ditched the old hybrid engine's **MGU-H** component as part of a major regulation overhaul, which brought back **turbo lag** — a delay between a driver pressing the throttle and the engine actually delivering power. That lag made race starts unpredictable and risky, since cars could bog down or lurch unevenly off the grid. To manage this, the FIA introduced a **five-second pre-start phase** before the usual light sequence, during which blue lights flash on the grid panels, letting drivers build up engine revs safely before the lights go out and the race begins.

cards.title: Christian Horner edges closer to an F1 return at Cadillac as owner Mark Walter's financial troubles force a sell-off
cards.what_happened: New reporting this week says Horner is edging closer to a move to Cadillac, but only on the condition that he acquires some form of **ownership stake** in the team, not simply a management role. The speculation comes as Cadillac owner Mark Walter faces mounting financial pressure: he recently sold the **LA Lakers for a record $12.5 billion**, just over a year after taking control of the team, and is now reportedly looking to sell his and business partner Todd Boehly's roughly **12.8% stakes each in Chelsea FC**. Walter's TWG Global is also said to be under a **US government and SEC investigation** into allegedly undisclosed loans between several of his companies. Cadillac CEO **Dan Towriss** has publicly denied the Horner reports, saying: "There have been no talks with Christian Horner. No plans to do that." No deal has been confirmed by either side.
key_points: Horner reportedly wants an **ownership stake** at Cadillac, not just a team-principal job.
Cadillac's CEO **Dan Towriss has denied** any talks with Horner are happening.
Owner **Mark Walter** just sold the **LA Lakers for $12.5 billion** and is now shopping his **Chelsea FC** stake too.
Walter's TWG Global is reportedly under a **US government/SEC investigation** into undisclosed inter-company loans.
Horner has ruled out **Red Bull or Racing Bulls**, the team that fired him last July, leaving few other landing spots on the grid.

depth.background: **Christian Horner** built Red Bull into one of Formula 1's most dominant teams over roughly two decades as team principal, before being removed from the role last July following internal turmoil. **Cadillac** is F1's newest team, entering the grid in 2026 under ownership tied to **Mark Walter's TWG Global**, a sports and investment group that also has stakes in the LA Dodgers and, until recently, the LA Lakers. Team principals in F1 typically run operations without owning equity in the team, but reports say Horner wants a different arrangement this time.

cards.title: Zandvoort hosts its last Dutch Grand Prix this weekend, going out with F1's first-ever sprint there
cards.what_happened: F1 confirmed that this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix will be **Zandvoort's last** on the calendar, ending an agreement that brought the track back for **six race weekends** since 2021. As part of the farewell deal, this final edition is also Zandvoort's **first-ever F1 Sprint weekend** — a shorter, separately-scored Saturday race format F1 has rolled out at select venues in recent years. The decision came down to economics: despite consistently sold-out crowds fueled by Verstappen's home-race popularity, organizers couldn't make the numbers work long-term, and passed on options to rotate the race with other circuits in favor of a clean exit. Verstappen himself has spoken candidly about the track's departure heading into the weekend.
key_points: This weekend's **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** will be the track's **final appearance** on the F1 calendar — it drops off after 2026.
The local promoter chose **not to renew** the race, after struggling to make the sell-out event financially viable despite Max Verstappen's popularity.
The farewell weekend is also Zandvoort's **first-ever F1 Sprint round** — a shorter Saturday race added to the format.
Zandvoort **returned to the F1 calendar in 2021**, driven largely by Max Verstappen's rise, and hosted **six race weekends** before this exit.
Verstappen, a Dutch national and the track's biggest draw, has given an **honest, resigned verdict** on the venue's departure ahead of the race.

depth.background: Zandvoort, a seaside circuit in a small Dutch holiday town, hadn't hosted a Formula 1 race since **1985** until it made a high-profile comeback in **2021** — timed almost perfectly with Max Verstappen's emergence as a championship contender and eventual four-time champion. The revival was a financial and cultural success story, selling out grandstands with a sea of Dutch orange every year, but running a modern F1 race is extremely expensive, and organizers reportedly explored options like **rotating the slot** with other circuits before ultimately deciding not to continue at all.

cards.title: Antonelli returns from the break with a 50-point title cushion, but Hamilton's Ferrari has closed the gap
cards.what_happened: F1 returns from its summer break with Antonelli still on top of the standings on **219 points**, a **50-point cushion** over Hamilton in second and Russell close behind in third. But the underlying form tells a different story: Antonelli's results over his last five races rank only fourth in the field, while **Ferrari has won two of the last five grands prix** and **McLaren finally converted its car's potential into a win in Hungary** — its first victory of the season. That combination has shifted the narrative from "is this a runaway title" to a genuine, if still Antonelli-favored, fight over the season's remaining **12 races**, starting with this weekend's Zandvoort finale for the circuit.
key_points: **Kimi Antonelli** leads the championship with **219 points** after 11 races — a **50-point lead** over second-placed Lewis Hamilton.
**George Russell** sits third, a further six points behind Hamilton, keeping Mercedes in the mix at the top.
Antonelli has **6 wins, 6 poles and 9 podiums** so far, but his form over the last five races ranks only **fourth-best** in the field.
**Ferrari has won two of the last five races** and **McLaren won for the first time in 2026 in Hungary**, both signs the title fight is tightening.
Bookmakers still favor Antonelli heavily (around 1/4), with Hamilton next (about 6/1) as F1 resumes at Zandvoort with **12 races remaining**.

depth.background: Kimi Antonelli, racing for Mercedes, opened the 2026 season as a breakout title contender, winning five of the early races and prompting fears the championship could turn into a runaway. Since then, Mercedes has hit reliability issues, and 43-year-old **Lewis Hamilton** — now in his second full season at Ferrari after leaving Mercedes — has found late-career form, closing what once looked like a comfortable gap. The sport's mandatory mid-season **summer break** gives every team a moment to reset, and this weekend's return at Zandvoort kicks off the second half of the season with the title picture more competitive than it looked at the year's midpoint.

prev_ref.title: Mercedes says grid penalties for title leader Antonelli and George Russell are now 'almost inevitable'

cards.title: Mercedes zeroes in on Monza as the venue for Antonelli's 'inevitable' engine grid penalty
cards.what_happened: Mercedes has confirmed Antonelli is now maxed out on four distinct engine elements, meaning his next component change of any kind is an automatic 10-place grid penalty. Rather than wait for it to happen at a random race, the team is trying to choose the least costly moment to take the hit, and has settled on the Italian Grand Prix at Monza as the leading candidate — its long straights make it one of the easier tracks on the calendar to recover lost positions. Team principal Toto Wolff said Monza would be 'a good place' for Antonelli to take an engine penalty, even though Monza is also Antonelli's home race. Teammate George Russell is in a similar position on his third set of components, and Mercedes says it will decide whose penalty comes first based on team strategy, not favoritism toward Antonelli's title bid.
key_points: Antonelli is now at the **max allocation** on four separate engine parts — one more change means an automatic **10-place grid penalty**
Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** calls Monza **'a good place'** to take the hit, since its long straights make overtaking easier
Antonelli leads the championship with **219 points**, a **50-point cushion** over Lewis Hamilton
Teammate **George Russell** faces the same dilemma; Mercedes says it **won't prioritize** Antonelli's title bid when deciding who takes a penalty first
Monza is also **Antonelli's home race**, adding pressure to how and when the team times the penalty

thread.previously: On August 17, Mercedes said both championship leader Kimi Antonelli (already on his fourth set of engine components) and George Russell (his third) would almost certainly need grid penalties in the second half of the season, and floated Monza as one possible venue for timing the hit.
thread.changed: Mercedes has now confirmed Antonelli is at the maximum allowance on four separate engine elements — the combustion engine, exhaust, energy store, and control electronics — meaning any further change triggers an automatic 10-place penalty. Team boss Toto Wolff has now specifically named the Italian Grand Prix at Monza as 'a good place' to take it, since the track's long straights make overtaking easier for a car running a fresh engine.

depth.background: F1 caps how many power-unit parts each driver can use per season — four combustion engines, four turbochargers, four exhaust systems, three energy stores, and three control electronics, among other limits. Fit one more than the allowance and the driver gets an automatic grid-position penalty, typically dropping them back about 10 places at their next race. Kimi Antonelli, a rookie in his first full title-contending season, currently leads the drivers' championship with 219 points, a 50-point lead over Lewis Hamilton, but reliability issues in the first half of the year have burned through his allotted parts faster than planned.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz is closing in on a new Williams deal, right before his home stretch verdict on 2027
cards.what_happened: Multiple F1 outlets report Sainz and Williams team principal James Vowles are in the final stages of agreeing a new contract, likely a one-year extension, with an announcement possible in the coming days before the Dutch Grand Prix weekend. The reversal follows Sainz reportedly rejecting an earlier offer worth roughly €30 million from Williams; sources now say his eventual salary will be a significant improvement on that figure. Given how much uncertainty still surrounds the 2027 driver market, Sainz is said to be pushing for performance-related clauses — bonuses or protections tied to results and championship position — rather than a flat salary alone. The reporting comes as Sainz has statistically been Williams' standout this season: a 9-2 qualifying advantage over teammate Alex Albon, and 6 of the team's 11 championship points.
key_points: Sainz and Williams are reportedly in the **final stages** of a new contract, with an announcement possible before this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.
Sainz has comprehensively **outqualified teammate Alex Albon 9-2** this season and scored **6 of Williams' 11 points** in a tough year for the team.
The new deal is expected to lean on **performance-linked clauses** tied to championship position, given how open the 2027 driver market still is.
It's a reversal from earlier this month, when Sainz reportedly **rejected** an initial Williams offer worth around **€30 million**.
Sainz joined Williams from Ferrari in 2025 on a deal that already guaranteed him through 2026, with an option year beyond.

thread.previously: Yesterday's reporting said Sainz was nearing a new one-year Williams deal after rejecting an earlier roughly €30 million offer, reversing his earlier reluctance to commit beyond 2026.
thread.changed: Talks have now reportedly reached their final stage, with sources describing an improved salary offer, performance-linked clauses under discussion, and an announcement possible before this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.

depth.background: Carlos Sainz left Ferrari for Williams ahead of the 2025 season on a deal guaranteeing two years — 2025 and 2026 — plus an option season after that. He arrived as the more experienced of Williams' two drivers, joining a team trying to rebuild from years near the back of the grid, and has emerged as its clear form driver this year even as Williams itself has struggled. Reporting a day earlier already suggested Sainz was close to a new one-year extension; talks have moved further since then.

cards.title: A wrist injury pulls Isack Hadjar out of Verstappen's home race — Liam Lawson gets the Red Bull seat back
cards.what_happened: Red Bull confirmed Isack Hadjar will miss the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort (August 21–23) after injuring his wrist during a gym session over F1's summer break. With the injury not serious enough to need a long-term replacement, Red Bull is temporarily promoting Liam Lawson — the same driver it demoted to Racing Bulls after just two races this season — back into the senior team to partner Max Verstappen. To cover Lawson's seat, reserve driver Yuki Tsunoda moves down to Racing Bulls alongside Arvid Lindblad, who has been closing the performance gap on Lawson in recent races. Red Bull says it hopes Hadjar can return in time for the Italian Grand Prix at Monza roughly two weeks later.
key_points: Red Bull's **Isack Hadjar**, 21, is set to miss this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix with a **wrist injury** picked up training during the summer break.
**Liam Lawson** — dropped by Red Bull's senior team earlier this season — gets a surprise recall to partner **Max Verstappen**.
Reserve driver **Yuki Tsunoda** steps back down to Racing Bulls to cover Lawson's seat alongside rookie **Arvid Lindblad**.
The injury isn't considered serious — Red Bull hopes Hadjar can return at **Monza**, two races later.
The timing stings: it's the **final-ever Dutch Grand Prix**, since Zandvoort's contract wasn't renewed past 2026, and Verstappen's home farewell.

depth.background: Formula 1 teams run a strict pecking order below their two race seats: a reserve driver (here, Tsunoda) is next in line, and beneath that sits the junior team — Racing Bulls — which develops young drivers like Lawson and Lindblad. Hadjar earned the second Red Bull seat this year after Red Bull dropped Lawson just two races into the 2026 season, one of the most abrupt driver swaps in recent F1 history. That demotion left Lawson back at Racing Bulls, competing with 18-year-old rookie Lindblad and F2 driver Nikola Tsolov for a longer-term future at Red Bull.

cards.title: Red Bull's junior program has three drivers fighting for one seat — and it's about to get messier
cards.what_happened: Lawson and Lindblad, both out of contract at Racing Bulls at the end of 2026, are being pushed into direct competition for whichever Red Bull-family seat opens up next, with team principal Alan Permane telling them they're free to race wheel-to-wheel with one condition: don't make contact. On competitive form, Lawson currently holds the upper hand, sitting 9th in the drivers' championship on 43 points against Lindblad's 23 points in 11th, and leads their head-to-head qualifying battle 6-5. But the picture isn't clean: Lindblad is actually marginally quicker on average lap time. Complicating things further, Formula 2 championship leader **Nikola Tsolov**, a 19-year-old Bulgarian and fellow Red Bull junior, is pushing hard for his own F1 opportunity. Tsolov is set to get his first real taste of a Formula 1 car in a Racing Bulls test at Imola on August 27, driving a 2025-specification car under rules that let him bank the superlicence points needed to eventually race in F1 — he currently has 25 of the 40 points required.
key_points: Racing Bulls teammates **Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad** are both out of contract at the end of 2026 and effectively racing each other for the next Red Bull opening.
Team boss Alan Permane's only rule for the pair: **'do not touch each other.'**
Lawson leads the standings, **9th on 43 points** to Lindblad's **11th on 23 points**, but Lindblad is marginally faster on raw pace.
A **third contender**, Formula 2 championship leader Nikola Tsolov, is closing in fast on a superlicence.
Tsolov gets his first real Formula 1 test in a Racing Bulls car at **Imola on August 27**.

depth.background: Red Bull has long run one of F1's most aggressive young-driver pipelines, using its junior team (currently branded Racing Bulls) as a proving ground before promoting drivers to the senior Red Bull team. That system has been unusually brutal this year — Red Bull has swapped drivers in and out of its senior seat repeatedly, and Lawson himself was demoted from the senior team early in the season after a rocky start, landing back at Racing Bulls. With Max Verstappen's own contract situation also unresolved, the driver most likely to get the next opening at either team is whoever wins the internal fight happening right now at Racing Bulls.

cards.title: Verstappen reportedly wants only a one-year Red Bull deal, resisting the team's push to erase his exit clause
cards.what_happened: Red Bull has tabled a revised contract offer to Max Verstappen worth roughly **$80 million per season**, running five years to **2033**, with **no exit clause** attached — a clear upgrade on his current pay and a bid to eliminate the uncertainty around his future. But reporting indicates Verstappen may prefer the opposite: signing only a **one-year extension** so he retains the flexibility to reassess his options each year, rather than tying himself to Red Bull for the rest of the decade. His existing contract's **exit clause** requires him to decide by **October** whether to invoke it, based on whether he's inside the top two of the standings at the year's midpoint. Neither Verstappen nor his management have issued an on-record response to Red Bull's new offer.
key_points: Red Bull's five-year, **~$80 million-a-season offer** would run **through 2033** and **remove Verstappen's exit clause** entirely.
Verstappen is instead said to prefer signing **only a one-year extension**, keeping maximum flexibility over his future.
His current deal runs to **2028**, but an **exit clause** lets him leave if he isn't in the **top two of the standings at mid-season** — a condition he must act on by **October**.
The new offer is a **notable raise** on his current reported ~€65 million annual pay.
**No official response** has come from Verstappen's camp on the record yet.

depth.background: Max Verstappen has driven for Red Bull since 2016 and won multiple world championships with the team, but speculation about a future move — including to Mercedes — has simmered as Red Bull's competitiveness has fluctuated. His current contract includes an unusual **exit clause**: if he isn't in the top two of the drivers' standings at the season's halfway point, he gets a window (closing this October) to notify the team if he wants to leave. Red Bull's new offer is widely seen as an attempt to lock him down long-term and remove that flexibility before it becomes a problem.

cards.title: McLaren's boss admits he feared Norris and Piastri's teammate rivalry could turn toxic — instead they're still getting along
cards.what_happened: McLaren team principal **Andrea Stella** said he felt real relief that **Norris and Piastri** have continued working well together in 2026, despite the pressure of their tight 2025 title fight. That cooperation is being tested from a different angle now: Mercedes technical figures say McLaren's recent upgrades have created a **'significant' gap** in performance between the two drivers' cars, which could reignite internal tension if one driver starts consistently outperforming the other. Norris's win at the **Hungarian Grand Prix**, with pole position too, was McLaren's **first win of the season** — a rare bright spot in an otherwise tough 2026 campaign. The team is bringing a new **rear-wing upgrade** to Zandvoort this weekend to try to close the gap to the front-runners for both cars.
key_points: Team principal **Andrea Stella** said he was relieved at how well **Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri** have worked together in 2026.
The concern followed a **hard-fought 2025 title fight** between the two teammates, which Norris won.

Norris's **Hungarian Grand Prix win** was McLaren's **first victory of a difficult 2026 season**.
McLaren is bringing a **new rear wing upgrade** to this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort to help both cars.

depth.background: Formula 1 teammates racing for the same championship often become each other's fiercest rivals, and tension between them can fracture a team from the inside — something McLaren experienced firsthand during Norris and Piastri's tight title battle in 2025, which Norris ultimately won. Going into 2026, there was no guarantee the pair would keep cooperating rather than letting that rivalry sour. McLaren's 2026 car, the MCL40, has also been a step behind expectations for much of the season.

cards.title: Cadillac denies Sergio Perez is leaving for Williams, as his camp opens talks for a 2027 seat
cards.what_happened: Reports emerged that **Sergio Perez's management has opened discussions with Williams** about a potential 2027 race seat, contingent on Carlos Sainz not remaining there. **Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss** moved quickly to shut the rumours down, stating **'we have great confidence in our relationship with Checo, and he will also be racing in the Cadillac next year.'** The complication is that Perez's current agreement with Cadillac effectively only guarantees his seat for **2026**, leaving the picture beyond that genuinely open. Perez, for his part, has been **openly critical of the pace of Cadillac's development** as the team remains without a single point through the opening half of the season.
key_points: Perez's management has **opened talks with Williams** about a **2027 seat** — contingent on Carlos Sainz not staying there.
Cadillac CEO **Dan Towriss** dismissed the rumours, saying Perez **'will also be racing in the Cadillac next year.'**
Perez's current Cadillac deal effectively **only covers 2026**, leaving his future beyond that unresolved.
Perez has been **openly critical of Cadillac's slow development**, with the rookie team still **pointless** heading into the summer break.

A debut season with zero championship points has fuelled speculation about whether Cadillac's top driver might look elsewhere, especially with **Williams** — where Carlos Sainz's own future beyond 2026 remains uncertain — seen as a possible landing spot.

cards.title: Cadillac's brand-new boss shuts down Perez-to-Williams rumours in his first big call
cards.what_happened: Speaking during his first round of media appearances since being named Cadillac's new team principal, **Marcin Budkowski** was asked directly about swirling rumours that Sergio Perez could leave for Williams. He said Perez **'has not only been driving exceptionally well, but he's been pushing the team very, very hard in the background'**, calling him crucial to providing stability in a young team. Cadillac CEO **Dan Towriss** went further, saying the team is **not distracted by the Williams rumours for a second** and expressing confidence Perez will stay. The statements come the same week Cadillac abruptly sacked founding boss Graeme Lowdon and installed Budkowski, and while Perez has yet to score a championship point in Cadillac's debut season, he currently leads teammate Bottas 9-5 in qualifying head-to-heads.

cards.title: Gabriel Bortoleto shuts down Carlos Sainz-to-Audi rumours: 'my seat is filled'
cards.what_happened: Gabriel Bortoleto addressed rumours linking Carlos Sainz to his Audi seat head-on, telling reporters plainly that **'the seat is filled'** and that he holds a **long-term contract with no clause** allowing the team to replace him. His comments came the same week Audi's racing director Allan McNish spoke positively about the pairing of Bortoleto's youthful energy with Hulkenberg's experience. Audi currently sits 8th in the constructors' standings after scoring points in its last three races, with Bortoleto outscoring the more experienced Hulkenberg 10 points to 2 through 11 rounds of the season.
key_points: Audi rookie **Gabriel Bortoleto** publicly rejected speculation that **Carlos Sainz** could take his seat, saying **'the seat is filled'**.
Bortoleto confirmed his **long-term Audi contract has no clause** that would allow him to be swapped out for Sainz.
Audi (formerly Sauber) sits **8th in the constructors' championship**, an improvement on its predecessor team.
Bortoleto has **10 points** this season to teammate **Nico Hulkenberg's 2**, across 11 rounds.
Audi's racing director **Allan McNish** praised the Hulkenberg-Bortoleto pairing as a strong blend of experience and youth.

depth.background: Audi took over the former Sauber team as a full manufacturer entry for the 2026 season, pairing experienced driver Nico Hulkenberg with rookie Gabriel Bortoleto. As one of F1's most competitive driver markets this year has heated up, with several experienced drivers like Carlos Sainz weighing their 2027 options, speculation has periodically linked Sainz to a possible Audi seat given the team's manufacturer ambitions.

cards.title: McLaren's new rear wing could widen the gap between its own two drivers at Zandvoort
cards.what_happened: McLaren is introducing a rear-wing update for both Norris and Piastri at this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, designed to fix how the MCL40 behaves as it transitions from straight-line to cornering mode — an issue that has been costing lap time at low-grip circuits. The team is deliberately holding back a more extensive rear-wing overhaul, internally referred to as the 'Macarena' wing, for Monza later in the season, a track that rewards straight-line speed rather than downforce. Norris currently leads Piastri **7-4** in qualifying head-to-heads and **4-0** in Sprint qualifying this year, and rivals — including Mercedes — have publicly noted that McLaren's recent upgrades appear to have widened rather than narrowed the performance gap between its two drivers.
key_points: McLaren is bringing a **rear-wing upgrade** for both cars at Zandvoort, targeting a downforce issue on the tight, high-banked circuit.
**Lando Norris** currently leads teammate **Oscar Piastri 7-4** in qualifying and **4-0** in Sprint qualifying this season.
Piastri has struggled to adapt to the **2026 regulations car**, particularly when the rear end slides on low-grip tracks.
A separate, bigger rear-wing redesign (dubbed 'Macarena') is being saved for **Monza**, a higher-speed circuit later this season.
Rivals including **Mercedes** have flagged that McLaren's own upgrades have exposed a **significant gap** between its two drivers.

depth.background: McLaren enters the second half of the 2026 season locked in a title fight but managing an awkward internal dynamic: teammates **Lando Norris** and **Oscar Piastri** are performing at clearly different levels under the same car, which raises delicate questions for a team that has publicly committed to letting both drivers race freely rather than favoring one. Zandvoort's tight, banked layout rewards a car that handles well in low-speed corners, an area where McLaren's current car (the MCL40) has shown a specific weakness that hurts both drivers, but reportedly Piastri more than Norris.

cards.title: Ferrari brings its biggest upgrade of the year as Hamilton tries to close a 50-point gap at F1's most emotional farewell race
cards.what_happened: Ferrari is bringing what's being described as its **major, second-half-of-season upgrade package** to the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort this weekend, aimed at closing the performance gap to championship leader Kimi Antonelli. Hamilton currently sits **second in the drivers' standings**, 50 points adrift of Antonelli after 11 races, but has shown clear improvement over his rocky first Ferrari season — highlighted by ending his win drought with a victory at the **Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix**. Adding to the reset, Hamilton will work with a **new race engineer** this weekend after his previous engineer, Riccardo Adami, moved into a role in Ferrari's driver-development pipeline. The upgrades land at a symbolically loaded venue: this is **Zandvoort's final scheduled Dutch Grand Prix**, as its contract with F1 expires this year.
key_points: **Ferrari** is bringing major car upgrades for the second half of the season as **Lewis Hamilton** chases an eighth world title.
Hamilton sits **second in the standings**, **50 points behind** championship leader Kimi Antonelli, after 11 rounds.
He's had a stronger 2026 than his difficult debut Ferrari season, snapping a win drought with victory at **Barcelona-Catalunya**.
Hamilton will also race with a **new race engineer** this weekend after Riccardo Adami moved to Ferrari's driver-development program.
The upgrades arrive at **Zandvoort**, hosting its **final-ever** Dutch Grand Prix before dropping off the calendar.

depth.background: **Lewis Hamilton** joined Ferrari for the 2025 season chasing a record eighth F1 drivers' title, but his first year at the team was widely seen as a struggle to adapt. Team boss **Fred Vasseur** has pointed to specific areas Ferrari needs to improve to keep Hamilton in the title fight, and the team has been building toward a package of upgrades for the second half of 2026 rather than making incremental tweaks. **Kimi Antonelli**, in only his second F1 season, has emerged as the surprise championship leader, putting pressure on established stars like Hamilton to close the gap in the remaining races.

The story breaks as F1 returns from its summer break with the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** — Verstappen's home race, and reportedly the event's last edition, since it's dropping off the 2027 calendar.

Red Bull, unwilling to lose a four-time world champion, has been trying to lock him down with a new long-term contract — but the terms of any deal, and whether the exit clause survives it, have become the central tension.

cards.title: Honda's long-awaited upgraded engine hits its performance target ahead of Aston Martin's Zandvoort debut
cards.what_happened: Honda's chief engineer, **Shintaro Orihara**, confirmed the manufacturer has met its **internal performance target** for the upgraded RA626H power unit ahead of its debut at the Dutch Grand Prix. The changes include a **revised pre-chamber** (to speed up combustion), a **reshaped combustion chamber and piston**, and **lubrication changes** aimed at reducing mechanical friction — all routes to extracting more usable power. The unit already ran on-track for the first time during an Aston Martin **filming day at the Hungaroring**, gathering data ahead of its planned race debut. Honda flagged one complication: Zandvoort's **Sprint race format** gives teams only a single free practice session, making it harder to properly evaluate a new engine spec under real conditions before it's raced.
key_points: Honda says its new-spec **RA626H power unit** has hit its **internal performance target** ahead of the Dutch GP.
The upgrade modifies the **pre-chamber, combustion chamber and piston shape** to burn fuel more efficiently, plus lubrication tweaks to cut friction losses.
It already ran on track during an Aston Martin **filming day in Hungary** before its planned **race debut at Zandvoort**.
Honda admits this weekend's **Sprint format**, which gives only one practice session, makes properly evaluating the new engine **harder**.
The upgrade is meant to build on Aston Martin's **aerodynamic gains** from its AMR26 car this year.

depth.background: In Formula 1, the engine ('power unit') and the aerodynamic package are separate battles — a team can have a great chassis but still lose lap time if its engine partner falls behind. Honda supplies **Aston Martin's** power units, and after a mixed start to the 2026 rules era, the manufacturer has been working toward a significant mid-season upgrade. Aston Martin, meanwhile, has reportedly made real strides on the **aerodynamic side** of its car (the AMR26), meaning a stronger engine could unlock gains the chassis is already capable of. Zandvoort's Dutch Grand Prix (August 21-23) marks the engine's intended competitive debut.

cards.title: Racing Bulls tells its two title-hopeful rookies they can race flat-out — with one rule: don't touch
cards.what_happened: Team principal Alan Permane confirmed that Racing Bulls will **not impose team orders** to protect one driver over the other, even though Lawson and Lindblad are directly competing with each other for results, for a place ahead of Tsolov in the pecking order, and ultimately for a possible Red Bull promotion. The only boundary Permane set is that the two must **not make contact** with each other while racing. Permane said the team expects to arrive at this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort '**even stronger**' than before the summer break.
key_points: Racing Bulls boss **Alan Permane** set just one rule for teammates **Liam Lawson** and **Arvid Lindblad**: don't touch each other.
The team is chasing its **best-ever Constructors' Championship finish** and won't order either driver to back off.
Both drivers are also racing for a possible future **Red Bull seat**, adding personal stakes to every on-track battle.
F2 champion **Nikola Tsolov** is a further threat to both drivers' longer-term F1 futures.
Permane says the team expects to come back **'even stronger' at Zandvoort** this weekend.

depth.background: Racing Bulls is Red Bull's sister/junior team, and this season it is fighting for its **best-ever finish** in the Constructors' Championship — the team title based on combined points from both drivers. Teammates **Liam Lawson** and 18-year-old rookie **Arvid Lindblad** are not just racing for the team; they are also both competing for the same prize of a future promotion to the senior **Red Bull** team if a seat opens up, with rising Formula 2 champion **Nikola Tsolov** also in the wings as a longer-term threat to both their prospects.

cards.title: Mercedes says grid penalties for title leader Antonelli and George Russell are now 'almost inevitable'
cards.what_happened: Mercedes has acknowledged that both Antonelli and Russell will almost certainly need grid penalties in the second half of the 2026 season because reliability failures in the first half burned through their allotted engine components faster than planned. Antonelli is already on his **fourth set** of power-unit components and Russell his **third**, meaning any further replacement triggers a penalty. Rather than debate whether to take the hit, the team is strategizing about **which race weekend** minimizes the damage — Mercedes team principal **Toto Wolff** has floated the **Italian Grand Prix at Monza** as a candidate, reasoning that even a back-of-grid start there is more recoverable than at a track like Zandvoort, Antonelli's title rival's home race. Mercedes has stated it will **not prioritize Antonelli's title campaign** over Russell when deciding the order.
key_points: Mercedes admits both **Kimi Antonelli** and **George Russell** will need grid penalties before the season ends.
Antonelli, the **championship leader with 219 points**, is already on his **fourth set** of engine components.
A grid penalty usually means starting **around 10 places back** — costly in a tight title fight.
Mercedes is choosing **when**, not if, to take the hit, with **Monza** floated as one option.
The team says it **won't favor Antonelli's title bid** over Russell when deciding whose penalty comes first.

depth.background: In Formula 1, each driver is allotted a limited number of engine parts (the 'power unit') for the entire season under FIA rules. Teams try to make each part last as long as possible, because fitting an extra one beyond the allowance triggers an automatic grid penalty at the next race — typically dropping a driver back around 10 places on the starting grid. **Kimi Antonelli**, a rookie in his first full title-contending season, currently leads the drivers' championship with **219 points**, a **50-point lead** over Lewis Hamilton.

depth.background: Christian Horner ran Red Bull's F1 team for two decades, winning multiple constructors' and drivers' championships, before being ousted from the role earlier in 2026 amid internal upheaval at the team. Since then, he has been widely reported to be exploring a return to the sport as a team owner rather than an employee, with his name repeatedly linked to various ownership and investment opportunities across the grid. Alpine, the Renault-owned French team, has struggled competitively in recent seasons, and investment firm **Otro Capital** holds a minority stake in the team that has reportedly been up for sale or restructuring — but Renault, as the majority owner, retains veto power over who else gets in.

cards.title: Mercedes admits it's fallen 'out of step' in F1's development war after front-loading everything into its launch car
cards.what_happened: Mercedes technical director **James Allison** explained that the team deliberately delayed locking in its car's aerodynamic and bodywork design **by several weeks longer than it ever had before**, pouring maximum development into getting the strongest possible car for the season's first race. That bet worked spectacularly at first: Mercedes finished **one-two in the opening two rounds** and won its **first six races** of 2026. But because the team emptied its development pipeline to achieve that early peak, it has since fallen behind — winning just **two of the next five races** as rivals, who paced their upgrades more evenly, caught up and overtook. Allison said F1's 2026 development rates are extraordinary, with aerodynamic gains in the wind tunnel running **six to seven times faster** than in 2025, worth roughly **half a second of lap time every couple of months** — meaning falling even one update cycle behind can be costly. Mercedes now finds itself "a race or two" behind its competitors in bringing new parts to the track.
key_points: Mercedes technical director **James Allison** says the team is now **"out of step"** with rivals in F1's 2026 development race
Mercedes deliberately delayed finalising its car's aero and bodywork by **several weeks** longer than ever before, to front-load development into the season opener
The gamble paid off early — Mercedes finished **one-two in each of the first two rounds** and won its **first six races**
Since then, Mercedes has won only **two of the next five races**, as rivals' updates caught up
Development rates across F1 in 2026 are running **six to seven times faster** than last season, worth roughly **half a second every two months**

depth.background: Formula 1's new 2026 technical regulations triggered an unusually intense "development war" among teams, where cars are evolving far faster mid-season than in a typical year because of loosened aerodynamic rules. Every team has to decide how to time its development spending across a season with a hard cost cap — front-load it for an early advantage, or spread it out to keep improving through the year. Mercedes chose an aggressive front-loaded strategy for its 2026 car, betting everything on being fastest out of the gate.

cards.title: Alpine brings a make-or-break upgrade to Zandvoort in its fight to avoid last place in the constructors' standings
cards.what_happened: As Formula 1 returns from its summer break for the **Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort, Alpine has brought a new upgrade package to the car, which **Pierre Gasly** says will be central to the team's effort to overtake **Racing Bulls** for fifth place in the 2026 constructors' championship. The update arrives alongside a broader wave of midfield upgrades this weekend — Aston Martin, for instance, has also brought a significant new package — as teams look to make gains with roughly a third of the season still to run. Zandvoort itself carries extra weight this year: it is expected to be the **last-ever Dutch Grand Prix** on the calendar for the foreseeable future, and forecasts suggest this year's race could see F1's current-generation cars run in wet conditions for the first time.
key_points: Alpine arrives at the **Dutch Grand Prix** with a new upgrade package for the car.
Driver **Pierre Gasly** calls it "key" to the team's push for **P5 in the constructors' championship**.
Alpine is currently battling **Racing Bulls** for that midfield position.
The upgrade lands as several other midfield teams, including Aston Martin, also bring updates to Zandvoort.
It's F1's first race back after the summer break, when small car upgrades can swing tight midfield battles.

depth.background: Formula 1's **constructors' championship** rewards every team, not just the front-runners — midfield finishes translate directly into prize money, so teams like Alpine and Racing Bulls fight hard over positions like fifth and sixth even though neither is competing for race wins. Alpine has struggled for consistent pace this season, and driver **Pierre Gasly** has repeatedly pointed to car upgrades as the team's main lever to close the gap on rivals ahead of it in the standings.

cards.title: A former F1 boss says Mercedes doesn't need Max Verstappen anymore — because it already found the next one
cards.what_happened: Speaking on the **"Up To Speed" podcast** with former driver David Coulthard and content creator Jolie Sharpe, former Haas team principal **Guenther Steiner** said Mercedes no longer has a compelling reason to pursue Max Verstappen, because the team believes it has already found its next superstar in **Kimi Antonelli**. Steiner said his own thinking on the matter changed noticeably after the **Hungarian Grand Prix**: "If you would have asked me three or four days ago, I would say going to McLaren is a sideways move [for Verstappen] — after Hungary, maybe it isn't a sideways move, but things changed since then," he said, pointing to Antonelli's continued strong form. Antonelli, still only 19, currently **leads the 2026 drivers' championship**. The comments land as F1 prepares to resume after its summer break at Zandvoort for the Dutch Grand Prix, with Verstappen's own contract situation — including an exit clause from Red Bull that is now active — still one of the sport's most closely watched storylines.
key_points: Ex-Haas boss **Guenther Steiner** says Mercedes no longer needs to chase Max Verstappen for a future seat.
His reasoning: Mercedes rookie **Kimi Antonelli**, 19, is already playing the role of "the next Max Verstappen."
Antonelli currently **leads the 2026 drivers' championship**.
Steiner says his view shifted specifically after the **Hungarian Grand Prix**, where Antonelli's form changed the calculus.
It comes as Verstappen's own Red Bull exit clause is **active** heading into F1's return from summer break.

depth.background: Max Verstappen's future has been one of Formula 1's biggest ongoing storylines in 2026: he holds a contract with Red Bull through 2028, but an **exit clause** in that deal became active once the team fell outside the top two in the constructors' standings at the summer break, fueling constant speculation about a possible move to Mercedes or McLaren. Mercedes, meanwhile, has been building its future around its own young driver pipeline, headlined by **Kimi Antonelli**, who stepped into a Mercedes seat this season at just 19 and has exceeded expectations.

cards.title: Franco Colapinto set to stay at Alpine for 2027, closing off one of the driver market's last open seats
cards.what_happened: Paddock sources now say Colapinto is in the closing stages of agreeing to **stay at Alpine for the 2027 season**, with an announcement widely expected before or around the summer-break-ending Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort. Alpine team boss **Steve Nielsen** said the team wants 'more' from the 23-year-old but confirmed the decision would be made purely **'on merit'** — pointing to Colapinto's improved consistency and his ability to regularly match or edge teammate Pierre Gasly, a big step up from his rockier rookie form earlier in the year.
key_points: Paddock sources say Colapinto is **'ever closer' to a 2027 Alpine deal**, expected before Zandvoort.
Alpine boss Steve Nielsen said the call will be made **'on merit'** — 'if he's good enough, he'll stay'.
Colapinto's current contract **runs out at the end of 2026**.
He has taken a **clear step forward this season**, regularly matching or beating teammate Pierre Gasly.
Keeping Colapinto removes one of the last uncertain seats in F1's 2027 driver market.

depth.background: Franco Colapinto is a young Argentine driver who joined Alpine after impressing as a late-season stand-in for Williams in 2024. His rookie full season with Alpine in 2026 was watched closely because his results would determine whether the team kept faith in him for 2027 — Alpine had been explicit that his seat wasn't guaranteed and would depend on performance against experienced teammate Pierre Gasly.

cards.title: Verstappen and Hadjar unveil Delftware-inspired helmets for F1's last-ever Dutch Grand Prix — Hadjar's honours his own broken trophy
cards.what_happened: Ahead of the final Dutch Grand Prix (August 21–23), Red Bull unveiled one-off **Delftware-inspired helmets, race suits, and boots** for Verstappen and Hadjar, drawing on the blue-and-white floral patterns of the Netherlands' famous pottery tradition. Verstappen's helmet and orange-striped suit are a tribute to his home country and fans, inscribed with **'Dankjewel Zandvoort'**. Hadjar's helmet goes further, incorporating an illustration of his **broken trophy from last year's podium celebration**, along with a cartoon of his reaction in the moment — turning what could have been an embarrassing mishap into a signature piece of his identity as a driver.
key_points: Red Bull unveiled special **Delft Blue-inspired helmets and race suits** for Verstappen and Hadjar.
It's the **final Dutch Grand Prix** on the F1 calendar — the race isn't being renewed beyond 2026.
Hadjar's design references his **own broken trophy** from his maiden podium at Zandvoort last year, which went viral.
Verstappen's helmet carries the message **'Dankjewel Zandvoort'** — 'thank you' in Dutch — for his final home race.
Verstappen has **won his home race three times** and has one more shot to match a long-standing record.

depth.background: The Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort has been one of F1's most passionate home-crowd events since Max Verstappen's rise turned it into an unofficial 'Orange Army' takeover each year. F1 has confirmed the race will **not continue on the calendar beyond 2026**, making this weekend Verstappen's last chance to win in front of his home fans at this specific track. Isack Hadjar, promoted to Red Bull for 2026 after a strong 2025 with sister team Racing Bulls, earned his maiden F1 podium at last year's Dutch Grand Prix — a moment that went viral when he **broke the ceremonial Delft Blue trophy** while celebrating.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz nears a new one-year Williams deal for 2027, reversing course after rejecting their earlier offer
cards.what_happened: Just a day after reports said Carlos Sainz had **rejected a Williams offer worth roughly €30 million a year**, Spanish outlet Marca now reports he is negotiating exclusively with the team on a **one-year contract extension** running through the end of **2027**. Sources say Williams is willing to make financial concessions and build in an exit clause to secure the shorter deal, and an announcement could land as soon as **this Thursday**, when teams gather for Zandvoort media day ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix. The short-term structure would let Sainz reassess his options again before an anticipated bigger driver-market shuffle in **2028**, when several current contracts expire together. Williams has been hedging regardless, with reports that **Sergio Perez's** camp has opened separate talks with the team about a possible 2027 seat.
key_points: Spanish outlet **Marca** reports Sainz is now negotiating **exclusively with Williams** on a **one-year extension through 2027.**
Just a day earlier, reports said Sainz had **rejected a roughly €30 million offer** from the team, reopening his options.
An announcement is possible **before Thursday's Zandvoort media day**, ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.
The shorter, one-year term would let Sainz **reassess his position** before an expected bigger driver shuffle in 2028.
Williams boss **James Vowles** has separately been holding talks with **Sergio Perez** as a possible alternative if Sainz leaves.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Sainz had reportedly rejected a roughly €30 million Williams offer, reopening speculation about his 2027 future.
thread.changed: Today, reports say Sainz is negotiating exclusively with Williams on a one-year extension, with an announcement possible before Thursday's Zandvoort media day.

depth.background: Carlos Sainz joined **Williams for 2025** after being dropped by Ferrari to make room for Lewis Hamilton, but his first two seasons at the smaller team have been difficult as Williams rebuilds under team principal **James Vowles**. Sainz has repeatedly said he'd use the summer break to calmly weigh his 2027 options, and speculation about a Williams exit — with Audi and other teams floated as alternatives — has run for weeks. F1's driver market is unusually active this year ahead of major **2027 regulation changes**, which has several drivers, including Max Verstappen, negotiating shorter deals to stay flexible.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz reportedly rejects Williams' 30 million euro offer, reopening his 2027 options
cards.what_happened: According to reports from Spanish outlet Marca and multiple F1 outlets, Sainz turned down Williams' latest contract proposal, said to be worth around **30 million euros a season**, because he wants a shorter-term deal that keeps his options open rather than locking in long-term. That has left talks ongoing rather than concluded, with Sainz reportedly considering whether **Red Bull, McLaren or Audi** could offer a more competitive package — with some reports suggesting he may be waiting to see whether Verstappen leaves Red Bull, which would open a seat there. The rejection has immediately revived talk that **Sergio Perez**, who Cadillac's leadership had firmly said would stay for 2027, could yet end up in the Williams conversation again.
key_points: Carlos Sainz has reportedly **rejected** a new Williams contract offer worth roughly **30 million euros per season**.
Sainz reportedly wants a **shorter deal with flexibility** to leave if a stronger seat opens up, rather than a long-term commitment.
Speculation now points to **Red Bull, McLaren or Audi** as possible alternative destinations for Sainz.
Some reports suggest Sainz is **waiting to see where Max Verstappen lands** before committing to his own next move.
The rejection **reopens the door** for Sergio Perez, who had been widely expected to lose out on the Williams seat.

thread.previously: We reported that Carlos Sainz was closing in on a new Williams deal for 2027 — a move that would effectively shut Sergio Perez out of that seat, since Williams was seen as his likeliest landing spot after Cadillac.
thread.changed: That deal has now stalled: multiple reports say Sainz has turned down Williams' latest offer, reportedly worth around 30 million euros a season, because he wants a shorter contract with an exit route rather than a long-term commitment — reopening speculation about Red Bull, McLaren, Audi, and reviving Perez's own hopes of a Williams seat.

depth.background: Sainz left Ferrari for Williams in 2025 and had appeared close to a new multi-year Williams deal for 2027, a move that was widely read as closing off Sergio Perez's main route back into a competitive seat after his exit from Red Bull. With this year's driver market unusually fluid — tied up in Verstappen's own Red Bull exit-clause saga — several drivers have reportedly been holding off on signing extensions until the bigger dominoes fall.
