cards.title: Ralf Schumacher says the Verstappen-Red Bull bond is 'broken' as a McLaren move edges closer
cards.what_happened: Schumacher told media this week that something has 'broken down' between Verstappen and the team, pointing specifically to Verstappen being criticised by senior Red Bull figures at the **Austrian Grand Prix** for not publicly ruling out activating his exit clause while they were present. Separately, sources cited by **GPBlog** say a Verstappen-to-McLaren deal is now in its **closing stages**, with speculation escalating since the British Grand Prix. Dutch media reporting suggests Verstappen could make his decision public at **Zandvoort**, the Dutch Grand Prix that marks his home race and, potentially, the circuit's last appearance on the F1 calendar. Red Bull, meanwhile, has already been reshuffling — hiring Mercedes' junior-programme chief **Gwen Lagrue** to replace long-time advisor Helmut Marko — seen by some as preparation for a driver-market shake-up.
key_points: Ex-F1 driver **Ralf Schumacher** says the relationship between **Verstappen and Red Bull** has genuinely **'broken down'**, not just cooled.
Verstappen was reportedly criticised internally for **refusing to rule out his exit clause** in front of team figures at the Austrian Grand Prix.
Sources tell **GPBlog** a move to **McLaren is close to being announced**, with speculation intensifying since the British Grand Prix.
Dutch media expect Verstappen could confirm his **2027 plans at Zandvoort** this weekend (Aug 21–23) — his home race, and the track's likely **final F1 appearance**.
The saga is now tangled with **Carlos Sainz's** own Williams contract situation (see below), as drivers wait to see where Verstappen lands first.

thread.previously: We reported that Max Verstappen's exit clause from Red Bull had been activated after he entered the summer break outside the championship's top two, but that a move to McLaren carried a catch: McLaren's engine situation could complicate the switch.
thread.changed: The tone has hardened. Former F1 driver Ralf Schumacher now says the trust between Verstappen and Red Bull has genuinely 'broken down' — citing internal criticism of Verstappen for refusing to rule out the clause at the Austrian Grand Prix — and multiple paddock sources say a McLaren deal is now close to being announced, possibly this week at Zandvoort.

depth.background: Verstappen, a four-time world champion, has a contract clause that lets him exit Red Bull if he's outside the championship's top two positions at the summer break — a threshold that was triggered this year. Since then, speculation has built steadily that he could move to McLaren for 2027, with reports pointing to friction inside Red Bull over both his form and his public silence on his own future.

cards.title: Max Verstappen is 'fed up' of repeating himself on F1's 2026 rules, as his future in the sport hangs in the balance
cards.what_happened: Speaking ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort — F1's return from its summer break, and potentially the track's final appearance on the calendar — Verstappen said he was "fed up" of repeating his criticism of the 2026 regulations, telling reporters "at one point, I'm also a little bit just fed up with repeating myself, because it's already hard enough just having to drive it." He described this season's racing as "very artificial," likening the unpredictable, track-dependent handling of the new cars to playing Mario Kart at different difficulty settings. He noted that while many dismissed his early-season complaints as simply him being unhappy on-track, more people in the paddock have since come around to seeing the same issues he flagged months ago. The comments land as his F1 future remains unresolved: Verstappen has yet to win a grand prix in 2026, sits sixth in the drivers' championship, but has taken three podiums in his last four races heading into a Zandvoort weekend where he has won three times before.
key_points: **Max Verstappen** says he's "fed up" of repeatedly criticizing F1's new 2026 regulations ahead of this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix.
He compared the racing under the new rules to "**Mario Kart**" — artificial and inconsistent from track to track.
"It's already hard enough just having to drive it," he said, describing the fatigue of explaining the same complaint over and over.
This comes as his **Red Bull exit clause is now active**, with his long-term future in the sport genuinely uncertain.
Verstappen has yet to win a race in **2026**, though three podiums in his last four starts suggest he's closing in on a first victory.

depth.background: Formula 1 overhauled its technical rules for 2026 with new aerodynamics and a fundamentally different power-unit format that splits engine power roughly 50/50 between a traditional combustion engine and an electric motor. The changes were meant to make the sport greener and closer-fought, but they've also made the cars trickier and, in the view of several drivers including four-time champion Verstappen, less satisfying to drive and less consistent from circuit to circuit. Verstappen has criticized these regulations publicly and repeatedly since the season began, arguing the racing product itself has suffered. Separately, his contract situation at Red Bull has become genuinely uncertain this year: an exit clause in his deal is now active, and he has reportedly turned down both a longer-term contract extension and a buyout offer from the team, while rival teams like McLaren and Mercedes are reported to be circling.

cards.title: Verstappen's active Red Bull exit clause draws a warning: McLaren's engine situation could be the catch
cards.what_happened: In an F1 driver-market roundup published yesterday, former Haas F1 team principal Guenther Haas warned that if Verstappen moves to McLaren for 2027, the team's **power-unit status** would be the biggest pitfall — McLaren currently uses a customer engine rather than building its own, which could leave Verstappen at a technical disadvantage compared to manufacturer teams like Mercedes or Ferrari under the new rules. The same roundup noted that F1's official seat-confirmation tracker shows **both Mercedes seats** for 2027 remain unconfirmed, keeping alive the possibility that Verstappen could instead partner (or replace) a Mercedes driver — the team widely seen as his other most plausible destination given its current championship form. Separately, Audi's rising junior driver Gabriel Bortoleto issued a statement confirming his contract status for the coming years, which the roundup said effectively ends speculation that linked Carlos Sainz to an Audi seat; Sainz instead remains on course for a move to Williams.
key_points: Former F1 team boss **Guenther Haas** (Haas F1 founder) warned Verstappen that a move to **McLaren** carries a specific risk: the team's **power-unit status**.
McLaren currently doesn't build its own engine and relies on an outside supplier — a factor that matters hugely under F1's new 2026 power-unit rules.
F1's own official update says **both Mercedes seats** for 2027 are still not 100% confirmed — keeping Mercedes alive as Verstappen's other likely option.
Separately, Audi ended its own share of the transfer-market noise: junior star **Gabriel Bortoleto** confirmed he's staying, quashing rumors that **Carlos Sainz** could join Audi instead of Williams.

thread.previously: We reported that the exit clause in Max Verstappen's Red Bull contract had become active, opening the door for him to leave, with McLaren reportedly circling as a landing spot for 2027.
thread.changed: A former F1 team boss has now publicly flagged the specific downside of a McLaren move — the team's power-unit arrangement — while a separate F1 update shows both Mercedes seats are also still not fully confirmed for 2027, keeping Verstappen's options genuinely open.

depth.background: Max Verstappen's contract situation has been F1's biggest storyline of the 2026 driver market. An exit clause in his Red Bull deal became active this year, and reports say he has turned down both a new long-term extension and a buyout offer from the team, leaving his future genuinely open as rival teams circle. McLaren, the reigning constructors' champion, and Mercedes — the team currently leading the 2026 drivers' championship through Kimi Antonelli — are seen as his two most realistic destinations if he leaves Red Bull. Under F1's new-for-2026 power-unit rules, the engine (which now splits power roughly 50/50 between combustion and electric) is a much bigger differentiator between teams than before, making a driver's choice of engine supplier more consequential than in past eras.

cards.title: McLaren's Stella cautions against calling Hungary win a 'turning point' as team heads to Zandvoort
cards.what_happened: Speaking as the team heads into the Dutch Grand Prix at **Zandvoort**, Stella pushed back on the 'turning point' framing of Norris's Hungary win, saying: **'It's far too early to say whether this is a turning point for McLaren or not. We just look at the facts.'** He pointed out that **other top teams have also been successfully introducing their own upgrades** this season, meaning McLaren's Hungary form could just as easily reflect a one-off convergence of car, track, and conditions rather than a genuine step forward. The comments follow McLaren's Hungarian GP breakthrough, where Norris converted pole into a commanding win — his first repeat win at a circuit and his first race with the number 1 on the car.
key_points: McLaren boss **Andrea Stella** says it's **'far too early'** to call Lando Norris's Hungarian GP pole-and-win a turning point.
Norris's Budapest victory was McLaren's **first pole and win of the 2026 season**, and his 12th career win.
Stella noted **rival teams are also introducing upgrades**, so a single strong weekend doesn't guarantee a trend.
The comments come as F1 returns from its summer break for the **Dutch GP at Zandvoort**, a Sprint-format weekend.
McLaren had earlier admitted its 2026 car was **too short** by design, with no full fix expected until 2027.

depth.background: McLaren enters the second half of the 2026 season having struggled with a car concept team principal **Andrea Stella** has admitted is fundamentally limited — reportedly too short in wheelbase — with a proper redesign not arriving until 2027. Against that backdrop, Norris's dominant win at the Hungarian Grand Prix, McLaren's first pole and victory of the year, was seen by many as a potential sign the team had turned a corner with in-season upgrades.

cards.title: Red Bull poaches Mercedes' junior-programme chief Gwen Lagrue to replace Helmut Marko
cards.what_happened: Mercedes confirmed the departure of **Gwen Lagrue**, who had run its junior driver academy for 11 years, rebuilding it after a period of decline into a pipeline that produced Grand Prix winners **George Russell** and **Esteban Ocon**, and identified **Kimi Antonelli** — this season's championship leader — as a young karting talent well before he reached Formula 1. Red Bull has now appointed Lagrue as Director of its Junior Programme starting in **2027**, filling the void left by **Helmut Marko's** exit at the end of 2025. The move was confirmed as F1 returns from its summer break.
key_points: **Gwen Lagrue** is leaving Mercedes after an **11-year spell** running its junior driver academy.
Red Bull has hired him to lead its **Junior Programme from 2027**, effectively replacing **Helmut Marko**, who left at the end of 2025.
Lagrue rebuilt Mercedes' pipeline into one of the strongest in motorsport, discovering and developing **George Russell, Esteban Ocon, and Kimi Antonelli**.
He reportedly spotted Antonelli as a **karting prodigy** long before Antonelli reached F1 and became this season's title leader.
The move hands Red Bull's famously demanding young-driver system to the man who built Mercedes' rival version of it.

depth.background: F1 junior programmes are how teams identify, fund, and fast-track young karting and junior-formula talent toward a race seat — done well, they're a competitive advantage that outlasts any single driver. **Helmut Marko** built Red Bull's programme into the sport's most feared and most productive, producing multiple world champions but also known for its ruthless, high-pressure approach to cutting drivers who don't perform. Marko stepped away at the end of 2025, leaving the programme without its longtime leader during a pivotal period for Red Bull's driver pipeline.

cards.title: Nico Hulkenberg nears a two-year Audi extension, closing off one of Carlos Sainz's remaining options
cards.what_happened: According to F1 journalist Marc Limacher, Hulkenberg is closing in on a **two-year extension with Audi**, a deal that would keep him with the German manufacturer beyond his current contract, which expires at the end of 2026. Audi is said to be prioritising **project continuity** over chasing a bigger name, valuing Hulkenberg's race pace and the quality of his technical feedback during this critical phase of the team's development. Hulkenberg has said he is happy to stay **'as long as I'm having fun, the stopwatch is accurate, and the team wants me.'** The move comes just as reports emerged that **Carlos Sainz** — who had also been linked to Audi — is instead nearing a **Williams deal for 2027**.
key_points: **Nico Hulkenberg**, 37, is in advanced talks for a **two-year contract extension** with Audi.
His current deal runs out at the **end of 2026**.
Audi is reportedly prioritising **continuity over a headline signing** during a critical development phase.
The extension would effectively close the door on **Carlos Sainz** joining Audi, days after Sainz was reported nearing a Williams move instead.
Hulkenberg has praised the quality of his technical feedback role in Audi's build-up as a **full works team**.

depth.background: **Audi** entered Formula 1 as a full manufacturer team in 2026, taking over what was previously the Sauber operation, and has been building its own engine and car programme from the ground up — a project where experienced technical feedback matters as much as outright pace. **Nico Hulkenberg** is one of the grid's most experienced drivers, valued for his ability to help develop a car through technical feedback during exactly this kind of early-stage manufacturer buildup.

cards.title: Ollie Bearman turns down an Aston Martin approach, commits to staying in the Ferrari driver programme through 2028
cards.what_happened: According to reporting from F1 journalist Marc Limacher, **Bearman turned down a significant offer from Aston Martin** and instead chose to extend his commitment to the **Ferrari Driver Academy through 2028**, continuing to race for Haas in 2027. Bearman confirmed his stance directly, saying: **'I'm very much committed to what Ferrari have offered me, and they have supported me since the very beginning, since I joined F3, and I'm only sitting here thanks to them.'** The decision takes one of the market's most sought-after young drivers off the table for rival teams.
key_points: **Ollie Bearman** has rejected a offer from Aston Martin, choosing to extend his **Ferrari Driver Academy** deal through 2028.
He will continue racing for **Haas** in 2027 under the extended arrangement.
Bearman said he remains **'very much committed'** to Ferrari, crediting them for his rise since his F3 days.
The decision removes Bearman as an option in F1's crowded 2027 **'silly season'** driver market.
It comes as fellow young driver moves — Sainz to Williams, Verstappen's Red Bull future — keep the market unsettled.

depth.background: **Ollie Bearman** is a young British driver who rose through Ferrari's junior driver programme and made his F1 debut as a late substitute in 2024 before securing a full-time seat with **Haas**, a team that effectively runs as a Ferrari customer outfit with Ferrari engines and close technical ties. With **eight of F1's 22 seats still unfilled for 2027**, teams up and down the grid — including Aston Martin — have been chasing rising young talent, making this year's driver market unusually fluid.

cards.title: F1 returns from its summer break at Zandvoort for what may be the last Dutch Grand Prix — and a shot at history for Verstappen
cards.what_happened: Formula 1 resumes racing this weekend (**August 21-23**) at Zandvoort after nearly a month off for the summer break, and reports indicate this will be the **final Dutch Grand Prix** on the calendar for the foreseeable future, as the event hasn't been renewed beyond 2026. For Verstappen, who has won at his home track three times since it returned, this is a farewell weekend with real stakes: a fourth win would let him **match Jim Clark's record** of home-race wins and would also be his **first win of the entire 2026 season**, after a year in which title leader Antonelli has built a 50-point championship lead over Lewis Hamilton. Verstappen has already unveiled a special helmet design for the occasion, and Red Bull drivers will wear special race suits. It's a **sprint-format weekend**, and weather forecasts suggest a real possibility of F1's first properly wet race since the 2026 generation of cars was introduced.
key_points: The Dutch Grand Prix **will not be renewed** on the F1 calendar after this year, making this the event's likely farewell.
Home hero **Max Verstappen** has won at Zandvoort three times and has a shot at a 4th win to match **Jim Clark's record**.
It would also be Verstappen's **first win of the 2026 season** if it happens.
It's a **sprint weekend**: a single practice session Friday, then sprint qualifying, sprint race and full qualifying on Saturday.
Forecasts suggest a real chance of F1's **first genuinely wet race** since the 2026 cars were introduced.

depth.background: The **Dutch Grand Prix** returned to F1's calendar in 2021 after a 35-year absence, driven largely by Verstappen's rise and the huge 'Orange Army' of Dutch fans who fill Zandvoort's dunes every year. F1 rotates and refreshes its calendar regularly to fit in new markets (like recent additions in the Middle East and Americas), which sometimes means older European races lose their slot even when they're popular with fans. Verstappen has dominated at his home track since the race's return, but has struggled for outright wins in the **2026 season** under new technical regulations, while Mercedes' **Kimi Antonelli** has built a big championship lead.

cards.title: Carlos Sainz nears a new Williams deal for 2027, effectively shutting Sergio Perez out of the seat
cards.what_happened: According to Spanish outlet **Marca** and multiple F1 outlets, Sainz and his management have used the summer break to focus exclusively on a **new one-year Williams contract** for 2027, after weighing other options and speaking extensively with team principal **James Vowles**. Williams reportedly wants the deal locked in before this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix and is prepared to increase Sainz's pay beyond his current **€13 million** salary to secure him. Sainz's side is also said to be pushing for an **exit clause** in the contract — a mechanism that would let him leave early if a better seat opens up, mirroring the clause that just triggered Max Verstappen's own Red Bull exit drama. With Sainz set to stay, **Sergio Perez's** management-led talks with Williams — explored as a contingency — now look set to go nowhere, even as Cadillac insists publicly that Perez isn't going anywhere.
key_points: Sainz is reportedly in the **final stages** of a new one-year contract with Williams for 2027.
Williams is said to be willing to raise his wage **above his current €13 million** to lock him in.
Sainz's camp reportedly wants an **exit clause**, similar to the one that triggered Max Verstappen's own market shake-up this year.
A deal is expected to be **announced before the Dutch Grand Prix** this weekend at Zandvoort.
Sergio Perez's management had opened **talks with Williams as a backup**, but that door is now closing.

depth.background: F1's driver market ('silly season') runs on a strict calendar most fans never see: contracts for the following year are usually settled by **late summer**, well before the season that they cover even starts, because teams need certainty to plan around sponsors, junior drivers and seat swaps. Carlos Sainz joined **Williams in 2025** after losing his Ferrari seat to Lewis Hamilton, and has spent the year weighing whether to stay or chase a return to a front-running team. Sergio 'Checo' Perez, meanwhile, moved to the new **Cadillac** team but has faced persistent rumors linking him elsewhere, including to Williams if Sainz departed.

cards.title: Toto Wolff backs F1's V8 return as a 'purist' — but says the FIA's timeline is unrealistic
cards.what_happened: In an interview, Mercedes team principal **Toto Wolff** said he supports the idea of F1 returning to **V8 engines** in a future rules cycle, calling it 'the best consensus' and adding 'as a purist, I like it.' He said his preferred version would be a naturally aspirated V8 paired with some form of **energy-recovery system** — a lighter version of the hybrid technology used today — and built to run on **sustainable fuel**, rather than a straightforward throwback engine. However, Wolff pushed back on FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's push for a **2029** introduction, calling that timeline unrealistic: 'Most manufacturers don't want to pay for a double program. A new engine in two years would cause costs to explode,' since teams would effectively have to develop two engines — today's and the new one — simultaneously.
key_points: Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** says he supports F1 bringing back **naturally aspirated V8 engines**
FIA president **Mohammed Ben Sulayem** wants the switch as early as **2029**, ending the turbo-hybrid era that began in **2014**
Wolff calls that timeline **unrealistic**, warning a new engine in two years would make costs 'explode'
He wants the V8 paired with an **energy-recovery system** and **sustainable fuel**, not a pure retro engine
Most manufacturers reportedly don't want to fund **two engine programmes at once**

depth.background: Formula 1 has used complex, expensive **turbo-hybrid V6 engines** since 2014 — powerful and efficient, but criticised by some fans and insiders for sounding quieter and being harder (and pricier) to build than the raw V8s and V10s of earlier eras. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been pushing to bring back a simpler, louder V8 for F1's next big engine cycle, aiming for as soon as **2029 or 2030/31**. Manufacturers like Mercedes, Ferrari, Honda and Audi have poured billions into today's hybrid engines and would need to plan and fund whatever comes next years in advance.

cards.title: Fernando Alonso says his Aston Martin future comes down to the 2027 rules, not this year's car
cards.what_happened: Fernando Alonso confirmed he will decide on his Formula 1 future — whether to continue with Aston Martin, or retire — sometime between the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort (August 21-23)** and the **Italian Grand Prix at Monza** the following week. Alonso has stressed that any upgrades or performance improvements to Aston Martin's current car will **not** be what determines his decision; instead, he says it hinges on F1's incoming **2027 technical regulations** and whether he believes the team can be competitive under them. He is in the final year of his current Aston Martin deal. Team principal Adrian Newey has publicly said he remains confident Alonso will stay, describing their working relationship as strong. Alonso has separately shut down rumours linking him to other teams throughout the year.
key_points: **Alonso**, in the final year of his Aston Martin contract, will decide his future between **Zandvoort and Monza**
He says the call is about F1's **new 2027 regulations**, not how competitive Aston Martin's current car is
Aston Martin boss **Adrian Newey** says he's confident of keeping the two-time world champion
Alonso has repeatedly ruled out speculation linking him to rival teams
He still wants to win a **third world title** — this one with Aston Martin

depth.background: **Fernando Alonso**, a two-time world champion now in his 40s, joined Aston Martin in 2023 partly on the promise that the team — bankrolled by billionaire owner Lawrence Stroll and headed technically by star designer **Adrian Newey** — would become a genuine title contender under F1's next big rules reset in **2027**. Aston Martin has struggled to match that ambition on-track through 2026, fueling periodic rumours linking Alonso elsewhere, all of which he has denied. F1's driver market always heats up around the summer break, when contracts for the following year are typically finalised.

cards.title: Ferrari rushes an all-new chassis to Zandvoort as Hamilton's late title bid heats up
cards.what_happened: Ferrari confirmed it will introduce an all-new chassis for Hamilton at the **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort (August 21-23)**, marking F1's return from its summer break. The new part is a direct evolution of the floor platform Ferrari debuted at the Barcelona race in June, fast-tracked after the team reviewed performance data from the Silverstone weekend. Engineers say the specific goal is to generate **more downforce** from the car's underbody, which should translate into extra cornering grip. The team is holding back its next **power-unit upgrade** — allowed under the FIA's ADUO engine-development rules — for Ferrari's home race at **Monza** (the Italian Grand Prix) rather than debuting it at Zandvoort. Hamilton currently trails Antonelli by **50 points** in the standings as the title fight resumes.
key_points: Ferrari brings an **'all-new chassis'** for Hamilton at the Dutch GP
It's an evolution of the floor first introduced at **Barcelona in June**
Goal: squeeze more **downforce** from the car's body and floor
Hamilton trails championship leader Antonelli by **50 points**
Ferrari saves its next **power-unit upgrade** for Monza, not Zandvoort

depth.background: **Ferrari** enters the second half of the 2026 season chasing Mercedes' **Kimi Antonelli**, an 19-year-old Italian who leads the drivers' championship, and rival **Lewis Hamilton**'s own teammate Charles Leclerc, currently fourth in the standings. Hamilton, in his second season at Ferrari after leaving Mercedes, won at the **Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix** in June, his first victory in red, reviving his title hopes. F1 teams are allowed to keep developing their cars through the season, and floor/chassis upgrades are one of the biggest ways to find extra grip and speed without a full redesign.

cards.title: Ex-F1 steward Johnny Herbert reveals 'Death to Herbert' abuse from Verstappen fans over Hamilton-bias claims
cards.what_happened: In new comments published on **August 16, 2026**, Herbert revealed that the single worst abuse he has ever received on social media came from Verstappen's fanbase, who accused him of favouring Lewis Hamilton whenever he criticised the Red Bull driver on air. He said some messages went as far as reading '**Death to Herbert**,' which he described as the low point of the online reaction. Herbert pointed to his role in the 2024 Mexican Grand Prix penalty decision as the moment the hostility intensified, noting the awkwardness of simultaneously working as a steward handing out penalties and as a pundit publicly discussing them. He pushed back directly on the bias accusation in the interview, standing by his commentary as independent analysis rather than favouritism.
key_points: Herbert says the **worst online abuse** he's received came from Verstappen fans
Messages included death threats reading '**Death to Herbert**'
Fans accuse him of being **biased toward Lewis Hamilton**
Backlash traces to a **20-second penalty** he gave Verstappen at the 2024 Mexican GP
Herbert was axed as an **FIA steward** in Jan 2025 over media conflicts, not this row

depth.background: **Johnny Herbert** is a former F1 driver who went on to become a TV pundit and, until January 2025, an **FIA steward** — one of the officials who rule on driving penalties during race weekends. Late in 2024, Herbert was part of the stewards' panel that handed Red Bull's **Max Verstappen** a 20-second penalty for an aggressive move on McLaren's Lando Norris at the Mexican Grand Prix, a decision Verstappen and his father publicly criticised. Herbert was later removed as a steward — officially because the FIA judged his paid media punditry, including work tied to a betting company, incompatible with the steward role. He has continued as a prominent F1 broadcaster and commentator since.

cards.title: Verstappen reportedly rejects Red Bull's 5-year offer, wants a 1-year 'prove it' deal instead
cards.what_happened: According to reports, Red Bull has put a **five-year contract offer** on the table for Verstappen, running through 2033. Verstappen, however, is said to want something shorter: a **one-year deal** that would let him evaluate whether Red Bull can actually deliver a competitive car under the new 2027 regulations before committing to anything longer-term — effectively a 'prove it' clause rather than a long-term commitment. Separately, Christian Horner's own bid to return to F1, reportedly with Alpine, is approaching a key veto deadline in September, adding pressure to an already chaotic Red Bull storyline. The team has struggled in 2026 following the departures of Horner and several other senior figures.
key_points: Red Bull has offered Verstappen a **five-year contract** through 2033, according to reports.
Verstappen instead reportedly wants a **one-year deal** to test whether Red Bull can build him a **competitive 2027 car** before committing longer.
His performance-based **exit clause is active** from August to October, after he fell outside the top two in the standings at the summer break.
**Christian Horner's** own hoped-for F1 return is approaching a **September veto deadline** at Alpine — adding another layer to Red Bull's turbulent year.
Red Bull has lost a string of senior figures in 2026, including **Horner, Adrian Newey, Helmut Marko, Rob Marshall and Jonathan Wheatley**.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported that Verstappen's Red Bull contract has a performance clause letting him explore other teams since he was 6th in the standings — about 110 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli — at the summer break, that the clause runs August to October, that he hadn't announced any decision to leave, and that only 8 of 2027's grid seats were fully confirmed.
thread.changed: New reporting now details the actual negotiation: Red Bull has offered a 5-year deal through 2033, but Verstappen reportedly wants just a 1-year contract to test the team's competitiveness first — while Christian Horner's own return to F1 is separately approaching a September deadline.

depth.background: Max Verstappen's Red Bull contract contains a performance clause that lets him explore other teams if he's outside the top two in the drivers' championship at the summer break — a threshold he crossed after sitting 6th, well off the pace, making him effectively a free agent for a window running from August to October. He hasn't announced any decision to leave or retire, but he's now widely seen as **F1's biggest 2027 storyline**, with McLaren repeatedly linked as a possible destination. The backdrop is a Red Bull team in upheaval: former team boss Christian Horner and several other senior figures — technical guru Adrian Newey, advisor Helmut Marko, and engineers Rob Marshall and Jonathan Wheatley — have all left the team during 2026.

cards.title: Mercedes says grid penalties are now 'almost inevitable' for both Antonelli and Russell — and Monza looks like the place to take the hit
cards.what_happened: Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord told media it is **'almost inevitable'** that both Kimi Antonelli, who leads the drivers' championship, and George Russell, currently P3, will take grid penalties before the season ends. His exact words: 'Looking at how many components we've used in the first half of the season, it's almost inevitable that at some point there will be penalties to take... it's realistically going to be hard to get to the end of the season on the existing hardware.' Team principal Toto Wolff has gone further, openly discussing where — not if — Mercedes takes the hit: 'Monza can be very special for Kimi, but on paper it looks like it's a good place to take an engine penalty, so I need to speak to Marco [Antonelli's father] on whether we want to take it there,' he said, half-joking that 'we'll take the pressure off in Monza by starting him from the back!' Monza's long straights make overtaking easier than at tracks like Zandvoort or Baku, making it the team's preferred venue to absorb a penalty.
key_points: Mercedes deputy team boss Bradley Lord says penalties for **both title contenders** are **'almost inevitable'** before season's end.
Kimi Antonelli is already on his **4th engine and exhaust**; George Russell on his **3rd set** — one more change triggers an automatic grid drop.
Team boss Toto Wolff is weighing taking the hit at **Monza** (Sept 4-6), where long straights make overtaking easiest.
Mercedes leads the **constructors' championship by 72 points**; Antonelli leads the drivers' standings by **50 points**.
The timing decision could hand track position — and a title-fight opening — to **Ferrari's Hamilton** or Red Bull's Verstappen.

depth.background: Formula 1's power-unit rules cap how many engine components (the ICE, exhaust, energy store, control electronics, among others) each driver can use per season — typically four — before further changes trigger an automatic grid-position penalty. Antonelli has already needed a 4th ICE and exhaust after reliability failures this year (a battery issue in Spain, an engine swap at Belgium), and Russell is on his 3rd set after a water leak forced an engine change in Hungary qualifying and a battery failure in Canada earlier in the season.

cards.title: Honda says its upgraded Aston Martin engine has hit its targets, arriving at Zandvoort as the second half of the team's revival plan
cards.what_happened: Honda has detailed the technical content of a new-specification engine for Aston Martin — sometimes called 'spec-2' — confirming it will debut at the **Dutch Grand Prix, August 21-23**, the first race back from F1's summer break. Honda's GM of Trackside Engineering, Shintaro Orihara, confirmed the engine has hit Honda's internal performance targets but declined to confirm exact horsepower figures, which media estimates put anywhere from **30 to 50 additional horsepower**. The changes include a redesigned combustion pre-chamber for a faster burn, a reshaped piston head for better combustion, and revised internal lubrication to reduce parasitic friction losses. This lands as the second half of a planned Aston Martin revival: the team already introduced a major aerodynamic 'B-spec' chassis at the Hungarian Grand Prix before the break, which immediately helped Alonso and Stroll compete in the midfield instead of running at the back.
key_points: Honda confirms a new-spec engine for Aston Martin has hit its **internal performance targets**, debuting at the **Dutch GP (Aug 21-23)**.
The upgrade redesigns the **combustion pre-chamber, piston shape, and internal lubrication** to cut friction and burn fuel faster.
Estimates of the power gain range from **30 to 50 horsepower**, though Honda won't confirm the exact figure.
Aston Martin's power unit has reportedly been down **over 100bhp** on rivals at points this season.
It follows a chassis 'B-spec' introduced at the **Hungarian GP** that already helped Alonso and Stroll fight in the midfield.

depth.background: Honda's 2026 return to F1 as Aston Martin's works engine partner has been rocky — the power unit has struggled with both performance and reliability, traced partly to Honda reassigning many of its F1 specialists to other projects ahead of the 2026 rules reset. Aston Martin, with an Adrian Newey-designed car and one of the grid's biggest budgets, has been arguably the season's most disappointing team relative to its ambitions, though a new aerodynamic package introduced at the Hungarian GP before the summer break already helped Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll compete with Williams and Haas rather than running last.

cards.title: Verstappen turned down an €8 million Red Bull buyout of his exit clause, deepening the McLaren speculation
cards.what_happened: Red Bull's leadership formally proposed **buying out Verstappen's exit clause for €8 million**, an offer that would have locked him into the team through **2028** and shut down the growing speculation about a move. Verstappen's management **declined the offer**. He currently sits **sixth in the championship, roughly 110 points behind leader Kimi Antonelli**, a gap that has fueled talk he's ready to leave a team he no longer sees as capable of winning. Multiple reports say **McLaren and Verstappen's camp are in advanced, closing-stage negotiations** for a switch, even though McLaren CEO Zak Brown has publicly waved off the rumors. Verstappen has until **October** to formally tell Red Bull whether he's activating the clause and leaving after this season; his manager has separately said Max would like to fulfill his existing contract through 2028 if things improve.
key_points: Red Bull's leadership offered Max **Verstappen €8 million** to buy out the exit clause in his contract — he **declined**.
The offer would have tied Verstappen to Red Bull through **2028**, removing his ability to leave at the end of this season.
His **exit clause activated** after he went into the summer break outside the championship's top two.
Verstappen must formally notify Red Bull by **October** if he intends to leave at season's end.
**McLaren** is reported by multiple paddock sources to be in the closing stages of talks to sign him, despite team boss Zak Brown publicly downplaying it.

thread.previously: Verstappen's performance-linked exit clause became active after he fell outside the championship's top two at the summer break, and McLaren was reported to be circling for a possible signing.
thread.changed: Red Bull has now made a concrete move to keep him — offering €8 million to buy out the clause and tie him to the team through 2028 — and Verstappen's camp has turned it down.

depth.background: F1 driver contracts increasingly include **performance-linked exit clauses** — provisions that let a driver leave early if the team underperforms, protecting top talent from being stuck in an uncompetitive car. Verstappen, a multiple world champion, has driven for Red Bull his entire top-flight career, but the team has struggled with **car development and consistency this season**, and his clause was written to trigger if he fell outside the championship's top two positions by the summer break. That threshold was crossed, activating his right to explore an exit.

prev_ref.title: Christian Horner's best shot at an F1 return hinges on a September veto deadline at Alpine

cards.title: Renault's CEO shuts down talk of Christian Horner joining an Alpine takeover bid
cards.what_happened: Renault Group CEO **François Provost** directly rebutted the Horner-Alpine connection, telling reporters **'there is no discussion today with Christian. We are assessing the options. I want the Renault Group to retain control of our team, regardless of who succeeds Otro.'** This followed earlier reports that Mercedes, another prospective buyer of the Otro stake, had **pulled out of talks** over valuation concerns, which had removed one obstacle some saw as standing between Horner and a deal. Despite Provost's public denial, other reports say Renault is prepared to **formally exercise its veto** specifically to block any Horner-linked consortium from acquiring the stake before September, when that veto power lapses.
key_points: Renault CEO **François Provost** said there is **'no discussion today with Christian [Horner]'** about Alpine.
Renault holds a **veto right** over the sale of Otro Capital's 24% Alpine stake — but that veto **expires in September**.
Provost said Renault wants to **retain control** of the Alpine team 'regardless of who succeeds Otro.'
Reports say Renault is prepared to actively use its veto to **block any Horner-linked buyer** before the deadline.
After September, Otro would be free to sell its stake to **any bidder**, veto-free, reopening the door for Horner.

thread.previously: Christian Horner's best shot at returning to F1 was said to hinge on Renault's veto power over Alpine's ownership expiring in September, after which Otro Capital could sell its stake freely.
thread.changed: Renault's CEO has now publicly denied any current talks with Horner and reports say Renault is prepared to actively use its veto to block a Horner-linked bid before that September deadline.

depth.background: Christian Horner, who led Red Bull's F1 team for nearly two decades before departing, has been searching for a way back into the sport as a **team owner or leader**, and has been linked to a consortium interested in buying a stake in Alpine (formerly Renault's factory F1 team). **Otro Capital** owns a 24% stake in Alpine and has been exploring a sale, but **Renault, as Alpine's parent company, holds veto power** over any change of ownership until a set deadline in September — after which Otro can sell to the highest bidder without Renault's approval.

cards.title: Formula 1's teenage title leader goes undercover at a German karting event — and wins
cards.what_happened: Antonelli entered a karting event in Germany under the alias 'Franz Antonelli' — a play on Verstappen's own pseudonym — reportedly outpacing other competitors at the session despite trying to stay under the radar. The appearance came in the closing days of F1's summer break, just before the grid reconvenes for the Dutch Grand Prix weekend at Zandvoort on August 21–23, where Antonelli will defend a 50-point lead over second-placed Lewis Hamilton and a 59-point lead over his own teammate George Russell.
key_points: Mercedes' **Kimi Antonelli**, F1's **19-year-old championship leader**, raced go-karts in Germany under the alias 'Franz Antonelli.'
The fake name is a **direct nod to Max Verstappen**, who used 'Franz Hermann' to race incognito in 2025.
Antonelli reportedly **smashed rival competitors' lap times** despite the disguise.
He heads into next week's **Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort** holding a **50-point championship lead** over Lewis Hamilton.
The stunt keeps alive an unofficial F1 tradition of stars **racing incognito** between race weekends.

depth.background: Kimi Antonelli was promoted to Mercedes' race seat and has become the sport's breakout story in 2026, becoming the youngest points leader in F1 history at just 19. The 'racing incognito' tradition traces back to Max Verstappen, who first used the pseudonym 'Franz Hermann' in May 2025 to enter karting events without drawing a crowd. Formula 1 is on its summer break before resuming at Zandvoort for the Dutch Grand Prix — confirmed as the venue's final scheduled appearance on the calendar after five years back on the F1 schedule, and the first time the race will run as a Sprint weekend.

cards.title: Red Bull fends off Cadillac's approach for chief engineer Paul Monaghan with a counteroffer
cards.what_happened: Reports suggested Paul Monaghan was on the verge of leaving Red Bull for **Cadillac**, F1's newest team, as it builds out its technical department ahead of a fuller 2027 push. Red Bull responded with a **counteroffer** substantial enough to persuade the **58-year-old** to stay, according to paddock reporting, and he was back working in the Red Bull garage at the **Hungarian Grand Prix** in Budapest. The near-miss underscores how aggressively Cadillac has been recruiting experienced engineering and technical staff from rival teams as it tries to compress years of institutional knowledge into a much shorter build-up.
key_points: Red Bull has reportedly kept veteran chief engineer **Paul Monaghan** from leaving for **Cadillac** by matching or beating its offer.
Monaghan, nicknamed **'Pedals'** in the paddock, has spent years in senior Red Bull technical roles and was back in the garage at the **Hungarian Grand Prix**.
Cadillac, F1's newest team, has been aggressively **poaching experienced engineering talent** from established outfits as it builds its operation from scratch.
The episode is part of a wider pattern this season of new and expanding teams raiding rivals' technical staff, not just their drivers.

depth.background: When a new Formula 1 team joins the grid — as Cadillac did this season — it typically has no existing engineering department, so it has to build one almost entirely by hiring away experienced staff from established rivals, often at a significant pay premium. This kind of quiet personnel story rarely gets headlines the way driver transfers do, but senior race and design engineers can matter just as much to a car's competitiveness. Paul Monaghan has spent years in senior technical roles at Red Bull, one of the grid's most successful teams, giving him exactly the pedigree a new team like Cadillac would want.

cards.title: F1's 2027 driver market blows wide open: only 8 of 22 seats are filled
cards.what_happened: An official F1 update confirmed that just **8 of the 22 seats** on the 2027 grid are currently filled, leaving **14 seats** open with the season not even past its summer-break halfway point. The update reaffirmed Max Verstappen's status: his Red Bull exit clause is active, and he's reportedly been warned by people close to the sport about the downsides of a move to McLaren, where seat politics and an already title-winning lineup could complicate his fit. Elsewhere, Audi's driver picture firmed up slightly — Gabriel Bortoleto's camp shut down speculation about an exit, saying his contract has **'no clauses,'** while veteran Nico Hülkenberg is expected to continue alongside him. Meanwhile Carlos Sainz's future at Williams and several other seats, including at teams still finalising 2027 plans, remain unresolved.
key_points: F1 has officially confirmed only **8 of the 22 seats** on the 2027 grid are locked in, with **14 seats** still undecided.
**Max Verstappen's** exit clause in his Red Bull contract is now active, and he's been publicly **warned about the downsides** of a rumoured move to McLaren.
**Audi** has moved to shore up its lineup, with Gabriel Bortoleto's camp shutting down exit talk and Nico Hülkenberg expected to partner him.
The uncertainty spans midfield and top teams alike, with **Carlos Sainz's** Williams future among several other seats still unresolved.
2026's 'silly season' is unusually wide open because so many contracts were written to expire together at the end of this year.

depth.background: Formula 1 driver contracts typically run one to three years, and a cluster of them were signed to expire at the end of **2026** — meaning an unusually large share of the 22-driver grid is up for renegotiation at once heading into 2027. Complicating things further, F1's new technical regulations take effect in 2027, prompting teams to rethink which drivers best suit the new cars before locking in long-term deals. Max Verstappen, a four-time champion, has an **exit clause** in his Red Bull contract tied to team performance that has now become active, making him the single biggest variable in the market and drawing interest from rivals including McLaren.

cards.what_happened: Verstappen went into F1's summer break sitting **6th** in the drivers' championship, well outside the top two — the threshold that activates an exit clause in his Red Bull contract, giving him a window from **August to October** to explore a move elsewhere. F1 says only **8 of the grid's drivers** are '100% confirmed' for 2027, leaving **14 seats** still open across the field.

thread.previously: We reported that Max Verstappen was expected to confirm he was staying at Red Bull through 2028 around the Dutch Grand Prix.
