cards.title: Sri Lanka names uncapped duo Mishara and Arachchige to plug its injury-hit batting for the Colombo Test
cards.what_happened: Sri Lanka Cricket announced its squad for the second Test against India, confirming **Kamil Mishara** and **Sahan Arachchige** — both uncapped at Test level — as direct replacements for the injured senior batters, alongside a squad that includes **four fast bowlers**. The selection confirms Sri Lanka will go into the Colombo Test with a batting order stripped of experience: no Mendis, no Chandimal, no Nissanka. Head coach Gary Kirsten's side will lean on the uncapped duo's recent domestic form as India, already 1-0 up after the Galle Test, look to close out the series.
key_points: Sri Lanka named its squad for the **2nd Test vs India** in Colombo, drafting in **uncapped batters Kamil Mishara and Sahan Arachchige**.
Both were picked on the back of **strong recent domestic form**, the stated reason for their inclusion.
The squad carries **four pacers**, a notably pace-heavy attack for a subcontinental Test.
The changes follow the injury exodus reported after Galle: **Kusal Mendis** (hamstring), **Dinesh Chandimal** (concussion protocol) and **Pathum Nissanka** (wrist recovery) are all unavailable.
Sri Lanka trails the two-Test series **1-0** after a **165-run defeat** in Galle, and now fields a batting order with almost no senior experience against India's in-form attack.
cards.moot: A team's real depth is only revealed when its first-choice players are unavailable all at once — how the replacements perform under that pressure tells you more about a system than any result with a full-strength side.

thread.previously: We reported that Sri Lanka would head into the second Test against India missing three senior batters — Kusal Mendis (hamstring), Dinesh Chandimal (concussion protocol) and likely Pathum Nissanka (wrist recovery) — and flagged the team announcement as the thing to watch for.
thread.changed: Sri Lanka has now named its actual replacement squad: uncapped batters Kamil Mishara and Sahan Arachchige have been drafted in, with the squad also carrying four pacers, resolving who steps into the vacated batting slots.

depth.background: India beat Sri Lanka by **165 runs** in the first Test in Galle, and Sri Lanka's top order — already thin on depth — lost three senior batters to injury in the space of a week: Mendis to a hamstring picked up in the **Lanka Premier League**, Chandimal to a first-Test concussion that triggers a mandatory **7-day stand-down**, and Nissanka to a lingering wrist injury. Coach **Gary Kirsten** has been trying to rebuild Sri Lanka's Test depth, and this squad announcement is the team's answer to that injury crisis ahead of the second Test starting **August 23** at Colombo's SSC ground.
depth.why_it_matters: Test debuts under this much pressure — replacing three senior players at once, away from home form, against a rampant Indian attack — either fast-track a career or expose a player badly; how Mishara and Arachchige perform will shape Sri Lanka's batting depth conversation for years, not just this series.
depth.ripple_effects: A strong showing could hand Sri Lanka two long-term Test batters and vindicate Kirsten's rebuilding approach; a heavy collapse would intensify scrutiny of Sri Lanka Cricket's bench strength and franchise-league injury management. Either way, India will be favourites to seal the series 2-0.
depth.why_now: The squad had to be finalised ahead of the second Test's start on August 23 in Colombo.
depth.watch_next: Watch whether Mishara or Arachchige gets a Test debut in the XI, and how they cope with India's pace and spin attack in the first innings.

cards.title: BCCI to decide Ajit Agarkar's own future as chief selector — with VVS Laxman floated as a replacement
cards.what_happened: The BCCI is set to meet chief selector Ajit Agarkar after the ongoing Sri Lanka series concludes to discuss extending his contract by one more year, as his current three-year term expires this September. The renewal talks arrive amid friction over Rohit Sharma's ODI future: selectors had reportedly told Rohit directly they planned to move on from him once England's white-ball series wrapped up, while BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly told a different story, saying Rohit **'will continue to represent the country as long as he is in the scheme of things.'** That mixed messaging has reportedly left selectors frustrated with the board's own secretary. Reports also suggest former India great **VVS Laxman** could be considered for the role if the BCCI opts not to continue with Agarkar.
key_points: The BCCI will meet **Ajit Agarkar** after the Sri Lanka series to discuss a **1-year contract extension**.
Agarkar completes **3 years** as selection chairman this September, the maximum before requiring renewal.
The talks are complicated by **tension over Rohit Sharma's ODI future** between selectors and the board.
Selectors reportedly told Rohit privately they'd **move on from him**, while the board's line to media said otherwise.
**VVS Laxman** is reportedly a name under consideration if the board decides against continuing with Agarkar.
cards.moot: In any large organization, mixed public messaging between different arms — here, selectors versus the board's communications office — is usually a sign of unresolved internal disagreement, not a communications slip.

depth.background: Ajit Agarkar, a former India fast bowler, has chaired the Board of Control for Cricket in India's (BCCI) men's selection committee since 2023, a period that included two ICC trophy wins — the 2025 Champions Trophy and the 2026 T20 World Cup. Under BCCI rules, a selection committee chairman serves an initial term and can be renewed for one further year. The renewal talks come at an awkward moment: selectors and the BCCI's own administration have reportedly given conflicting signals to the media about whether veteran batter Rohit Sharma still has a future in the ODI side, exposing a rift between the selection panel and the board's public messaging.
depth.why_it_matters: This isn't just about one man's job — it's a test of whether the BCCI will back its own selection committee's judgment on sensitive calls like retiring a legend, or let public-relations messaging from the board's administrative side undercut the selectors it appointed.
depth.ripple_effects: How this is resolved will shape who controls the narrative around India's next generation of team transitions — selectors or the board's communications office — and could influence how openly future selectors are willing to make unpopular calls. A change at chief selector this close to major series would also add uncertainty to India's squad-building process.
depth.why_now: This is surfacing now because Agarkar's three-year term expires next month, forcing the BCCI to decide before the deadline, right as the Rohit Sharma tension is at its most public.
depth.watch_next: The outcome of the BCCI's post-Sri Lanka-series meeting with Agarkar, and whether Rohit Sharma's ODI status is formally clarified one way or the other.

key_terms.definition: The BCCI official who leads the panel responsible for picking India's national cricket squads — effectively the most influential behind-the-scenes role in Indian cricket.

cards.title: Mohammad Rizwan refuses to sign his PCB contract after being demoted and stripped of the ODI captaincy
cards.what_happened: Pakistan's star wicketkeeper-batter Mohammad Rizwan has refused to sign the PCB's newly announced central contract for the coming season, becoming the only one among 30 contracted players to hold out. The board restructured its grading system, eliminating the elite Category A entirely and placing Rizwan — along with Babar Azam — in Category B instead. Sources say Rizwan has put two demands to the board: reinstating Category A for senior, high-performing players, and giving national captains clearly defined authority and stability, free from board interference. The PCB has reportedly rejected both demands and does not plan to renegotiate. The dispute follows Rizwan's removal as ODI captain, which came after head coach Mike Hesson wrote to the board describing him as **'difficult to deal with'** and prone to complaining about squad selection during a tour of the West Indies.
key_points: Rizwan is the **only one of 30 contracted players** who has not signed the PCB's new central contract.
The board scrapped the top **Category A** grade entirely, demoting Rizwan (and Babar Azam) to **Category B**.
He's reportedly demanding **Category A be reinstated** and that captains get **clear autonomy** over team decisions.
The PCB has **rejected his demands** and says it won't renegotiate or revisit the decision.
Head coach **Mike Hesson** reportedly recommended removing Rizwan as ODI captain, calling him **'difficult to deal with.'**

depth.background: In Pakistan cricket, the PCB (Pakistan Cricket Board) issues annual central contracts that rank players into pay grades — historically topped by 'Category A' for the country's biggest stars. Rizwan had been Pakistan's ODI captain and one of its most consistent performers across formats in recent years, alongside Babar Azam. The PCB's central contract system has been a recurring flashpoint in Pakistan cricket, with frequent leadership changes and player grievances over pay, selection, and board interference — a pattern that has repeated across multiple board regimes.

cards.title: England seamer Kate Cross announces retirement after being left out of the T20 World Cup squad
cards.what_happened: Cross confirmed that the current season will be her last as a professional cricketer, ending a career that brought her 102 international caps and 140 wickets for England across Tests, ODIs and T20Is, plus 239 wickets for Lancashire across all formats. Her career highlight came on Test debut in Perth in 2014, where she took match figures of 6-70 to help England successfully defend the Ashes in Australia. In 2024 she reached the milestone of 400 career wickets across First-Class, List A and T20 cricket, and climbed to a career-high world No. 2 in the ICC's ODI bowling rankings. The announcement follows her being left out of England's squad for the 2026 T20 World Cup and losing her central contract at the end of last summer — she said she'd felt she 'wasn't good enough' to continue after that setback. In her own words: 'This summer is going to be my last playing professional cricket. It's incredibly hard to imagine ever saying goodbye to playing the sport that has been such a huge part of my life and shaped me into the person I am today.'
key_points: **Kate Cross** will retire from professional cricket at the end of the 2026 season.
She made her England debut in **2013** and went on to win **102 caps** across all formats, taking **140 wickets**.
Her standout moment: **6 wickets in the match** on her Test debut in Perth, helping England retain the Ashes.
Cross was **left out of England's squad for the 2026 T20 World Cup** and lost her central contract last summer.
She said it's 'incredibly hard to imagine' saying goodbye to a sport that **'shaped me into the person I am today.'**

depth.background: Kate Cross made her senior county debut for Lancashire aged just 13 and became the first female player to enter the Lancashire Academy a year later, building a career that spanned well over a decade at the top of English women's cricket. She debuted for England in 2013 and delivered one of her career-defining performances on her Test debut in Perth in early 2014, where match figures of 6-70 helped England retain the Ashes on Australian soil. In recent years, though, she fell out of England's central contract list and, more recently, missed selection for the 2026 T20 World Cup squad — signs that her international career was drawing to a close even before Friday's announcement.

prev_ref.title: Pakistan's latest batting collapse puts stand-in captain Salman Agha's leadership under the microscope

cards.title: Pakistan collapse to an innings defeat inside 3 days, piling more pressure on stand-in captain Salman Agha
cards.what_happened: England completed a crushing innings-and-103-run victory over Pakistan at Headingley, wrapping up the match in under three days. Pakistan collapsed twice: bowled out for **171** in their first innings, then **135** in their second, unable to survive even 38 overs the second time round. England had posted **366 for 8** in reply to Pakistan's first innings, with contributions from Harry Brook (91), Jordan Cox (73), Root (66) and Zak Crawley (51). **Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue** shared 16 wickets between them across the match — eight apiece — while Jofra Archer added three more scalps. The win is the joint-second fastest of Root's 66-Test captaincy reign, underlining just how one-sided the contest became. Pakistan now travel to Lord's for the second Test starting the following Thursday, with Agha's captaincy under fresh scrutiny after back-to-back batting collapses.
key_points: England won the 1st Test at Headingley by **an innings and 103 runs**, inside just three days.
Pakistan were bowled out twice — for **171 and then 135** — after England posted 366 for 8.
**Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue** took eight wickets each across the match; **Jofra Archer** chipped in with three more.
It's the **joint-second fastest win** of Joe Root's 66-match tenure as England Test captain.
Pakistan's stand-in captain **Salman Agha**, filling in for the injured Babar Azam, now faces mounting scrutiny.

thread.previously: We reported that Pakistan's batting collapse on the rain-hit opening day at Headingley — bowled out for 171 — had already put stand-in captain Salman Agha's leadership under scrutiny.
thread.changed: Pakistan collapsed again in their second innings, folding for 135 to lose by an innings and 103 runs inside three days — turning early concern about Agha's captaincy into a much bigger crisis heading into the Lord's Test.

depth.background: Pakistan arrived at Headingley already weakened, with regular captain Babar Azam ruled out with a hand injury and Salman Agha elevated to lead the side in his place. Agha's leadership had already come under the microscope after Pakistan's batting looked fragile on the rain-hit opening day, when England bowled them out cheaply first time round. England, under Joe Root's captaincy, have built a reputation this era for aggressive, fast-scoring 'Bazball' cricket that tends to bowl out fragile opposition batting line-ups quickly once on top.

cards.title: Sri Lanka's batting line-up is gutted by injuries and a concussion-substitution rule, days before the Colombo Test
cards.what_happened: Sri Lanka heads into the second Test against India in Colombo with its batting line-up badly depleted by injuries. **Kusal Mendis** is unavailable with a hamstring injury picked up during last month's Lanka Premier League, and coach **Gary Kirsten** confirmed he **'is not going to be available for a while.'** Veteran **Dinesh Chandimal** suffered a concussion while fielding in the first Test and was replaced under ICC concussion-substitute protocols by Pasindu Sooriyabandara — a rule that also bars a concussed player from returning to action for **seven days**, ruling Chandimal out of the second Test too. **Pathum Nissanka**, still working back from wrist surgery in June, is also considered unlikely to play. The timing is brutal for Sri Lanka: it already trails the series **1-0** after losing the first Test in Galle by **165 runs**, and now must try to level things up fielding a batting order missing three of its most experienced players.
key_points: Three key batters are out for the second Test: **Kusal Mendis** (hamstring), **Dinesh Chandimal** (concussion) and likely **Pathum Nissanka** (wrist surgery recovery)
Chandimal was concussed while fielding and replaced by Pasindu Sooriyabandara — under ICC rules, a **concussion substitute can't play for 7 days**, ruling him out
Mendis picked up his hamstring injury during the **Lanka Premier League** last month and coach Gary Kirsten says he **'is not going to be available for a while'**
India already leads the two-match series **1-0**, having won the first Test in Galle by **165 runs**
Sri Lanka must now field a batting line-up missing three of its most experienced players against a red-hot Indian attack

depth.background: Sri Lanka is hosting India for a two-match Test series, with the first Test in **Galle** ending in a **165-run win for India**. Sri Lanka's top order has been thin on experience for some time, making its senior batters — wicketkeeper **Kusal Mendis**, opener **Pathum Nissanka**, and veteran **Dinesh Chandimal** — disproportionately important to its chances of competing. Head coach **Gary Kirsten**, the former India and South Africa batting great now coaching Sri Lanka, has been trying to rebuild the side's Test-match depth and consistency after a difficult run of results.

cards.title: A 33-year-old who has waited a decade may take Kuldeep Yadav's place in the Colombo Test
cards.what_happened: Reports on **20 August 2026** indicated India are set to hand **Saransh Jain** his **Test debut** in the second Test against Sri Lanka in **Colombo**, starting **23 August**. He would come in for **Kuldeep Yadav**, who had a difficult first Test in **Galle**: **25 overs, 103 runs conceded, one wicket**, unable to find rhythm on a surface that offered spin. Jain, now **33** and playing for **Madhya Pradesh**, carries a substantial first-class record — **188 wickets in 54 matches at 27.30**, plus **2,223 runs** including **two centuries and 14 fifties** — and was the standout performer of Madhya Pradesh's **2025-26 Ranji Trophy** campaign with **30 wickets**. He earned the call-up as a replacement for the injured **Washington Sundar**. India go into the match **1–0 up**, having won in Galle by **165 runs** on the back of **Manav Suthar's ten-wicket haul**, with **Shubman Gill** captaining after being passed fit from a finger injury and **Jasprit Bumrah** absent with a knee problem.
key_points: **Saransh Jain**, 33, is set for a Test debut in Colombo from **23 August**
He would replace **Kuldeep Yadav**, who took **1 for 103** off 25 overs in Galle
Jain has **188 first-class wickets** at an average of **27.30** from 54 matches
He was called up only as cover for the **injured Washington Sundar**
India lead the two-Test series after winning the first by **165 runs**

depth.background: **Kuldeep Yadav** is a left-arm wrist-spinner — a rare, high-risk, high-reward type of bowler who turns the ball away from right-handers using his wrist rather than his fingers. He has been in and out of India's Test side for years precisely because that method produces either match-winning spells or expensive ones. **Saransh Jain** is the opposite kind of cricketer: an **off-spinner** who turns the ball with his fingers, a dependable lower-order batter, and a **Madhya Pradesh** domestic professional who has been grinding through the **Ranji Trophy** since his early twenties without an India cap. He was named in this squad only because **Washington Sundar** was injured — the classic route by which a long-serving domestic player finally gets a look.

cards.title: BCCI moves the Duleep Trophy final out of its own academy so fans can actually watch it
cards.what_happened: The BCCI confirmed on **20 August 2026** that the final of the **2026-27 Duleep Trophy**, scheduled for **6 to 10 September**, has been moved from the Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru to the **M.A. Chidambaram Stadium in Chennai**. The stated reason is spectator access: the CoE carries **restrictions on crowd attendance**, and the board decided the tournament's showpiece deserved a venue where fans can turn up. The **rest of the tournament stays at the CoE**, beginning on **Sunday 23 August** with East Zone against North East Zone and North Zone against West Zone. The board is also widening coverage — **all matches will be streamed live**, with television coverage of one quarter-final, one semi-final and the final. The six zonal sides are led by **Ishan Kishan (East)**, **Kanhaiya Wadhawan (North)**, **Ruturaj Gaikwad (West)** and **Tilak Varma (South)**, among others.
key_points: Final shifted from Bengaluru's **Centre of Excellence** to Chennai's **Chepauk**
Reason: the academy has **restrictions on public access** — no real crowds
Final runs **6–10 September**; the tournament starts **23 August**
Every match will be **streamed live**, with TV for a quarter-final, semi-final and the final
Six zonal teams, captained by **Ishan Kishan, Ruturaj Gaikwad, Tilak Varma** and others

depth.background: The **Duleep Trophy** is India's oldest surviving zonal first-class competition, in which teams representing **North, South, East, West, Central and North East** zones play multi-day cricket. For the last few seasons the **BCCI** — the Board of Control for Cricket in India, which runs the domestic game — has staged it at the **Centre of Excellence (CoE)** in Bengaluru, the board's own training academy. That is convenient for pitch control and player management, but the CoE is a **closed campus**: it was built as a training facility, not a stadium, and it cannot let large numbers of the public in. The result has been a marquee domestic final played in front of almost nobody. **Chepauk** — the M.A. Chidambaram Stadium in Chennai — is one of India's oldest Test grounds and seats tens of thousands.

cards.title: India–Pakistan set for September 5 as Women's Asia Cup schedule lands amid the BCCI–Naqvi trophy row
cards.what_happened: Organizers **announced the schedule** for the **Women's Asia Cup 2026**, confirming the tournament will run from **August 28 to September 13** at the **Dubai International Stadium**, with **eight teams** split into two groups of four. India will open against **Thailand**, face **Hong Kong**, and then meet arch-rivals **Pakistan on September 5** in the tournament's headline fixture. **Harmanpreet Kaur** will lead a **15-member** Indian squad. The **top two** from each group advance to the **semi-finals on September 10 and 11**, with the **final on September 13**. The fixtures dropped while the **BCCI's dispute with ACC chairman Mohsin Naqvi** — over trophy handovers from earlier events — remained unresolved, keeping cricket's India–Pakistan politics in the frame even as the on-field schedule firms up.
key_points: Women's Asia Cup 2026 runs **Aug 28–Sep 13** at Dubai International Stadium.
The marquee **India–Pakistan clash is set for September 5**.
**Harmanpreet Kaur** captains a 15-member Indian side.
Fixtures land while the **BCCI feuds with ACC chief Mohsin Naqvi** over trophies.
Top two from each group of four reach the **Sep 10–11 semis**.

depth.background: The **Asia Cup** is the continent's flagship cricket tournament, run by the **Asian Cricket Council (ACC)**, whose chairman is **Mohsin Naqvi** — who also heads the **Pakistan Cricket Board**. India and Pakistan do not play bilateral series because of political tension, so they only meet at multi-nation events, which makes every **India–Pakistan** fixture a massive commercial and emotional draw. The women's edition is being held in the **neutral venue of Dubai** for that reason. It arrives against the backdrop of a simmering **governance standoff**: the BCCI has been locked in a dispute with Naqvi over the handover of tournament trophies, with the men's title still reportedly unclaimed — a row that has spilled into the build-up to the women's event.

cards.title: Gavaskar demands the IPL make trade fees public, warning secret deals hide salary-cap breaches
cards.what_happened: **Sunil Gavaskar** publicly urged the **BCCI** to make **IPL trade fees public**, arguing that the financial details of trades are known only to the **player, the franchises involved, and the board** — leaving every other team **in the dark**. His core point: because the money is hidden, **no one can tell** whether a club has **stayed within or breached the salary cap** that is supposed to keep the competition fair. He tied the concern to the busy 2026 trade window and the speculation around marquee moves. 'The IPL is the greatest T20 league in the world, and it's therefore crucial that **full transparency** is maintained so that there's **no finger-pointing** at it from those jealous of it,' Gavaskar wrote. The comments amount to a call for the league to **open its books** on trades, a governance question that touches the credibility of every deal.
key_points: Gavaskar wants **IPL trade fees disclosed**, not kept secret.
He argues rival teams **can't verify** whether the salary cap was breached.
Only the **player, franchise and BCCI** currently know the numbers.
The call follows a flurry of **high-profile trades** in the 2026 window.
His worry: hidden money invites **finger-pointing** at the league's integrity.

depth.background: The **IPL** (Indian Premier League) is cricket's richest T20 competition, and each franchise must build its squad within a **salary cap** — a fixed limit on total player spending meant to keep teams on a level field. When one team 'trades' a player to another, money often changes hands, but the **financial terms are kept confidential** between the two clubs, the player, and the **BCCI** (the Board of Control for Cricket in India, which runs the league). A hectic 2026 trading window — including the **Rishabh Pant–Kuldeep Yadav swap** and swirling talk of a **Hardik Pandya** move — has put those secret sums under the spotlight. **Sunil Gavaskar**, a former India captain and one of the game's most respected voices, has now waded in.

cards.title: Ajinkya Rahane retires from all cricket, leaving KKR without a captain
cards.what_happened: Rahane announced his **retirement from international cricket and all formats with immediate effect** via a social-media post, saying **'today, I feel the timing is right for me to move on.'** Over his career he represented India in **85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is**. Because the announcement covers **all formats**, it also ends his **IPL** playing days — and his tenure as **KKR captain**, a role he'd held for **two seasons**. That immediately opens up a **captaincy vacancy at Kolkata Knight Riders** heading into IPL 2027, with reports already floating names like Rinku Singh as a possible successor. The exit marks the end of a steady, understated career built more on temperament than flash.
key_points: Former India captain **Ajinkya Rahane, 38**, retired from **all formats** with immediate effect.
He announced it via **social media**: 'the timing is right for me to move on.'
He played **85 Tests, 90 ODIs and 20 T20Is** since his 2011 debut.
His exit also ends his **IPL** career — he was **KKR's captain** for two seasons.
It leaves **Kolkata Knight Riders** hunting a new leader for 2027.

depth.background: **Ajinkya Rahane** was one of India's most dependable middle-order Test batters of the last decade, remembered above all for **captaining India to a historic 2021 series win in Australia** while stand-in skipper. In recent years he moved into a franchise-elder role, leading the **Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR)** in the IPL for the past **two seasons**. At 38, with international selection long behind him, a retirement decision had been widely anticipated — the question was timing. His departure closes a **15-year career** that began with his India debut in **August 2011**.

cards.title: St Lucia Kings lose star spinner Noor Ahmad after Afghanistan's board yanks his NOC
cards.what_happened: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board revoked Noor Ahmad's NOC**, ruling him out of the **CPL 2026** season with the St Lucia Kings. Reports indicate **visa-related issues** meant Noor **never traveled to the West Indies** for the league, and once the board withdrew its clearance, he was **no longer permitted to take part**. The loss stings the Kings: Noor was the **leading wicket-taker with 22 wickets in 12 games** when they lifted the trophy in **2024**. To fill the gap, **St Lucia Kings signed wicketkeeper-batter Tim Seifert** for the rest of CPL 2026. The episode sits within a wider pattern of Afghan players facing NOC hurdles for overseas leagues this year.
key_points: The **Afghanistan Cricket Board (ACB)** revoked **Noor Ahmad's NOC** for CPL 2026.
The **'no-objection certificate'** is the board's permission to play foreign leagues.
Without it, Noor is **no longer eligible** for the Caribbean Premier League.
He was the tournament's **leading wicket-taker (22 in 12)** when the Kings won in 2024.
St Lucia Kings signed **Tim Seifert** as his replacement.

depth.background: To play in a foreign franchise league like the **Caribbean Premier League (CPL)**, an international cricketer needs an **NOC ('no-objection certificate')** from their home board — official permission to go. Boards can grant or **pull** that permission, which gives them real power over where their stars earn money. **Noor Ahmad** is Afghanistan's prized **left-arm wrist-spinner** and a genuine match-winner in T20 leagues worldwide. He'd been signed by the **St Lucia Kings**, whom he helped win the 2024 title as the competition's top wicket-taker. The ACB pulling his NOC is exactly the kind of board-versus-player money-and-control story that plays out behind franchise cricket.

prev_ref.title: Two cricket teams in crisis, two comeback captains: Root and Babar collide today at Headingley

cards.title: England bowl Pakistan out for 171 on a rain-hit opening day at Headingley, piling pressure on a fragile batting line-up
cards.what_happened: On a rain-disrupted opening day at Headingley, England **bowled Pakistan out for just 171 runs**, with seamers **Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue combining for 10 wickets** to rip through the batting line-up. England then reached **112 for 2** in their reply by the close of play, already building a commanding position in the match despite the interrupted overs. The collapse extends a pattern of fragile batting performances that has plagued Pakistan's Test side through this difficult stretch, adding fresh scrutiny to the team just as it tries to stabilize under restored leadership.
key_points: Pakistan were bowled out for just **171** on the rain-interrupted opening day of the first Test at Headingley.
England seamers **Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue shared 10 wickets** between them.
England closed the day at **112 for 2** in reply, already well ahead in the match.
Play was repeatedly interrupted by rain, compressing the day's overs.
The result deepens the pressure on Pakistan's batting after a build-up already clouded by fitness and form concerns.

thread.previously: We reported that England and Pakistan were starting a three-Test series at Headingley with two comeback captains, Joe Root and Babar Azam, both trying to stabilize teams that had been through recent turmoil, with Babar only just cleared to play after a hand injury.
thread.changed: Play has now happened — England bowled Pakistan out for 171 thanks to Robinson and Tongue's 10 combined wickets, and reached 112 for 2 in reply, putting England firmly on top after a rain-hit first day.

depth.background: England and Pakistan are playing the first of a **three-Test series** at Headingley in Leeds, with both sides entering out of form — Pakistan sit eighth in the World Test Championship table with only two wins in six matches, while England, seventh, are coming off a home series loss to New Zealand. **Joe Root** is captaining England for the first time since giving up the role in 2022, and **Babar Azam** returned as Pakistan's Test captain after being restored to the role, having been cleared to play despite a hand injury picked up in a warm-up match. Both boards are betting that bringing back experienced former captains can stabilize teams that have each been through recent turmoil.

cards.title: BCCI faces a repeat trophy standoff with ACC chief Mohsin Naqvi as the Women's Asia Cup nears, with India's men's trophy still unclaimed
cards.what_happened: With the **Women's Asia Cup 2026** set to run from **August 28 to September 13** in Dubai, cricket administrators are already bracing for a repeat of last year's men's trophy standoff if **Harmanpreet Kaur's** defending-champion India side wins the title. The men's Asia Cup trophy from last year's final — which India's team refused to accept directly from Naqvi, also skipping handshakes with Pakistan's players and the presentation ceremony — has still not been formally handed over to India more than a year later. One proposed solution being discussed is for Naqvi to step aside from the presentation duties and let another ACC official hand over any trophy India might win this time, but the BCCI has not publicly stated whether it would even accept a trophy in a ceremony involving Naqvi at all.
key_points: The **Women's Asia Cup 2026** runs **August 28 to September 13** in Dubai, and could revive last year's India-Naqvi trophy standoff if India's women win.
In last year's **men's Asia Cup final**, India's team refused to accept the trophy from **Mohsin Naqvi**, skipped the presentation, and declined handshakes with Pakistan's players.
That men's trophy has **still not been handed over to India**, more than a year later.
One proposed workaround has **Naqvi step aside** and let another ACC official present the trophy instead.
The **BCCI has not revealed** its position on whether it would accept a trophy from Naqvi if India's women win this time.

depth.background: **Mohsin Naqvi** is both Pakistan's interior minister and the president of the **Asian Cricket Council (ACC)**, the body that governs cricket across Asia and runs the Asia Cup. India and Pakistan's cricket rivalry is unusually fraught because the two countries don't play bilateral cricket outside ICC and ACC events, given broader political tensions, which means moments like trophy presentations become rare, highly charged flashpoints. Last year, after India's men beat Pakistan in the Asia Cup final in Dubai, the India team led by Suryakumar Yadav refused to accept the trophy from Naqvi and skipped the podium ceremony entirely — an unprecedented snub that left the trophy in limbo.

cards.title: Pakistan's latest batting collapse puts stand-in captain Salman Agha's leadership under the microscope
cards.what_happened: On the opening day of the first Test at Headingley, Pakistan looked settled after **Abdullah Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq** put on **91 runs** together — the only real resistance of the innings — before the middle and lower order collapsed, losing their last **eight wickets for just 74 runs** to be bowled out for **171** in 48.1 overs. England's seamers **Ollie Robinson** and **Josh Tongue** took five wickets apiece, exploiting conditions that, while difficult, were described by observers as not unplayable. England responded by reaching **112 for 2** by the close of a rain-affected day, taking firm control of the match. The collapse immediately became the story of the day, with observers noting Pakistan's now-familiar pattern of promising partnerships undone by sudden capitulations, unfolding under a stand-in captain thrust into the role by injury.
key_points: Pakistan collapsed from a promising **91-run partnership** to being bowled out for just **171** on day one at Headingley, losing their **last 8 wickets for 74 runs**.
**Salman Ali Agha** is standing in as captain after **Babar Azam** was ruled out with a hand injury, putting him in charge for a must-not-lose opener.
England's **Ollie Robinson (5/51)** and **Josh Tongue (5/46)** did the damage, bowling Pakistan out in just **48.1 overs**.
It's the latest in a pattern: Pakistan were also routed by **Bangladesh** and have struggled repeatedly against high-quality pace bowling overseas this year.
England closed day one at **112/2**, already in firm control of the match.

depth.background: Pakistan's Test side has been searching for stability all year, cycling through injury absences and leadership changes while struggling against quality seam bowling away from home. Babar Azam, the team's talisman, was ruled out of this series opener with a hand injury, handing the captaincy to all-rounder **Salman Ali Agha** — himself no stranger to controversy, having previously picked up ICC demerit points for on-field conduct. This tour of England, running from **August 19 to September 13**, was seen as a chance for Pakistan to prove their overseas game had improved after a rocky year that included a heavy ODI series defeat in Bangladesh.

cards.title: Jordan Cox's Test chance against Pakistan is a full-circle moment born from a career-altering injury
cards.what_happened: With Jacob Bethell now injured and unavailable, Jordan Cox has been promoted to bat at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan at Headingley — the very role once denied to him by injury, now his because of someone else's. Cox has spoken this week about drawing on advice from Virat Kohli, his former captain at Royal Challengers Bengaluru, who told him to focus on enjoying the occasion rather than being weighed down by its importance. Cox described the moment as bringing a sense of **"clarity"** to his game, even as it puts him in an unfamiliar top-order role for England, two years after the injury that first cost him this exact opportunity.
key_points: **Jordan Cox** is batting at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan, filling in for the injured **Jacob Bethell**.
It's a **full-circle moment**: Bethell's own Test debut two years ago only happened because Cox broke his thumb in the nets days before his scheduled debut.
Cox credits advice from **Virat Kohli**, his former Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain, for helping him handle the pressure of Test selection.
Kohli reportedly told Cox to **enjoy the occasion** rather than let its significance overwhelm him.
Cox finally made his delayed Test debut at **The Oval in June**, batting at number seven as cover for a suspended Ben Stokes.

depth.background: Jordan Cox was on the verge of a Test debut against New Zealand two years ago, only to fracture his thumb in the nets just days before the match — forcing him to call his own father and tell him not to fly out to watch. **Jacob Bethell** stepped into the vacated spot instead, and went on to build his own England Test career from that opportunity. Cox finally got his own Test debut this June, at The Oval, playing at number seven as cover while Ben Stokes served a suspension. He also spent time playing IPL cricket for **Royal Challengers Bengaluru**, where he crossed paths with Virat Kohli, one of the format's most storied players, who has become an unlikely mentor figure to him.

cards.title: BCCI president Mithun Manhas faces police probe over alleged date-of-birth fabrication
cards.what_happened: A **Special Railway Magistrate's Court in Jammu** directed police at Nowabad police station to open a **preliminary inquiry** into a complaint against **BCCI president Mithun Manhas**, alleging he recorded different dates of birth at different points in his cricketing career. The complaint says Manhas's school records — from Maharaja Hari Singh Agriculture Collegiate School in Nagbani, Jammu — list his birth date as **December 9, 1977**, while the **Delhi & District Cricket Association's** official records list **October 12, 1979**, a gap of roughly two years. The complainant, **Sudershan Mehta**, has a history of conflict with Manhas, including a separate pending criminal defamation case against him. The court has asked police to submit their inquiry report by **September 3, 2026**. The underlying age-fabrication allegation remains an unproven complaint, not an established fact.
key_points: A Jammu court ordered police to investigate a complaint that **BCCI president Mithun Manhas** used **two different birth dates** at different points in his career.
His school records reportedly list his birth date as **December 9, 1977**; the Delhi & District Cricket Association's site lists **October 12, 1979** — a **two-year gap**.
The complaint was filed by **Sudershan Mehta**, a former J&K Cricket Association official and longtime Manhas critic, who also has a separate defamation case pending against Manhas.
Police must report back to the court by **September 3, 2026**.

depth.background: **Age fraud** — young cricketers or their guardians misstating birth dates to stay eligible for junior age-group tournaments — has been a persistent, sensitive issue in Indian domestic cricket for years. **Mithun Manhas** is a former India domestic cricketer who now serves as **president of the BCCI**, the Board of Control for Cricket in India — the world's richest and most powerful cricket board. The complainant, **Sudershan Mehta**, is a former Joint Honorary Secretary of the **Jammu & Kashmir Cricket Association** and has a long-running rivalry with Manhas, including a separate criminal defamation case he has filed against Manhas and JKCA officials.

prev_ref.title: Mumbai Indians deny active Hardik Pandya trade talks, say nothing moves until their season review ends

cards.title: Hardik Pandya reportedly closing in on a KKR move — with the captaincy attached
cards.what_happened: Fresh reporting says Pandya is now believed to be closing in on a switch to **Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR)** ahead of IPL 2027, with some insider accounts suggesting he could be installed as KKR's captain — a notable escalation from earlier reports that only described "interest" or "talks." KKR has been described as the frontrunner among as many as seven interested franchises, ahead of Chennai Super Kings, which had reportedly offered players plus cash. Mumbai Indians have not confirmed any deal, maintaining their position that no trade decisions will be made until their internal season review concludes. Adding complexity: Pandya has previously been reported as unwilling to join KKR unless the franchise parts ways with coach **Abhishek Nayar**, over friction that reportedly traces back to Pandya's earlier fallout with Rohit Sharma.
key_points: Pandya is reportedly **closing in on a move to KKR**, with insiders suggesting he could be named **KKR's captain**.
**Seven IPL franchises** have been circling the India all-rounder, with **KKR and CSK** the two frontrunners.
**Mumbai Indians** — Pandya's current team and the side he currently captains — have not confirmed any deal and say their season review is still ongoing.
A KKR move would reunite Pandya with the club that gave him his IPL start, but tension reportedly persists over **KKR coach Abhishek Nayar**, whom Pandya has clashed with before.
No trade has been officially completed — this remains insider reporting, not a confirmed deal.

thread.previously: We reported Mumbai Indians pushed back on claims that trade talks over Hardik Pandya were underway, insisting nothing would move until their post-season review finished.
thread.changed: New reporting says Pandya is now believed to be closing in on a move to Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) for IPL 2027 — with insiders suggesting he could take over as KKR's captain, a significantly bigger claim than the earlier "talks are underway" reports.

depth.background: Hardik Pandya is one of Indian cricket's most valuable all-rounders and currently captains Mumbai Indians (MI) in the IPL, having returned to the franchise in a high-profile trade back in 2024. Every IPL offseason now includes a formal trade and auction window where franchises can move contracted players, and speculation about star players moving is a fixture of the build-up to each new season — MI have previously and repeatedly denied that talks over Pandya were serious, even as reports of interest from multiple franchises kept building.

prev_ref.title: BCCI's selectors are furious at the board's own secretary over a Rohit Sharma retirement denial

cards.title: Rohit Sharma is picked for the West Indies ODIs, but the selectors who wanted him gone still feel burned
cards.what_happened: India's chosen squad for the upcoming **West Indies ODI series** confirms Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli both remain in the fold for the 50-over format, resolving — for now — the retirement speculation that had built up. But the underlying tension hasn't resolved: selectors are reportedly still upset that BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** publicly reaffirmed Rohit's place in the team's plans just before the squad announcement, which they saw as reversing an internal lean toward transitioning away from him, seemingly in reaction to public and social-media pressure. That friction is reportedly now bleeding into a separate decision: chief selector **Ajit Agarkar** completes three years in the role this September and is eligible for a one-year extension, with BCCI office-bearers expected to take up that decision once the ongoing Sri Lanka Test series ends — with Rohit's ODI future said to be one of the sticking points behind the scenes.
key_points: **Rohit Sharma**, 38, has been retained in India's ODI squad for the **West Indies series**, alongside **Virat Kohli**, 36 — both now play only the 50-over format.
Selectors reportedly feel **"betrayed"** that BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly backed Rohit after internal discussions had leaned toward moving past him for the **2027 World Cup**.
Shubman Gill, 25, has separately been named India's new **ODI captain**, taking over the role from Rohit.
The rift is now tangled up with chief selector **Ajit Agarkar's** own future — his three-year term ends in September and BCCI is due to discuss his extension.
Selectors believe the board's public stance shifted **in response to social-media backlash**, not fresh cricketing judgment.

thread.previously: We reported that BCCI selectors were furious after board secretary Devajit Saikia publicly denied Rohit Sharma was being pushed toward retirement — a denial selectors felt was made under social-media pressure and contradicted the board's own internal direction.
thread.changed: Today's reporting confirms the practical outcome: Rohit Sharma has in fact been kept in India's squad for the West Indies ODIs alongside Virat Kohli, both playing ODI-only roles. The friction hasn't gone away — it's now reportedly spilling into chief selector Ajit Agarkar's own position, with BCCI office-bearers expected to discuss his one-year extension, due in September, against the backdrop of this same disagreement.

depth.background: India's chief selector picks the national squads, but the **BCCI (Board of Control for Cricket in India)** — the sport's governing body — sits above the selection committee and can shape or override its direction through its office-bearers. Rohit Sharma has already retired from **Test and T20I cricket**, leaving ODIs as his last format, and with the **2027 ODI World Cup** on the horizon, selectors have been debating whether a 38-year-old should still be central to that plan. Shubman Gill's rise — already India's Test captain — into the ODI captaincy as well signals the succession is already underway even as Rohit keeps playing.

cards.title: A DRS scare and alarm bells: inside Australia's reckoning after its historic loss to Bangladesh
cards.what_happened: In the first Test in Darwin, Bangladesh dominated a full-strength Australian side across all four days, winning by nine wickets to record one of the most one-sided Test wins away from home in the sport's recent history. Australia had gone into the match having won 11 of its previous 13 Tests and sitting top of the World Test Championship standings, making the defeat land as a genuine shock rather than a minor upset. On Day 1, Steve Smith was given not out on a caught-behind review off Ebadot Hossain that looked close on the stump-mic audio; Smith later admitted in a post-match interview that he believed he had actually edged it, joking 'technology saved me today.' Australian newspapers have since run scathing post-mortems on the batting collapse and team culture, and the second and final Test of the series begins August 22 in Mackay, Queensland, with Australia's established stars now under real pressure to respond.
key_points: Australia lost to Bangladesh by **nine wickets** in Darwin — one of the most humiliating defeats in Australian Test history
A full-strength Australian side that had **won 11 of its last 13 Tests** and topped the World Test Championship table was outplayed in every department
Star batter **Steve Smith** survived a contentious caught-behind review on Day 1, later admitting **'I think so, yeah'** when asked if he had actually nicked it
Bangladesh, ranked **ninth in the world**, had managed just **one win in 26 previous SENA-country Tests** and hadn't played a Test in Australia for **23 years**
Australian media has torn into the result, with the second and final Test starting **August 22 in Mackay** now billed as a must-win response

depth.background: Australia entered this series against Bangladesh as overwhelming favorites — a settled, in-form Test team against a side that had almost no history of winning in seam-friendly conditions overseas (the 'SENA' countries: South Africa, England, New Zealand, Australia). Test cricket's Decision Review System (DRS) uses replays, ball-tracking, and stump-microphone audio to help umpires check close calls like edges behind the wicket; a 'not out' review that looks close on the audio, as happened with Smith, often reignites cricket's long-running 'Spirit of Cricket' debate about players walking versus relying on technology.

cards.title: Manav Suthar's 10-wicket haul seals India's 165-run win over Sri Lanka — and quiets the noise around Gill's captaincy
cards.what_happened: India completed a 165-run victory over Sri Lanka on the fifth and final day in Galle, bowling the hosts out for 206 in their second innings. Left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, playing just his second Test, took 6 for 55 to finish with a 10-wicket match haul, turning the game with a triple-wicket maiden in the 76th over that broke a key partnership, bowled Jayasuriya for a golden duck, and had Kumara caught behind. The win — built on Padikkal's first-innings 167 and contributions from Rishabh Pant — gave India a 1-0 lead in the two-match series and was India's 600th Test match overall. Captain Shubman Gill, who had faced criticism over his captaincy, called the win "very satisfying," explaining the team wasn't sure the match would even finish given the weather and had targeted around 400 in the third innings before pushing for the result.
key_points: India beat Sri Lanka by **165 runs** in Galle, taking a **1-0 lead** in the two-Test series.
Spinner **Manav Suthar**, playing only his **second Test**, took a **10-wicket match haul** (6-55 in the second innings).
Sri Lanka were bowled out for **206**, with Suthar breaking the game open via a **triple-wicket maiden** in the 76th over.
It was India's landmark **600th Test match** — and a statement win for captain **Shubman Gill**, whose leadership had been under scrutiny.
Gill credited the bowlers and a tricky pitch, saying the team "**responded well**" despite uncertainty over whether the match would even finish.

thread.previously: Yesterday, India had bowled Sri Lanka out for 284 to take a 178-run first-innings lead, a position of strength that had temporarily quieted criticism of Gill's captaincy.
thread.changed: India completed the win today — by 165 runs — with Manav Suthar's 10-wicket match haul sealing it, turning Gill's 'for now' reprieve into a clear, result-backed vindication.

depth.background: Shubman Gill took over India's Test captaincy in a transition year and has faced persistent public scrutiny over his tactical decisions and results, with critics questioning whether the team's newer, younger core could deliver away from home. Devdutt Padikkal's first-innings 167 had already set up a commanding 178-run lead by the fourth day, but Test matches can swing quickly on turning subcontinent pitches, and Sri Lanka's second-innings fightback kept the result in doubt into the final day.

cards.title: BCCI's selectors are furious at the board's own secretary over a Rohit Sharma retirement denial
cards.what_happened: According to multiple reports this week, India's selection committee had privately told Rohit Sharma they intended to move on from him in ODIs once the England series concluded. BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia then went public saying there had been no such discussion and that Rohit would continue as a regular member of the side for as long as he remained part of India's plans — a statement selectors are said to have found frustrating, since it publicly contradicted their own call without consulting them first. That tension now feeds into a separate, higher-stakes conversation: Agarkar's own three-year term as chairman of selectors runs out in September, and under the current rules he's eligible for a one-year extension. The BCCI is reportedly keen to keep him in the role through the 2027 World Cup given his record — two ICC titles during his tenure — but a formal decision is expected only after the board meets him directly, with some reports floating VVS Laxman as an alternative if talks don't go smoothly.
key_points: Selectors had reportedly told **Rohit Sharma** they planned to move on from him after the England ODI series.
BCCI secretary **Devajit Saikia** then publicly said Rohit remains a **'regular member'** of the ODI team, contradicting that plan.
The selection committee, led by **Ajit Agarkar**, is said to be unhappy the board undercut their call in public.
Agarkar's own three-year term as chief selector **expires in September**, and the BCCI is set to meet him about an extension.
Reports suggest the board wants Agarkar to stay through the **2027 ODI World Cup**, but the rift adds uncertainty.

depth.background: India's chief selector, a role currently held by former fast bowler **Ajit Agarkar** since 2023, leads the panel that picks the national team and is meant to make those calls independent of the board's day-to-day management. Rohit Sharma, India's ODI captain for years, has already retired from Tests, and speculation about his ODI future has followed him through this year as India builds toward the 2027 ODI World Cup. In July, after Rohit played a match-winning innings at Lord's, Saikia had publicly waved off retirement talk — but the selectors' actual internal plan, according to these new reports, was reportedly the opposite.

cards.title: Hardik Pandya reportedly won't join KKR unless the franchise drops coach Abhishek Nayar — a grudge that traces back to Rohit Sharma
cards.what_happened: As **Kolkata Knight Riders** emerge as the frontrunner to sign Hardik Pandya from Mumbai Indians ahead of **IPL 2027**, reports say Pandya has set a personal condition on the move: he is reluctant to join if **Abhishek Nayar** remains part of KKR's coaching staff, with one report citing a **99% chance** he won't go through with the switch if Nayar stays. The friction reportedly goes back to 2024, when Pandya replaced **Rohit Sharma** as Mumbai Indians captain — a move Nayar's close friend Rohit was visibly upset about in a video that went viral at the time. Separately, Pandya is said to want the freedom to make his own decisions and lead in his own style, suggesting he is angling for the **KKR captaincy** itself as part of any deal. Multiple other franchises, including **CSK** (offering Shivam Dube, Rassie van der Dussen-alternative Tony de Zorzi/Ryan Brevis, plus cash) and **DC** (floating an Axar Patel swap), remain in the mix.
key_points: Pandya is said to have set a condition for a **KKR** move: he won't join if **Abhishek Nayar** stays as part of the coaching setup.
One report puts the odds at **99% Pandya won't join KKR** if Nayar remains in charge.
The tension reportedly stems from Nayar's **close bond with Rohit Sharma**, whom Pandya replaced as Mumbai Indians captain in 2024.
A **viral 2024 video** captured Rohit venting to Nayar about MI's abrupt captaincy switch to Pandya.
Pandya also reportedly wants **freedom to lead the team his own way** — suggesting he wants the KKR captaincy too.

thread.previously: We reported KKR had rejected Mumbai Indians' first offer for Hardik Pandya, with seven IPL franchises circling the trade.
thread.changed: New reporting reveals Pandya has set a personal condition on any KKR move — that coach Abhishek Nayar, who is close to Rohit Sharma, must not remain in the setup — and that Pandya also wants the captaincy.

depth.background: **Hardik Pandya** was installed as Mumbai Indians captain in 2024 in a surprise move that displaced **Rohit Sharma**, a switch that drew a hostile reaction from MI's fanbase and reportedly strained dressing-room relationships at the time. **Abhishek Nayar**, previously India's assistant coach before being let go, is known to be close to Rohit personally, and has since returned to KKR's coaching staff. With Pandya's IPL future now up for grabs ahead of the 2027 season, KKR has emerged as the frontrunner among several interested franchises — but old loyalties inside the dressing room are complicating the move.

cards.title: Moeen Ali quietly reversed his retirement from English domestic cricket after his overseas T20 gamble ran into trouble
cards.what_happened: Moeen Ali initially retired from **English domestic cricket** specifically to secure NOCs for the **Global Super League** and the **Caribbean Premier League**, prioritizing the overseas T20 paycheck route. He has since **reversed that decision**, signing with **Yorkshire** ahead of this year's **T20 Blast** and registering for **The Hundred** draft with a base price of **£75,000** — putting him back in the domestic English pipeline he'd stepped away from. The move comes alongside other veteran comebacks in the same window: **James Anderson**, who retired from international cricket, has also entered The Hundred draft in an attempt to revive his playing career, having not played competitively since July.
key_points: Moeen had **retired from English domestic cricket** to free himself up for the **Global Super League** and **Caribbean Premier League**, chasing lucrative overseas T20 deals.
He has now **reversed that decision** and signed for **Yorkshire** ahead of the T20 Blast.
He's also **registered for The Hundred draft** at a base price of **£75,000**.
The saga shows the tension between chasing **overseas T20 leagues** and staying eligible for **domestic county deals** back home.
It comes as **James Anderson** has also entered The Hundred draft, aiming to revive his playing career after international retirement.

depth.background: English all-rounder **Moeen Ali** originally stepped away from domestic English cricket so he could obtain **No-Objection Certificates (NOCs)** — official clearance the ECB requires before an English player can sign for lucrative overseas T20 leagues like the Caribbean Premier League or the Global Super League, since playing at home and abroad at the same time can create scheduling and release conflicts. Giving up domestic status was meant to simplify that path, but it also meant losing his place in England's T20 Blast and Hundred pipeline.

cards.title: Joe Root scraps England's midnight curfew for the Pakistan Tests, and Nasser Hussain calls it 'a grown-up decision'
cards.what_happened: Root abolished the team's midnight curfew as his first act back as captain, telling players to behave like **'grown adults'** instead of policing them with a fixed rule. Former England captain **Nasser Hussain** endorsed the move on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, calling it **'just a grown-up decision'** and arguing that if players don't act responsibly, the right response is to **fine them first, and drop them if it continues** — rather than impose blanket restrictions on the whole squad. Hussain added that needing a curfew in the first place 'shows how bad a place they were in.' The change comes as Root leads England into the opening Test of a three-match series against Pakistan at Headingley, his first Test in charge since 2022.
key_points: Root scrapped the **midnight curfew** in his **first act since returning as England Test captain**.
The curfew was brought in after **Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke it**, missing a Test after a nightclub incident.
Former captain **Nasser Hussain** backed the call, saying **'a professional sporting outfit shouldn't need a curfew.'**
Root wants players treated as **'grown adults'**, with fines and then being dropped as the real deterrent instead of blanket rules.

depth.background: England's Test team introduced player-behaviour guidelines, including a midnight curfew, after a string of off-field alcohol-related incidents during the **'Bazball' era**. The rule became a flashpoint when then-captain **Ben Stokes and bowler Gus Atkinson** were left out of a Test against New Zealand after being caught breaking it following a nightclub visit. **Joe Root** has now returned to the England Test captaincy for a second stint — having previously stepped down in 2022 — and this Pakistan series, starting today at Headingley, is his first assignment back in charge.
